`evaluation/condition_ci.py` imports it, so any interval in this paper
can be recomputed from the committed per-utterance reports without
decoding anything again. Intervals are drawn with `r boot_b_txt`
replicates, above the module default of `r big(boot_default)`, because
a percentile bound carries a Monte Carlo error of its own, which falls
as the replicates rise. Even at this count a bound moves in the fourth
decimal with the seed, so one lying near a rounding threshold can print
either way in the third. Both modules write the
replicate count and the seed into the artefact they produce, and every
figure quoted from them below is read back out of that record, so a
reported interval cannot become detached from the settings that
produced it.

For LibriSpeech test-clean, an exploratory sensitivity analysis also
resampled whole readers, identified by the reader prefix of each
utterance's identifier. Each of `r big(sc_level$bootstrap)` replicates,
under seed `r sc_level$seed`, sampled
`r num_word(sc_level$n_readers)` readers with replacement and retained
all their utterances. WER sums and utterance counts were pooled across
the sampled readers before dividing, preserving the corpus macro
estimand and weighting readers by their utterance counts. Historical
condition comparisons used each utterance's paired difference and
sampled the same readers on both sides. These percentile intervals
describe sensitivity to clustering within the observed sample; they
estimate neither uncertainty from corpus selection or reference errors
nor coverage for a wider population of speakers.

The experiments that follow draw on these corpora in different
combinations, and their designs are fixed here so that the Results can
be read for what they found. The condition sweep of [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer) scores
`r num_word(n_sweep_conditions)` conditions, every registered one, on
all `r num_word(n_sweep_suites)` corpora for
`r num_word(n_sweep_models)` models,
`openai/whisper-large-v3`, `openai/whisper-medium` and
`distil-whisper/distil-large-v3`, at one decoding pass per corpus and
model, giving `r big(nrow(sweep_agg))` corpus-level figures.
[The Dispersion Across Speakers section](#sec-speakers) repartitions
that sweep's LibriSpeech test-clean report by reader and adds no new
decoding. Filler preservation ([the Filler Preservation section](#sec-disfluency)) is scored from the
verbatim hypotheses that sweep kept for its Whisper Large v3 decoding
of the `r big(dcond("raw", "n_utterances"))` AMI test utterances, and
so adds no new decoding either.
The multilingual wave of [the Post-Processing Beyond English section](#sec-multilingual) runs
Whisper Large v3 over `r num_word(length(ml$languages))` further FLEURS
test splits, Polish
(`r ml_utt("pl_pl")` utterances), Spanish (`r ml_utt("es_419")`, the
`es_419` split), Italian (`r ml_utt("it_it")`), German
(`r ml_utt("de_de")`), French (`r ml_utt("fr_fr")`) and Dutch
(`r ml_utt("nl_nl")`), scoring the raw hypothesis
against the production composite in
`r num_word(length(ml$benchmark$arms))` successive states of the code,
the last of them the code the condition sweep ran.

The remaining experiments each rest on one source of material.
Diarisation in
[the Speaker Diarisation and Timestamp Alignment section](#sec-benchmark-der) scores `pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1` on the
`r num_word(der_summary$n_meetings)` meetings of the AMI test split,
reconstructed on their true timeline from the utterance-level release,
with a forgiveness collar `r der_collar` s wide in total, which is
`r der_collar / 2` s either side of each reference boundary. Its two
tuning parameters, the clustering threshold and the minimum pause,
were chosen on the `r num_word(der_dev_meetings)` meetings of the AMI
development split, which the dataset calls `validation`, over a
`r num_word(der_scan_n)`-point scan followed by a
`r num_word(der_grid2_n)`-point grid,
`r if (der_defaults_both) "each" else "the latter"` scored beside the
pipeline's defaults, so that no hyperparameter was selected on the split it is
reported on.
Timestamp alignment is measured with Whisper Large v3 on the first
`r big(ts_first)` utterances of the AMI test split, of which
`r big(ts_summary$n)` are scored. On the remaining
`r num_word(ts_summary$n_skipped)`, the recogniser never closed its
last segment with an end timestamp, which leaves no end boundary to
compare.
The masking
benchmark of [the Evaluating the Masking Layer section](#sec-masking) uses no audio at all. It injects
`r big(ms$n)` constructed cases. Under seed `r ms$seed` it draws up to
`r num_word(ms$n_per_cell)` names from each language and name type of
an in-dictionary pool and from each group of a held-out one, and sets
every name drawn in title case and in lower case, bare and possessive,
in each of `r num_word(length(ms$by_position))` carrier positions,
among them the opening of a quotation and of a parenthesis.
Voice anonymisation in [the Anonymising the Voice section](#sec-anonymisation) takes
`r big(anon$n_utterances)` utterances of the AMI test split, the first
`r num_word(anon$per_meeting_cap)` usable ones, in order of start time,
of each of its `r num_word(length(anon_ami$meetings))` meetings, spoken
by `r num_word(anon$n_speakers)` people. It warps each at McAdams
coefficients of `r and_list(names(anon$by_alpha))`, takes speaker
embeddings from `pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM`, the
embedding model of the diarisation pipeline, loaded on its own for the
reason [the Anonymising the Voice section](#sec-anonymisation) gives, and transcribes every version with
Whisper Large v3.
The `r big(ts_first)` utterances of the
timestamp benchmark all fall within one
`r num_word(length(ts_ami$speakers))`-speaker meeting,
`r ts_ami$meetings`, a limitation [the Speaker Diarisation and Timestamp Alignment section](#sec-benchmark-der) returns to.
A determinism check transcribes the first `r big(det_n)` AMI test
utterances, all from meeting `r det_meetings`, twice under one seed and
again under a second, on each of `r num_word(det_n_own_cards)` cards and
on a processor, and what it produced is compared with the
condition sweep's transcripts of the same utterances. The Discussion
sets out what that check can and cannot establish.

The whole manuscript is written as a Quarto document. Figures,
tables and the results quoted in the text are generated at render time
from the committed JSON and comma-separated values (CSV) artefacts the evaluation modules
produce, except where the text names another source, so a regenerated
artefact changes the reported numbers without any being retyped, and
a missing or malformed one stops the
render instead of leaving an older figure in its place. The full
test suite, the Slurm submission scripts and the post-processing
implementation are catalogued in the repository linked at the end
of the paper.

# Results

The five tests set out in the Introduction are reported in turn, from
the accuracy of the workflow on English through to the reach of its
privacy features.

## Word Error Rate and the Cost of Post-Processing {#sec-wer}

Accuracy comes first, measured on LibriSpeech test-clean, which is drawn
from the speakers that a reference recogniser found easier to
transcribe [@panayotovLibrispeechASRCorpus2015].
@tbl-corpus-summary gives the totals the headline figures are computed
over, with a bootstrap interval on the corpus macro average.

```{r load-wer-ci, include=FALSE}
# Percentile bootstrap over the scored utterances. The committed
# wer_ci.csv was written, from the repository root, by
#   python -m evaluation.bootstrap_ci
#     --report output/evaluation/wer_report.csv --bootstrap 10000
#     --output output/evaluation/wer_ci.csv
# which also writes wer_ci_provenance.json beside it, recording the
# report's digest and the commit the command ran at.
# The replicate count and the seed are columns of the artefact, checked
# in the setup chunk, because the interval shifts in the fourth decimal
# with the replicate count and the seed. The lower bound lies on a
# rounding threshold (0.057500 pooled over two million replicates), so
# its third decimal depends on the seed: about half of all seeds print
# 0.057 and the rest 0.058. The earlier decode these files held put the
# bound just above the threshold (0.057575 pooled), and at this seed it
# printed 0.058. The data moved it by less than a ten-thousandth, which
# is no change worth reporting. The artefact holds one interval, drawn
# on the report the setup chunk ties to post_raw.
stopifnot(nrow(wer_ci) == 1, wer_ci$n == wer_summary$summary$files)
# The headline table describes the raw output of Whisper Large v3 on
# LibriSpeech test-clean. Other entry points write the same canonical
# file name, so a summary of any other run under it is refused rather
# than rendered as the headline (audit finding EWER-11).
local({
  wb <- wer_summary$benchmark
  if (is.null(wb) ||
      !identical(wb$dataset, "librispeech_asr") ||
      !identical(wb$config, "clean") || !identical(wb$split, "test") ||
      !identical(wb$model, "openai/whisper-large-v3") ||
      !(is.null(wb$condition) || identical(wb$condition, "raw")))
    stop("wer_summary.json is not the raw Whisper Large v3 run on ",
         "LibriSpeech test-clean that the headline table describes",
         call. = FALSE)
})
ci_lo    <- wer_ci$ci_lo
ci_hi    <- wer_ci$ci_hi
ci_width <- ci_hi - ci_lo
wsum     <- wer_summary$summary
# The caption and the prose below say the interval is wider than the
# difference any production or diagnostic condition makes on this
# corpus; the canonical normaliser, a different order of size, is not
# one of them.
lsc_cond_max <- local({
  g <- sweep_agg[sweep_agg$suite == "librispeech_clean" &
                 sweep_agg$model_slug == "whisper-large-v3", ]
  keep <- condition_layer(g$condition) %in%
    c("Production atomic", "Production composite", "Diagnostic ablation")
  max(abs(g$macro_wer[keep] -
            mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_clean", "raw")))
})
if (!(lsc_cond_max < ci_width))
  stop("A production or diagnostic condition now moves test-clean by as ",
       "much as the width of the corpus interval; rewrite the caption of ",
       "@tbl-corpus-summary and the paragraph that quotes the interval",
       call. = FALSE)
corpus_cap <- paste0(
  "WER = word error rate. Whisper Large v3, raw output. ",
  "The interval on the macro average is a ",
  "95% percentile bootstrap over the ", big(wer_ci$n), " scored ",
  "utterances. It is given because it is wider than the difference any ",
  "production or diagnostic condition makes on this corpus.")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-corpus-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Corpus Summary for LibriSpeech test-clean"
summary_table <- tribble(
  ~Quantity,                ~Value,
  "Utterances scored",      big(wsum$files),
  "Reference words",        big(wsum$total_reference_words),
  "Macro-averaged WER",     sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", f3(wsum$macro_wer),
                                    f3(ci_lo), f3(ci_hi)),
  "Micro-averaged WER",     f3(wsum$micro_wer)
)
kable(summary_table)
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r corpus_cap`

```{r perfile-dispersion, include=FALSE}
# Diagnostics for the paragraph below.  The macro average weights every
# utterance equally, so utterances with few reference words, where a
# single error is already a large rate, carry it.  Computed here rather
# than quoted so that the claim tracks the artefact.
disp <- local({
  d <- wer_report |> filter(!is.na(wer), !is.na(reference_words))
  short <- d |> filter(reference_words < 10)
  # Unrounded: over an even number of utterances the median can fall
  # halfway between two lengths, and round() would then take it to the
  # even whole number below or above.
  list(median_words = median(d$reference_words),
       n_short      = nrow(short),
       pct_words    = sum(short$reference_words) / sum(d$reference_words),
       share_macro  = sum(short$wer) / sum(d$wer),
       r_len        = cor(d$reference_words, d$wer),
       pct_perfect  = mean(d$wer == 0))
})
```

That result is unsurprising in its direction and informative in its
magnitude. The macro-averaged and micro-averaged rates sit some
distance apart, and the corpus and the way it is scored explain that
distance where the model does not. The macro average weights every
utterance equally, and this release is made of short ones. The median
utterance length is `r format(disp$median_words)` reference words, and
the `r big(disp$n_short)`
utterances of fewer than 10 words, which hold only
`r pc0(disp$pct_words)` of the reference
words, contribute
`r pc0(disp$share_macro)` of the macro average. Where the
reference is a handful of words a single substitution is already a
large rate, so error falls as utterances lengthen
(*r* = `r r_apa(disp$r_len)`) and the
worst-scoring utterances are almost all very short. Many of their
errors are quotation marks, not misrecognised words. The scoring
normaliser keeps the apostrophe, and with it the single quotation
marks that Whisper Large&nbsp;v3 writes around the books' dialogue and
the references do not carry, so each mark counts as an error, and a
short line of quoted speech is charged heavily for it. Roughly
`r pc0(disp$pct_perfect)` of utterances are
scored as exact, so the median per-utterance rate is zero and the
upper quantiles tabulated in [Appendix C](#sec-appendix-c) are small
fractions over small denominators, which is a different thing from
points on a continuum.
The distribution is plotted in @fig-perfile. Dispersion between
utterances therefore describes how the corpus is segmented and scored
at least as much as which passages are hard. The dispersion a
researcher needs is between speakers, and [the Dispersion Across Speakers section](#sec-speakers) reports it.

\needspace{0.75\textheight}

```{r fig-perfile, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Distribution of Per-File Word Error Rate on LibriSpeech test-clean"}
ecdf_data <- wer_report |>
  filter(!is.na(wer)) |>
  arrange(wer) |>
  mutate(cdf = (row_number() - 0.5) / n())

mean_lines <- tibble(
  mean = c(wsum$micro_wer, wsum$macro_wer),
  averaging = c("Micro-averaged mean", "Macro-averaged mean"))

ggplot(ecdf_data, aes(x = wer, y = cdf)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(data = mean_lines, aes(xintercept = mean, linetype = averaging),
             colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = NULL,
    breaks = mean_lines$averaging,
    values = c("Micro-averaged mean" = "solid",
               "Macro-averaged mean" = "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01),
                     limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(x = "Per-file word error rate",
       y = "Cumulative share of files") +
  theme_paper()
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* Empirical cumulative distribution of per-file word error rate on LibriSpeech test-clean. The solid vertical line marks the micro-averaged corpus mean, and the dashed line the macro-averaged mean.

```{r wer-invisible, include=FALSE}
# The conditions the scoring normaliser cannot see, as the sweep marks
# them (wer_invisible, audit finding EWER-03), named as the prose names
# the stages. A newly marked condition without a name here stops the
# render, and so does a marked condition that no longer scores as the
# raw output in every cell, which the paragraph below says each does by
# construction.
invisible_names <- c(
  filler_bracket       = "the filler bracketing",
  common_phrase_fix    = "the common-phrase normaliser",
  whitespace_normalise = "the whitespace normaliser",
  sentence_capitalise  = "the sentence capitaliser",
  pronoun_i_fix        = "the pronoun capitaliser",
  punct_space_fix      = "the punctuation-spacing tidier",
  case_fold            = "case folding")
if (!all(wer_invisible_conds %in% names(invisible_names)))
  stop("No name for the wer_invisible condition(s) ",
       toString(setdiff(wer_invisible_conds, names(invisible_names))),
       call. = FALSE)
if (!wer_invisible_as_raw)
  stop("A condition the sweep marks wer_invisible no longer scores as ",
       "the raw output in every cell", call. = FALSE)
# The paragraph beside @tbl-condition-ci counts the others besides the
# filler bracketing.
stopifnot("filler_bracket" %in% wer_invisible_conds)
n_invisible <- length(wer_invisible_conds)
# The paragraph says why the production stages among them are in the
# sweep; case folding is a diagnostic, which the composite does not chain.
n_invisible_prod <- sum(condition_layer(wer_invisible_conds) ==
                          "Production atomic")
stopifnot(n_invisible_prod > 0)
```

The post-processing conditions form a three-layer registry. The
production layer comprises the atomic stages of
`clean_transcription_text` together with the Unicode strip and the
repetition repair that precede it, and the composite
`pipeline_full`, which is the chain `transcription.py` applies when
run with `--fix-spurious-repetitions`. Repetition repair is off by
default, in the command-line tool and the desktop application alike,
so a default run delivers the composite without that one step. A
diagnostic layer comprising filler removal, deduplication
windowing, punctuation stripping and case folding probes the
contribution of normalisation choices that the production pipeline
deliberately does not make. The `whisper_norm` condition applies the
published Whisper English text normaliser, including its
British-to-American spelling map, to both sides, which is the
normalisation behind the original Whisper evaluation tables
[@radford2022whisper], and it serves as a reference point for
comparisons with published benchmark figures.
`r Num_word(n_invisible)` of the conditions change only case, spacing,
square brackets or punctuation other than the apostrophe:
`r and_list(unname(invisible_names[wer_invisible_conds]))`. The
scoring normaliser removes all of those from both sides, so each of the
`r num_word(n_invisible)` scores exactly as the raw output by
construction, in every corpus and for every model, and a null
difference for any of them says nothing about whether it helps or
harms a reader. The `r num_word(n_invisible_prod)` production stages
among them are registered so that the composite decomposes exactly
into the stages it chains, not because word error rate can measure
them. Macro WER for every
condition on LibriSpeech test-clean is shown in @fig-conditions, and
the full numeric grid across all five corpora is given in
Appendix&nbsp;A.

\needspace{0.75\textheight}

```{r fig-conditions, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Post-Processing Costs on LibriSpeech test-clean"}
ls_all  <- sweep_agg |>
  filter(suite == "librispeech_clean",
         model_slug == "whisper-large-v3",
         condition %in% condition_order)
raw_wer <- ls_all$macro_wer[ls_all$condition == "raw"]
norm_pp <- 100 * (ls_all$macro_wer[ls_all$condition == "whisper_norm"] - raw_wer)

ls_panel <- ls_all |>
  filter(!condition %in% c("raw", "whisper_norm")) |>
  mutate(delta_pp  = 100 * (macro_wer - raw_wer),
         condition = factor(condition, levels = rev(condition_order)),
         layer     = droplevels(factor(condition_layer(as.character(condition)),
                                       levels = layer_levels)))

# Okabe-Ito, which stays distinguishable under the common forms of
# colour blindness; shape repeats the encoding for greyscale printing.
layer_cols   <- c("Production atomic"    = "#0072B2",
                  "Production composite" = "#000000",
                  "Diagnostic ablation"  = "#E69F00")
layer_shapes <- c("Production atomic"    = 16,
                  "Production composite" = 17,
                  "Diagnostic ablation"  = 15)

ggplot(ls_panel, aes(x = delta_pp, y = condition,
                     colour = layer, shape = layer)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = 0, yend = condition), linewidth = 0.35,
               colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = 0.7, hjust = 1.05, size = 2.85,
           colour = "grey35",
           label = sprintf("whisper_norm omitted: %s pp",
                           minus(sprintf("%.1f", norm_pp)))) +
  # No fixed accuracy: the labels take as many decimals as the spacing
  # of the breaks needs, so that ticks a fortieth of a point apart are not
  # printed alike, and a negative tick takes a true minus as the prose does.
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(style_negative = "minus"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.08))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = layer_cols) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = layer_shapes) +
  labs(x = "Change in macro-averaged WER against raw baseline (percentage points)",
       y = NULL, colour = "Layer", shape = "Layer") +
  theme_paper() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(9, "pt"))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* WER = word error rate; pp = percentage points. Change in macro-averaged word error rate against the raw baseline for each production and diagnostic post-processing condition on LibriSpeech test-clean (Whisper Large v3). Points to the right of zero cost accuracy, points to the left gain it. Conditions are ordered as they apply in the production pipeline, and are coloured and shaped by layer. The canonical Whisper normaliser is omitted because it is an order of magnitude larger, at the value given in the annotation, and it is shown across all five corpora in @fig-suites.

```{r condition-deltas, include=FALSE}
# What each production stage costs against the raw baseline, read from
# the grid in Appendix A for the layer as it now stands and from the
# preserved pre-fix aggregate for the layer before the contraction
# repair, so that the paragraphs below cannot drift from either. The
# stages are those the registry places in the production layer, the
# pronoun capitaliser among them now that the sweep scores it (audit
# finding EWER-13).
production_conds <- condition_order[
  condition_layer(condition_order) %in%
    c("Production atomic", "Production composite")]
atomic_conds <- condition_order[condition_layer(condition_order) ==
                                  "Production atomic"]
delta_vs_raw <- function(grid, k, suite = "librispeech_clean",
                         model = "whisper-large-v3") {
  g <- grid[grid$model_slug == model & grid$suite == suite, ]
  one(g$macro_wer[g$condition == k], paste(model, suite, k)) -
    one(g$macro_wer[g$condition == "raw"], paste(model, suite, "raw"))
}
cd <- list(n_atomic = length(atomic_conds))
# "Each of the production stages, and the composite that chains them,
# scores exactly as the raw output" on test-clean, and the repaired stage
# does so on every corpus.
if (any(abs(vapply(production_conds, \(k) delta_vs_raw(sweep_agg, k),
                   numeric(1))) > 1e-12) ||
    any(abs(vapply(unique(sweep_agg$suite),
                   \(s) delta_vs_raw(sweep_agg, "contraction_fix", s),
                   numeric(1))) > 1e-12))
  stop("A production stage no longer scores as the raw output where the ",
       "paragraphs on @fig-conditions say it does", call. = FALSE)

# What the contraction stage cost on each corpus BEFORE it was repaired,
# read from the preserved pre-fix aggregate rather than recalled. The
# range is quoted in the paragraph that reports the repair, so that the
# size of the defect is on the page beside its absence, and the
# test-clean value is quoted again in the Discussion.
pf <- sweep_agg_prefix |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$model_slug == "whisper-large-v3",
                .data$condition %in% c("raw", "contraction_fix")) |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(c("suite", "condition", "macro_wer"))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "condition", values_from = "macro_wer") |>
  dplyr::mutate(delta = .data$contraction_fix - .data$raw)
stopifnot(nrow(pf) == n_sweep_suites, !anyNA(pf$delta))
pf_min <- min(pf$delta)
pf_max <- max(pf$delta)
pf_lsc <- one(pf$delta[pf$suite == "librispeech_clean"],
              "pre-repair contraction cost on test-clean")
# The composite's excess on test-clean then, and the most any other
# stage moved the score; the first sweep did not score the pronoun
# capitaliser. The paragraphs say the stage cost more than the whole of
# that excess and raised the error rate in every cell of the first
# sweep, every model and corpus.
pf_comp      <- delta_vs_raw(sweep_agg_prefix, "pipeline_full")
pf_other_max <- max(abs(vapply(
  setdiff(intersect(atomic_conds, sweep_agg_prefix$condition),
          "contraction_fix"),
  \(k) delta_vs_raw(sweep_agg_prefix, k), numeric(1))))
pf_cells <- dplyr::inner_join(
  sweep_agg_prefix[sweep_agg_prefix$condition == "contraction_fix",
                   c("model_slug", "suite", "macro_wer")],
  sweep_agg_prefix[sweep_agg_prefix$condition == "raw",
                   c("model_slug", "suite", "macro_wer")],
  by = c("model_slug", "suite"), suffix = c("_fix", "_raw"))
stopifnot(pf_lsc > pf_comp, pf_comp > 0,
          nrow(pf_cells) == n_sweep_models * n_sweep_suites,
          all(pf_cells$macro_wer_fix > pf_cells$macro_wer_raw))
# A figure the prose gives as a bound ("no more than") is a bound only if
# printing it did not round it down.
pp_bound <- function(x) {
  s <- ppt(x)
  if (as.numeric(s) < 100 * x)
    stop("The bound ", s, " rounds ", signif(100 * x, 4), " down; reword the ",
         "sentence that quotes it", call. = FALSE)
  s
}
pf_other_txt <- pp_bound(pf_other_max)

# The per-utterance signature of the contraction repair, which is what
# identifies its cost as a defect rather than an orthographic
# mismatch. A stage that mismatches the reference would trade errors
# both ways; this one only ever adds substitutions. Read from the
# pre-repair reports in sweep_reports/, joined by utterance id.
cf_j <- dplyr::inner_join(pre_raw, pre_contraction, by = "name",
                          suffix = c("_raw", "_fix"))
stopifnot(nrow(cf_j) == nrow(pre_raw), nrow(cf_j) == nrow(pre_contraction))
cf_n        <- nrow(cf_j)
cf_worse    <- sum(cf_j$wer_fix > cf_j$wer_raw)
cf_better_n <- sum(cf_j$wer_fix < cf_j$wer_raw)
cf_better   <- if (cf_better_n == 0) "none" else big(cf_better_n)
cf_subs     <- sum(cf_j$substitutions_fix - cf_j$substitutions_raw)
cf_ins      <- sum(cf_j$insertions_fix - cf_j$insertions_raw)
cf_del      <- sum(cf_j$deletions_fix - cf_j$deletions_raw)
stopifnot(cf_ins == 0, cf_del == 0)   # the claim in the text
```

@fig-conditions shows the layer as it now stands, and on this corpus
none of it moves the score: each of the
`r num_word(cd$n_atomic)` production stages, and the composite that
chains them, scores exactly as the raw output. It was not so when the
stages were first scored. The contraction repair then cost
`r ppt(pf_lsc)` percentage points on its own, more than the whole of
the composite's `r ppt(pf_comp)`-point excess, while none of the other
stages moved the score by more than `r pf_other_txt` points. The
repair was written to restore apostrophes that the Whisper tokeniser
splits off, and the natural reading of its cost is that it introduced
an orthographic mismatch with the reference. That reading is wrong,
and the per-utterance records say so plainly. Of the
`r big(cf_n)`
utterances, the unrepaired stage left
`r cf_worse` worse and
`r cf_better`
better, and the whole of its effect was
`r cf_subs` additional substitutions with no
insertions and no deletions. A stage that only ever substitutes, and
never once helps, is not mismatching the reference orthography. It is
replacing words that were already right.

That is what the repair table turned out to be doing. Its keys were
meant to be misspellings the recogniser produces, but seven of them
were themselves ordinary English words, so the stage rewrote correct
text wherever they appeared. The commonest of them was `were`, which
became `we're`, and the next was the possessive `its`, which became
`it's`. The rest were `wont`, `cant`, `shed`, `wed` and `id`. Whisper Large v3
writes these contractions with their apostrophes already, which is why
the repair never had an artefact to fix and why not one test-clean
utterance improved under it. In the first sweep the stage raised the
error rate on every corpus, for each of the
`r num_word(n_sweep_models)` models. The scoring normaliser preserves
the apostrophe, so each rewrite is scored as the substitution it is.

This matters twice over. It is a fault in the workflow that reached
users and not only the benchmark, since the stage ran over every
English transcript the tool produced. The offending keys have been
removed,
under an invariant that no key may be a word that is already correct
English, and a test enforces that against the table instead of
against a handful of examples. The five corpora were then decoded again
on the repaired pipeline, and decoded once more after further
corrections elsewhere in the code. The figures reported here and in
[Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a) are from that last pass. The repair
holds: the contraction stage now scores exactly as the raw output on
this corpus and on each of the other four, having cost between
`r ppt(pf_min)` and `r ppt(pf_max)` points across the five before it
was repaired.
It also bears on the argument of
this paper, because the layer was offered on the claim that it is at
worst harmless, and it was not harmless. Neither the design review nor a
test suite of several hundred cases found this. What found it was
scoring each stage separately against a reference corpus and asking
why one of them cost anything at all, which is the case for measuring
a defensive layer instead of asserting it, and a stronger case than a
null result would have been.

The filler bracketing introduces square brackets and might be expected
to mismatch the reference in just the way the contraction repair was
assumed to, but it cannot, because the scoring normaliser turns a
bracket into a space and so scores a bracketed filler exactly as the
bare one. Its word error rate therefore says nothing about it either
way.
The diagnostic conditions are not all inert, even on this corpus of
read speech. Case folding and punctuation stripping leave
every utterance's score as it was, but filler removal and the
deduplication window each cost a little, because they delete words
from the hypothesis alone, and in read text some of the words they
delete are in the reference too.

These differences are small in absolute terms, and whether they are
larger than the noise in the estimates is a separate question that the
corpus-level interval cannot answer. A percentile bootstrap over the
scored utterances puts the corpus macro average at
`r f3(wsum$macro_wer)` with a 95% interval of
[`r f3(ci_lo)`, `r f3(ci_hi)`], a width of about
`r ppt(ci_width)` percentage points, which is
wider than the difference any production or diagnostic condition makes
on this corpus. Comparing two
such intervals would be the wrong test, however, because every
condition is scored on the same utterances, so the between-utterance
variance that dominates the corpus estimate is shared between any two
conditions and cancels when they are compared directly.

```{r load-condition-ci, include=FALSE}
# Paired bootstrap over the shared utterances. Two sets of intervals are
# read, because the section reports a repair and a repair needs a before
# and an after. Each was written, from the repository root, by the
# command beside it. The module requires an explicit output path, so
# omitting it cannot overwrite the pre-repair record with post-repair
# intervals (audit findings REGEN-01, ESTATS-07).
#
#   condition_ci_postfix.csv  the pipeline as it now stands, over every
#                             non-baseline condition, since the re-run
#                             retained a per-utterance report for every
#                             one of them:
#     python -m evaluation.condition_ci
#       --reports output/evaluation/sweep_reports_postfix
#       --baseline raw --bootstrap 10000
#       --output output/evaluation/condition_ci_postfix.csv
#
#   condition_ci.csv          the pipeline as it stood when the defect
#                             was still in it, over the six conditions
#                             whose per-utterance reports survived that
#                             sweep. This is the measurement that found
#                             the defect and it is quoted as history,
#                             not as a current property of the layer:
#     python -m evaluation.condition_ci
#       --reports output/evaluation/sweep_reports
#       --baseline raw --bootstrap 10000
#       --output output/evaluation/condition_ci.csv
#
# Both files are loaded, and their replicate counts checked, in setup.
row_of <- function(tab, k, label) {
  r <- tab[tab$condition == k, ]
  if (nrow(r) != 1)
    stop(label, " has ", nrow(r), " rows for condition ", k, call. = FALSE)
  r
}
cci_pre_row <- function(k) row_of(cci_pre, k, "condition_ci.csv")
cci_row     <- function(k) row_of(cci, k, "condition_ci_postfix.csv")
cci_pre_fmt <- function(k) {
  r <- cci_pre_row(k)
  sprintf("%s percentage points, 95%% CI [%s, %s]",
          sgn2(100 * r$delta), sgn2(100 * r$ci_lo), sgn2(100 * r$ci_hi))
}
cci_fmt <- function(k) {
  r <- cci_row(k)
  sprintf("%s percentage points, 95%%&nbsp;CI [%s, %s]",
          sgn2(100 * r$delta), sgn2(100 * r$ci_lo), sgn2(100 * r$ci_hi))
}
# How much narrower the paired intervals are than the interval on the
# level. A condition whose interval has zero width is left out: its
# stage changes no score on this corpus, so its interval measures the
# absence of any change and not the sharpness of the test, and averaging
# such intervals in inflated the ratio as inert stages were added to the
# table (audit finding MS-03). The canonical normaliser is left out too,
# as the one condition of a different order of size.
cci_zero_width <- cci$ci_hi == cci$ci_lo
cci_ratio_rows <- !cci_zero_width & cci$condition != "whisper_norm"
stopifnot(any(cci_ratio_rows), all(cci$delta[cci_zero_width] == 0))
cci_width_ratio <- round(ci_width / mean(cci$ci_hi[cci_ratio_rows] -
                                         cci$ci_lo[cci_ratio_rows]))
cci_n_zero  <- sum(cci_zero_width)
cci_n_ratio <- sum(cci_ratio_rows)

# Support for the two paragraphs on selection and multiplicity below.
# Every delta and p value quoted there is read from the same artefact
# the table is drawn from, so the prose cannot drift from the rows.
cci_pp <- function(k) sgn2(100 * cci_row(k)$delta)
# A bootstrap p value cannot resolve below twice the reciprocal of the
# replicate count, so a replicate distribution wholly on one side of
# zero is reported at that floor and not at an invented precision. The
# values it can take are multiples of that floor, so one below .001
# keeps its fourth decimal instead of printing as .000.
p_floor <- function(b) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.4f", 2 / b))
p_txt <- function(p, b) {
  if (p < 2 / b) return(paste0("<", p_floor(b)))
  sub("^0", "", sprintf(if (p < 0.001) "%.4f" else "%.3f", p))
}
cci_p <- function(k) {
  r <- cci_row(k)
  t <- p_txt(r$p_value, r$bootstrap)
  if (startsWith(t, "<")) sub("^<", "< ", t) else paste("=", t)
}
cci_k <- nrow(cci)
# What the paragraphs below say of the rows. Every production stage and
# the composite changes no utterance's score (an interval of zero width
# and a difference of zero); so do case folding and punctuation
# stripping. The rows whose intervals exclude zero are the canonical
# normaliser and the two diagnostic conditions that delete words, each a
# cost. Each clears a Bonferroni threshold over the table even at the
# far end of its Monte Carlo error, and each point value clears one over
# the model's whole grid, but filler removal's p rests on so few
# replicates at or below zero that its Monte Carlo error spans that
# second threshold. Every other row is an exact null with p = 1.
cci_null   <- cci_zero_width & cci$delta == 0 & cci$p_value == 1
cci_excl   <- cci$condition[cci$excludes_zero == 1]
bonf_table <- 0.05 / cci_k
bonf_grid  <- 0.05 / ((n_sweep_conditions - 1) * n_sweep_suites)
bonf_grid_txt <- sub("^0", "", formatC(bonf_grid, format = "fg", digits = 3))
# The Monte Carlo error of a bootstrap p value: an exact (Garwood) 95%
# Poisson interval on the count of replicates on the far side of zero,
# of which the p value is twice the share, given on the scale of p.
p_mc <- function(p, b) {
  k <- round(p * b / 2)
  2 / b * c(lo = if (k == 0) 0 else qgamma(0.025, k),
            hi = qgamma(0.975, k + 1))
}
fs        <- cci_row("filler_strip")
fs_beyond <- round(fs$p_value * fs$bootstrap / 2)
fs_mc     <- p_mc(fs$p_value, fs$bootstrap)
stopifnot(
  all(cci_null[cci$condition %in% c(production_conds, "case_fold",
                                    "punct_strip")]),
  setequal(cci_excl, c("whisper_norm", "dedup_window", "filler_strip")),
  all(cci_null | cci$excludes_zero == 1),
  all(cci$delta[cci$condition %in% c("dedup_window", "filler_strip")] > 0),
  all(vapply(cci_excl, \(k) p_mc(cci_row(k)$p_value,
                                  cci_row(k)$bootstrap)[["hi"]],
             numeric(1)) < bonf_table),
  all(cci$p_value[cci$excludes_zero == 1] < bonf_grid),
  bonf_grid < bonf_table,
  fs_beyond >= 1, fs_mc[["lo"]] < bonf_grid, bonf_grid < fs_mc[["hi"]])
# The production stages the scorer can see, which the paragraph on
# filler bracketing names, and none of which changes a score here.
visible_names <- c(unicode_strip   = "the Unicode strip",
                   repetition_fix  = "the repetition repair",
                   undefined_tag   = "the undefined-token tagger",
                   contraction_fix = "the contraction repair")
visible_conds <- setdiff(atomic_conds, wer_invisible_conds)
if (!setequal(visible_conds, names(visible_names)))
  stop("The production stages the scorer can see are no longer ",
       toString(names(visible_names)), call. = FALSE)
cci_conditions     <- and_list(paste0("`", sort(cci$condition), "`"))
cci_pre_conditions <- and_list(paste0("`", sort(cci_pre$condition), "`"))
# Every condition the sweep scored is paired against the baseline: the
# selection paragraph below says so, and a sweep whose reports were not
# all kept would make it false.
stopifnot(setequal(c("raw", cci$condition), unique(sweep_agg$condition)))
# Built here so that the caption's utterance and replicate counts come
# from the artefact the table is drawn from, not from a number typed
# into the caption or read from another file (MS-16, REGEN-03).
cci_n <- unique(cci$n)
cci_b <- unique(cci$bootstrap)
stopifnot(length(cci_n) == 1, length(cci_b) == 1)
cci_n_txt <- big(as.integer(cci_n))
cci_b_txt <- big(as.integer(cci_b))
cci_cap <- sprintf(paste0(
  "CI = confidence interval; pp = percentage points. Changes in macro-averaged word error rate ",
  "are measured against the raw baseline on ",
  "LibriSpeech test-clean (Whisper Large v3, %s shared utterances, ",
  "%s replicates). Positive deltas are costs. Intervals are marginal ",
  "and uncorrected for multiplicity, and *p* values are two-sided ",
  "bootstrap values reported at the resolution the replicate count ",
  "supports. Pairing by utterance removes the between-utterance ",
  "variance shared by the two conditions, which is why every interval ",
  "here but the canonical normaliser's is far narrower than the ",
  "interval on the corpus estimate in @tbl-corpus-summary. The ",
  "canonical Whisper normaliser is included for scale."),
  cci_n_txt, cci_b_txt)
# "Far narrower": at most a fifth of the corpus interval's width.
stopifnot(all((cci$ci_hi - cci$ci_lo)[cci$condition != "whisper_norm"] <=
                ci_width / 5))

# How far the figures moved between the first decoding and the one
# reported, for Whisper Large v3, the model the paired intervals
# describe and the only one the paragraph speaks for: the raw baseline;
# every production and diagnostic condition both decodings scored, apart
# from the repaired stage and the composite that includes it; those two,
# which must have moved by more than the others' printed bound on every
# corpus; and the canonical normaliser, whose scoring changed in between
# (it now uses the published spelling map, audit finding EWER-05). The
# paragraph gives each as a bound in percentage points.
decode_shift <- local({
  lv   <- "whisper-large-v3"
  keep <- c("suite", "condition", "macro_wer")
  j <- dplyr::inner_join(
    sweep_agg_prefix[sweep_agg_prefix$model_slug == lv, keep],
    sweep_agg[sweep_agg$model_slug == lv, keep],
    by = c("suite", "condition"), suffix = c("_pre", "_post"))
  j$moved <- abs(j$macro_wer_post - j$macro_wer_pre)
  stopifnot(all(table(j$condition) == n_sweep_suites))
  repaired <- c("contraction_fix", "pipeline_full")
  others <- setdiff(j$condition[condition_layer(j$condition) %in%
                                  c("Production atomic",
                                    "Production composite",
                                    "Diagnostic ablation")], repaired)
  list(raw      = max(j$moved[j$condition == "raw"]),
       others   = max(j$moved[j$condition %in% others]),
       repaired = min(j$moved[j$condition %in% repaired]),
       norm     = max(j$moved[j$condition == "whisper_norm"]))
})
shift_txt <- lapply(decode_shift[c("raw", "others", "norm")], pp_bound)
stopifnot(decode_shift$repaired > as.numeric(shift_txt$others) / 100)
```

Pairing by utterance and resampling a single index per replicate
exploits that cancellation, and the effect is large. The intervals on
the differences (@tbl-condition-ci) are on average roughly
`r cci_width_ratio` times narrower than the interval on the level,
over the `r num_word(cci_n_ratio)` conditions besides the canonical
normaliser whose intervals have any width at all, and that is what
makes the test sharp enough to be worth running. The other
`r num_word(cci_n_zero)` intervals have zero width because the
condition changes the score of no utterance on this corpus, and an
interval of that kind records the absence of any change, not the
precision of the comparison.

Run against the pipeline as it stands, the composite and the
contraction repair are among those `r num_word(cci_n_zero)`, and so is
every other stage the composite chains. None of them changes the score
of a single utterance on this corpus, so each costs nothing, with an
interval of zero width. Besides the canonical normaliser, the only
conditions whose intervals exclude zero are the two diagnostic ones
that delete words, the deduplication window at
`r cci_fmt("dedup_window")` and filler removal at
`r cci_fmt("filler_strip")`, and the production pipeline applies
neither. On clean read speech the layer as it now stands has no cost
this test can detect.

That is not what this test reported when it was first run, and the
difference is the substance of this section. On the pipeline as it stood
then, the composite cost
`r cci_pre_fmt("pipeline_full")`,
and the contraction repair
`r cci_pre_fmt("contraction_fix")`,
which is where the defect described above was found. Repairing it,
together with the further corrections made before the last decoding,
took the composite's cost to nothing. For Whisper Large v3, the model
these intervals describe, the raw baseline moved by no more than
`r shift_txt$raw` percentage points on any corpus between that first
decoding and the one reported here. The production and diagnostic
conditions that both decodings scored moved by no more than
`r shift_txt$others` points, except the repaired stage and the
composite that includes it, which moved by more than that on every
corpus. The canonical normaliser moved as well, by up to
`r shift_txt$norm` points, because it is now scored with its published
spelling map.

The utterance-level intervals treat successive utterances from one
reader as independent. Resampling whole readers instead, in the
exploratory sensitivity analysis, widened the 95% interval on the raw
corpus macro average to
[`r f3(sc_level$ci_lo)`, `r f3(sc_level$ci_hi)`], against
[`r f3(ci_lo)`, `r f3(ci_hi)`] under utterance resampling, without
changing the point estimate. The pre-repair costs remained positive:
the composite's reader-cluster interval was
[`r ppt(sc_pair("pipeline_full")$ci_lo)`,
`r ppt(sc_pair("pipeline_full")$ci_hi)`] percentage points and the
contraction repair's was
[`r ppt(sc_pair("contraction_fix")$ci_lo)`,
`r ppt(sc_pair("contraction_fix")$ci_hi)`]. The defect's direction thus
survived this change in resampling unit, while the original corpus
interval understated the sensitivity associated with repeated speech
from the same readers.

The filler bracketing is the stage that does the preservation work the
defensive layer is offered for, and @tbl-condition-ci cannot show
whether it does that work well or badly. The scoring normaliser turns
its square brackets into spaces, so a bracketed filler scores exactly
as the bare one and the stage's word error rate equals the baseline's
by construction, as it does for the
`r num_word(length(setdiff(wer_invisible_conds, "filler_bracket")))`
other conditions that change only case, spacing or punctuation other
than the apostrophe. A null
difference for any of them is guaranteed by the method and is no
evidence that the stage is harmless. A null means something only for
the production stages the scorer can see,
`r and_list(unname(visible_names[visible_conds]))`, and on this corpus none
of them changes the score of a single utterance. Whether marking the
fillers keeps them is a separate question, which [the Filler Preservation section](#sec-disfluency)
answers by scoring the fillers themselves.

Every condition the sweep scored kept its per-utterance report, so all
`r num_word(cci_k)` non-baseline conditions in @tbl-condition-ci are
paired against the baseline and none was chosen by which files
happened to survive. That was not true of the first sweep, whose
pre-repair intervals are quoted above. It kept per-utterance reports
for only `r num_word(nrow(cci_pre))` conditions besides the baseline,
`r cci_pre_conditions`, so those are the only ones that could be paired
at the time, and every other condition was scored at corpus level alone.

The intervals need reading with the same care, because
`r num_word(cci_k)` conditions are compared against one baseline here,
inside a sweep that covers `r num_word(n_sweep_conditions)` conditions
on `r num_word(n_sweep_suites)` corpora, and no
correction for multiplicity was applied at any point in the analysis. Each interval
is a marginal 95% percentile interval valid for its own comparison,
and each *p* value is the raw two-sided bootstrap value for that
comparison, so the probability that at least one row of the table
crosses a 5% threshold by chance is higher than 5%, and higher again
across the full grid. For this table a correction would change no
conclusion. `r Num_word(length(cci_excl))` rows have intervals that
exclude zero, the canonical normaliser at
`r cci_pp("whisper_norm")` percentage points, *p*
`r cci_p("whisper_norm")`, the deduplication window at
`r cci_pp("dedup_window")`, *p* `r cci_p("dedup_window")`, and filler
removal at `r cci_pp("filler_strip")`, *p* `r cci_p("filler_strip")`.
Each would clear a Bonferroni threshold of .05 divided by the
`r num_word(cci_k)` comparisons in the table. On their point values all
`r num_word(length(cci_excl))` would also clear .05 divided by the
`r num_word((n_sweep_conditions - 1) * n_sweep_suites)` comparisons that
`r num_word(n_sweep_conditions - 1)` non-baseline conditions on
`r num_word(n_sweep_suites)` corpora would involve for this model,
which is `r bonf_grid_txt`. Filler removal's *p* of
`r p_txt(fs$p_value, fs$bootstrap)`, however, rests on
`r num_word(fs_beyond)` of the `r cci_b_txt` replicates falling at or
below zero, too few to place it firmly on either side of that
threshold. Every other
row, the whole production layer among them, is a difference of exactly
zero with an interval of zero width and *p* = 1.000, on which a
correction has nothing to act. The filler bracketing is outside the
question altogether, since the scorer cannot see what it does.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-condition-ci
#| tbl-cap: "Paired Changes in Word Error Rate Against Raw Output on LibriSpeech test-clean"
cci |>
  arrange(delta) |>
  transmute(
    Condition = condition,
    `Delta (pp)` = sgn2(100 * delta),
    `95% CI` = sprintf("[%s, %s]", sgn2(100 * ci_lo), sgn2(100 * ci_hi)),
    # Uncorrected two-sided bootstrap p values, floored at the
    # resolution the replicate count supports: with b replicates the
    # smallest attainable two-sided value is 2/b, so anything below it
    # is reported as a bound and not as a smaller number (p_txt, in
    # load-condition-ci, which the prose quotes through as well). The
    # header is the italic symbol APA 7 asks for.
    `*p*` = mapply(p_txt, p_value, bootstrap)
  ) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r cci_cap`

```{r published-comparison, include=FALSE}
# The Whisper Large v2 figures on LibriSpeech test-clean and test-other
# that Radford et al. report, as the paragraph below quotes them, beside
# this evaluation's macro and pooled rates under the same normaliser.
# The paragraph says both put the workflow below them on both splits.
published_v2 <- c(librispeech_clean = 0.027, librispeech_other = 0.052)
norm_rate <- function(suite, field = "macro_wer") {
  one(sweep_agg[[field]][sweep_agg$model_slug == "whisper-large-v3" &
                           sweep_agg$suite == suite &
                           sweep_agg$condition == "whisper_norm"],
      paste(field, "of whisper_norm on", suite))
}
stopifnot(all(vapply(names(published_v2), \(s)
                     max(norm_rate(s), norm_rate(s, "micro_wer")) <
                       published_v2[[s]], logical(1))))
```

The `whisper_norm` condition reduces WER on test-clean by roughly a
factor of
`r num_word(round(mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_clean", "raw") / mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_clean", "whisper_norm")))`
relative to the baseline, because it rewrites both sides further than
the scoring normaliser does. It removes the quotation marks described
above, which the scoring normaliser keeps and the raw rate counts as
errors against references that have none, and those marks account for
most of the reduction. It also writes contractions, numbers, spellings
and abbreviated titles the same way on both sides.

That condition exists to allow comparison with published figures, so
the comparison is worth making explicitly. Under it the present
evaluation puts Whisper Large&nbsp;v3 at
`r pct(norm_rate("librispeech_clean"))`
on LibriSpeech test-clean and
`r pct(norm_rate("librispeech_other"))`
on test-other. @radford2022whisper report
`r pct(published_v2[["librispeech_clean"]])` and
`r pct(published_v2[["librispeech_other"]])` for Whisper
Large&nbsp;v2 under greedy decoding, which is the decoding
configuration used here. Two caveats keep this from being a like-for-like
result. The published figures are for v2, since v3 postdates that
paper, and an improvement is what a later model is expected to deliver.
More importantly, the quantities differ. The figures reported here are
macro averages over utterances, while published benchmark numbers are
pooled over words, and the two diverge substantially on this corpus
because it is made of short utterances. Pooled over words, the present
figures are `r pct(norm_rate("librispeech_clean", "micro_wer"))` and
`r pct(norm_rate("librispeech_other", "micro_wer"))`. Either way the
workflow comes in below the earlier model's published figures on both
splits, which is the direction a later model should take them. The
comparison should therefore be read as showing that the workflow
behaves as the published results lead one to expect, not as a measured
difference between model versions.

```{r raw-pooled, include=FALSE}
# The paragraph below says that FLEURS has the lowest raw macro rate as
# scored but that pooled over words test-clean has the lower rate, so
# that the order of the two turns on how they are scored. Re-scored from
# the sweep's hypotheses (ARC job 8917985, not committed) with the
# quotation marks set aside, test-clean's macro rate is also the lower
# (0.028 against 0.047), and under the Whisper normaliser it already is.
raw_micro <- function(suite)
  one(sweep_agg$micro_wer[sweep_agg$model_slug == "whisper-large-v3" &
                            sweep_agg$suite == suite &
                            sweep_agg$condition == "raw"],
      paste("raw micro WER on", suite))
stopifnot(
  mw("whisper-large-v3", "fleurs", "raw") <
    mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_clean", "raw"),
  raw_micro("librispeech_clean") < raw_micro("fleurs"),
  norm_rate("librispeech_clean") < norm_rate("fleurs"))
```

The cross-corpus picture in @fig-suites extends the headline result.
As scored, FLEURS read speech yields the lowest macro-averaged rate,
followed by LibriSpeech test-clean, but that order turns on how the two
are scored. The macro average weighs test-clean's short utterances
heavily, and with them the quotation marks described above, so that
pooled over words test-clean has the lower rate,
`r f3(raw_micro("librispeech_clean"))` against
`r f3(raw_micro("fleurs"))`. LibriSpeech test-other, drawn from the
speakers that a reference recogniser found harder to transcribe
[@panayotovLibrispeechASRCorpus2015], raises the macro rate
from `r f3(mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_clean", "raw"))` to
`r f3(mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_other", "raw"))`. VoxPopuli
accented English raises it
further, and AMI meeting speech sits at the top, where overlapping
speakers and dense spontaneous disfluency combine.

\needspace{0.75\textheight}

```{r fig-suites, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Word Error Rate Across Five English Corpora"}
focus_conds  <- c("raw", "pipeline_full", "whisper_norm")
focus_labels <- c("raw" = "Raw",
                  "pipeline_full" = "Production composite",
                  "whisper_norm" = "Whisper canonical")

# Order suites by the raw output's macro WER as scored (ascending); the
# raw-pooled chunk above says why FLEURS and test-clean fall in this order.
suite_difficulty <- sweep_agg |>
  filter(model_slug == "whisper-large-v3", condition == "raw") |>
  arrange(macro_wer) |>
  pull(suite)

cross <- sweep_agg |>
  filter(model_slug == "whisper-large-v3",
         condition %in% focus_conds) |>
  mutate(Suite     = factor(suite_labels[suite],
                            levels = suite_labels[suite_difficulty]),
         Condition = factor(focus_labels[condition],
                            levels = focus_labels))

ggplot(cross, aes(x = Suite, y = macro_wer, fill = Condition)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.78), width = 0.72) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01),
                     limits = c(0, NA),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.04))) +
  # Same layer palette as @fig-conditions, so a colour means the same
  # thing in both figures.
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Raw"                  = "#767676",
    "Production composite" = "#000000",
    "Whisper canonical"    = "#009E73"
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Macro-averaged word error rate",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_paper() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* Macro-averaged word error rate across five corpora (Whisper Large v3) for three representative conditions: the raw model output, the production composite and the canonical Whisper normaliser. Corpora are ordered left to right by the raw output's macro-averaged rate as scored, from read speech to spontaneous meeting audio. On AMI the normaliser's bar leaves out the utterances whose reference it empties.

```{r suite-order, include=FALSE}
# The paragraph above walks the corpora in this order of raw macro error
# rate as scored. If the scorer stops charging quotation marks, test-clean
# moves ahead of FLEURS: re-derive the paragraph, this order and the
# captions of @fig-suites and @tbl-models.
stopifnot(identical(suite_difficulty,
                    c("fleurs", "librispeech_clean", "librispeech_other",
                      "voxpopuli_accented", "ami")))
```

```{r normaliser-gains, include=FALSE}
# The composite's signed change against raw, and the relative reduction
# the canonical normaliser buys, by corpus, for Whisper Large v3.
ng <- sweep_agg |>
  filter(model_slug == "whisper-large-v3",
         condition %in% c("raw", "pipeline_full", "repetition_fix",
                          "whisper_norm")) |>
  select(suite, condition, macro_wer) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = macro_wer) |>
  mutate(norm_gain  = (raw - whisper_norm) / raw,
         comp_delta = pipeline_full - raw)
stopifnot(nrow(ng) == n_sweep_suites, !anyNA(ng))
gain_of    <- function(s) pct(ng$norm_gain[ng$suite == s])
ng_delta_of <- function(s) ppt(abs(ng$comp_delta[ng$suite == s]))
# What the two paragraphs below say of these figures. The composite
# scores exactly as raw everywhere but AMI, where it improves on raw by
# what the repetition repair alone improves, every other production
# stage scoring there as raw does, and the repetition repair moves no
# other corpus. The normaliser's gain is largest by far, more than twice
# any other, on the two LibriSpeech splits, and on the other three it
# follows the order of raw difficulty in neither direction. "Most of that
# gain is the single quotation mark" and "most of the rest" are said in
# words, because no committed artefact holds the hypotheses. Re-scored
# from the sweep's hypotheses (ARC job 8917985, not committed) with
# apostrophes at token edges set aside on both sides, the raw macro rate
# falls from 0.0621 to 0.0285 on test-clean and from 0.0840 to 0.0512 on
# test-other, against 0.0221 and 0.0434 under the normaliser, which
# leaves no apostrophe; those apostrophes, nearly all of them quotation
# marks, are thus 84% and 81% of the two gains. The rest, 0.64 and 0.79
# points, was split by rebuilding the normaliser (transformers'
# EnglishTextNormalizer with the Hub's normalizer.json less its "mm"
# entry, which reproduces every whisper_norm reference and hypothesis in
# the dump on both splits) and switching its parts off, one at a time and
# together: numbers account for 0.24 and 0.30 points, abbreviated titles,
# which it writes out (mr as mister), 0.18 and 0.23, spellings 0.12 and
# 0.08 and contractions 0.06 and 0.08, nearly additively, so numbers,
# spellings and titles together are 85% and 77% of the rest. On AMI alone
# the normaliser scores fewer utterances than raw, and the difference is
# the count the disfluency summary records it dropping.
ng_ls  <- ng$suite %in% c("librispeech_clean", "librispeech_other")
ng_ami <- ng$suite == "ami"
# On AMI the normaliser empties the references made only of fillers, and
# an utterance is scored only under the conditions that leave its
# reference non-empty, so the ratio of the two AMI corpus rates would mix
# the normaliser with the removal of those utterances (EWER-09). The AMI
# gain is read instead from normaliser_gain_ami.csv, which condition_ci
# --gains-output computed from the sweep's AMI reports for raw and
# whisper_norm over the utterances both score. Its counts and its
# all-utterance columns must be the matrix's, and the utterances the
# normaliser drops must be harder than the rest under raw scoring, as the
# paragraph below says. The gain is replaced before ng_3 is taken, so the
# checks below test the figure the text prints, while ng$raw and
# ng$whisper_norm stay the corpus rates plotted in @fig-suites.
ng_shared <- row_of(norm_gain_ami, "whisper_norm", "normaliser_gain_ami.csv")
stopifnot(
  ng_shared$n_shared == n_utt("ami", "whisper_norm"),
  ng_shared$n_shared + ng_shared$n_baseline_only == n_utt("ami"),
  ng_shared$n_condition_only == 0,
  abs(ng_shared$macro_baseline_all - ng$raw[ng_ami]) < 1e-6,
  abs(ng_shared$macro_condition_all - ng$whisper_norm[ng_ami]) < 1e-6,
  abs(ng_shared$macro_gain_all - ng$norm_gain[ng_ami]) < 1e-6,
  ng_shared$macro_baseline_all > ng_shared$macro_baseline_shared,
  ng_shared$macro_gain_all > ng_shared$macro_gain_shared)
ng$norm_gain[ng_ami] <- ng_shared$macro_gain_shared
ng_3   <- ng[!ng_ls, ]
ami_dropped <- n_utt("ami") - n_utt("ami", "whisper_norm")
stopifnot(
  all(abs(ng$comp_delta[!ng_ami]) < 1e-12),
  ng$comp_delta[ng_ami] < 0,
  abs(ng$pipeline_full[ng_ami] - ng$repetition_fix[ng_ami]) < 1e-12,
  all(abs(ng$repetition_fix[!ng_ami] - ng$raw[!ng_ami]) < 1e-12),
  all(abs(vapply(setdiff(atomic_conds, "repetition_fix"),
                 \(k) delta_vs_raw(sweep_agg, k, suite = "ami"),
                 numeric(1))) < 1e-12),
  min(ng$norm_gain[ng_ls]) > 2 * max(ng$norm_gain[!ng_ls]),
  !identical(order(ng_3$norm_gain), order(ng_3$raw)),
  !identical(order(ng_3$norm_gain), order(-ng_3$raw)),
  identical(ng_3$suite[order(ng_3$raw)],
            c("fleurs", "voxpopuli_accented", "ami")),
  all(vapply(ng$suite[!ng_ami], \(s) n_utt(s, "whisper_norm") == n_utt(s),
             logical(1))),
  ami_dropped > 0,
  ami_dropped == dcond("whisper_norm", "n_utterances_dropped"))
```

The production composite scores exactly as the raw baseline on the
four read and accented corpora. On AMI it improves on the baseline by
`r ng_delta_of("ami")` points, and the repetition repair, the one stage
a default run leaves out, makes exactly that improvement on its own,
while every other stage scores there as the raw output does. That is
the same repetition suppression @tbl-models shows at much larger scale
for a weaker model, appearing here in miniature on the one corpus
difficult enough to provoke it.

The gain delivered by the canonical Whisper normaliser tracks
transcription convention, which orders the corpora differently from
acoustic difficulty. It is largest
by far on the two LibriSpeech splits
(`r gain_of("librispeech_clean")` and
`r gain_of("librispeech_other")`), whose references are unpunctuated
audiobook text with numbers written out. Most of that gain is the
single quotation mark, which Whisper writes around the books' dialogue
and the scoring normaliser keeps as an apostrophe. Most of the rest
comes from numbers, spellings and abbreviated titles such as *Mr* and
*Mrs*, which the normaliser writes the same way on both sides.
Elsewhere it is worth far less, and not in order of difficulty:
`r gain_of("fleurs")` on FLEURS, the corpus with the lowest raw macro
rate as scored, `r gain_of("voxpopuli_accented")` on accented
VoxPopuli and `r gain_of("ami")` on AMI meeting speech, the corpus with
the highest. The AMI figure is taken over the
`r big(ng_shared$n_shared)` utterances scored both with and without the
normaliser. The normaliser empties `r big(ami_dropped)` of the
`r n_utt_txt("ami")` AMI references, for the reason given in
[the Filler Preservation section](#sec-disfluency), and those utterances drop out of its average while the
raw rate keeps them. Under raw scoring they are harder than the rest,
so the two corpus rates plotted in @fig-suites, which cover different
utterances, would put the gain at `r pct(ng_shared$macro_gain_all)`. On
the other four corpora both rates are taken over the same utterances. Figures computed under this
normaliser are therefore not straightforwardly comparable across
corpora whose references were transcribed to different conventions,
which bears on the interpretation of headline benchmark figures
published in the broader literature.

Exploratory rescoring confirms that much of the normaliser's apparent
gain depends on edge apostrophes. On fixed shared utterances, the relative
macro-WER reduction on test-clean fell from
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_clean", "whisper-large-v3", "original")` to
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_clean", "whisper-large-v3", "edge_apostrophe")`
for Large v3,
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_clean", "distil-large-v3", "original")` to
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_clean", "distil-large-v3", "edge_apostrophe")`
for Distil-Large v3 and
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_clean", "whisper-medium", "original")` to
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_clean", "whisper-medium", "edge_apostrophe")`
for Medium. Large v3's test-other reduction fell from
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_other", "whisper-large-v3", "original")` to
`r ss_gain_txt("librispeech_other", "whisper-large-v3", "edge_apostrophe")`,
while its AMI reduction stayed at about
`r ss_gain_txt("ami", "whisper-large-v3", "original")`.
No reference became newly empty. The rule also removes edge elisions
and terminal possessive marks, so this exploratory comparison cannot
establish reference correctness. No sampling interval was computed.

The picture in @fig-suites is for Whisper Large&nbsp;v3, and the
near-invariance of the production composite to the raw baseline proves
to be a property of that model, with the post-processing contributing
nothing to it. Repeating the full sweep for the smaller `whisper-medium` and
for the distilled `distil-large-v3` exposes a pronounced interaction
between the model and the value of the defensive layer
(@tbl-models).

```{r model-scaling, include=FALSE}
# `mw()` and `f2()` are defined in the setup chunk, because the
# published-figure comparison earlier in this section already uses them.
med_ami_gain <- mw("whisper-medium", "ami", "raw") -
                mw("whisper-medium", "ami", "pipeline_full")
med_lsc_gain <- mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_clean", "raw") -
                mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_clean", "pipeline_full")
# The part of that test-clean gain the repetition repair delivers alone.
med_lsc_rep  <- mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_clean", "raw") -
                mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_clean", "repetition_fix")
# The same model on test-other, harder for it than test-clean.
med_lso_raw  <- mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_other", "raw")
med_lso_gain <- med_lso_raw -
                mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_other", "pipeline_full")

# What the two paragraphs below say in words, checked against the grid
# the table is drawn from. "Exactly" is equality to the last binary
# digit, the tolerance the setup chunk uses for the same cells.
same_wer <- function(a, b) abs(a - b) < 1e-12
read_accented <- c("librispeech_clean", "librispeech_other", "fleurs",
                   "voxpopuli_accented")
stopifnot(
  # Large v3 and its distilled counterpart: the composite scores as the
  # raw output on the read and accented corpora, and better on AMI
  all(vapply(c("whisper-large-v3", "distil-large-v3"), \(m) all(vapply(
    read_accented, \(s) same_wer(mw(m, s, "pipeline_full"), mw(m, s, "raw")),
    logical(1))) && mw(m, "ami", "pipeline_full") < mw(m, "ami", "raw"),
    logical(1))),
  # Whisper Medium: helped on test-clean, nearly all of it by the
  # repetition repair, and helped "only" a little on test-other, whose raw
  # rate is the higher of the two: a gain above zero, under a tenth of the
  # test-clean one and not printed as zero at the three decimals quoted
  med_lsc_gain > 0, med_lsc_rep / med_lsc_gain > 0.95,
  med_lso_raw > mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_clean", "raw"),
  med_lso_gain > 0, med_lso_gain < med_lsc_gain / 10,
  sprintf("%.3f", med_lso_gain) != "0.000")

# The caption of @tbl-models says the repaired contraction stage costs
# nothing in every model-by-corpus cell, and prints the share of Whisper
# Medium's raw excess over Large v3 that the composite removes on AMI and
# on VoxPopuli (0.86 and 0.50 on the committed grid). The bounds below
# keep the paragraph's reading of them: more than three quarters on AMI
# and some, but less than three quarters, on VoxPopuli. The text's "much
# of the damage" holds of both. The check keeps
# these true of the grid the table is drawn from. The text adds that
# only Whisper Medium collapsed: no other model's raw macro WER reaches
# 1, the signature of collapse it names, on any corpus.
med_excess_removed <- function(s)
  (mw("whisper-medium", s, "raw") - mw("whisper-medium", s, "pipeline_full")) /
  (mw("whisper-medium", s, "raw") - mw("whisper-large-v3", s, "raw"))
stopifnot(med_excess_removed("ami") > 3 / 4,
          med_excess_removed("voxpopuli_accented") > 0,
          med_excess_removed("voxpopuli_accented") < 3 / 4)
contraction_cells <- dplyr::inner_join(
  sweep_agg[sweep_agg$condition == "contraction_fix",
            c("model_slug", "suite", "macro_wer")],
  sweep_agg[sweep_agg$condition == "raw",
            c("model_slug", "suite", "macro_wer")],
  by = c("model_slug", "suite"), suffix = c("_fix", "_raw"))
stopifnot(nrow(contraction_cells) == n_sweep_models * n_sweep_suites,
          all(same_wer(contraction_cells$macro_wer_fix,
                       contraction_cells$macro_wer_raw)),
          mw("whisper-medium", "ami", "raw") > 1,
          all(sweep_agg$macro_wer[sweep_agg$condition == "raw" &
                                    sweep_agg$model_slug !=
                                      "whisper-medium"] < 1),
          med_ami_gain > 0,
          mw("whisper-medium", "voxpopuli_accented", "pipeline_full") <
            mw("whisper-medium", "voxpopuli_accented", "raw"))
# The caption's sentence on quotation marks is in words, because no
# committed artefact holds the hypotheses. Re-scored from the sweep's
# test-clean hypotheses (ARC job 8917985, not committed) with apostrophes
# at token edges set aside on both sides, Whisper Large v3 loses 842
# errors, Distil-Large v3 711 and Whisper Medium 176, nearly all of them
# quotation marks (836, 706 and 169; the rest are possessive plurals such
# as Anders' and elided forms such as 'Tis), and the raw macro rates of
# 0.062, 0.061 and 0.066 become 0.028, 0.034 and 0.061.
models_cap <- paste0(
  "WER = word error rate. The production composite is `pipeline_full`. Corpora ",
  "are ordered by Whisper Large v3's raw macro-averaged rate as scored. ",
  "On the LibriSpeech rows the raw rates carry the charge for quotation ",
  "marks described in [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer), which falls heavily on Whisper Large v3 ",
  "and Distil-Large v3 and lightly on Whisper Medium. The composite is ",
  "near-neutral for Whisper Large v3 and Distil-Large v3, which do not ",
  "collapse into repetition loops, but removes ",
  pc0(med_excess_removed("ami")),
  " of Whisper Medium's excess over Whisper Large v3 on conversational ",
  "speech, where Whisper Medium does, and ",
  pc0(med_excess_removed("voxpopuli_accented")), " on accented speech. ",
  "Every row is from the ",
  "repaired pipeline: all ", num_word(n_sweep_models), " models, each at ",
  "the precision its checkpoint stores, were decoded again after the ",
  "contraction repair of [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer), and that stage now costs nothing in ",
  "each of the ", num_word(nrow(contraction_cells)), " model-by-corpus ",
  "cells.")
```

For Whisper Large v3 and its distilled counterpart, the composite scores
exactly as the raw output does on the read and accented corpora and
improves on it on AMI. Whisper Medium behaves quite differently on degraded audio. Its
raw macro WER climbs to
`r f2(mw("whisper-medium", "voxpopuli_accented", "raw"))` on
accented VoxPopuli and to `r f2(mw("whisper-medium", "ami", "raw"))`
on AMI meeting speech, the latter a signature of the decoder
collapsing into repetition loops. The model card of Whisper Large v3
identifies repetitive output as a limitation of Whisper's
sequence-to-sequence architecture [@openaiWhisperLargev3ModelCard2023]. The production composite
suppresses those loops and returns the same model to
`r f2(mw("whisper-medium", "voxpopuli_accented", "pipeline_full"))` and
`r f2(mw("whisper-medium", "ami", "pipeline_full"))` respectively, a
reduction of `r f2(med_ami_gain)` in macro WER on the conversational
corpus.

This falls short of a clean scaling law in two respects. The
composite also helps Whisper Medium on LibriSpeech test-clean, which
is not a degraded corpus at all, by `r sprintf("%.3f", med_lsc_gain)`,
and nearly all of that comes from the repetition repair, the one step
a default run omits. On LibriSpeech test-other, where the same model's
raw error rate is higher
(`r f3(med_lso_raw)` against
`r f3(mw("whisper-medium", "librispeech_clean", "raw"))`), the
composite lowers it by only `r sprintf("%.3f", med_lso_gain)`.
Difficulty of the audio therefore does not by itself predict where the
layer earns its place. More important, the AMI collapse was produced
by a decoder carrying none of Whisper's own anti-repetition safeguards,
since the benchmark passes only the language and task to `generate` and
leaves the temperature fallback, the compression-ratio threshold and
the log-probability threshold at their inactive defaults. Those heuristics
exist in the reference implementation precisely to interrupt loops, so
part of what the defensive layer recovers here is a failure the
decoder could have been configured to avoid. What the comparison
establishes is narrower than a scaling law and still useful. When a
model does collapse, a text-level layer recovers much of the damage,
and of the three models tested here only Whisper Medium did.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "Word Error Rate by Model, Corpus, and Post-Processing Condition"
model_order  <- c("whisper-large-v3", "whisper-medium", "distil-large-v3")
model_labels <- c("whisper-large-v3" = "Whisper Large v3",
                  "whisper-medium"   = "Whisper Medium",
                  "distil-large-v3"  = "Distil-Large v3")
mc_tab <- sweep_agg |>
  filter(condition %in% c("raw", "pipeline_full"),
         model_slug %in% model_order) |>
  mutate(Model = factor(model_labels[model_slug],
                        levels = unname(model_labels[model_order])),
         Corpus = factor(suite_labels[suite],
                         levels = unname(suite_labels[suite_difficulty])),
         Condition = ifelse(condition == "raw", "Raw", "Composite")) |>
  select(Model, Corpus, Condition, macro_wer) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = Condition, values_from = macro_wer) |>
  arrange(Model, Corpus) |>
  transmute(Model, Corpus,
            Raw = sprintf("%.3f", Raw),
            `Production composite` = sprintf("%.3f", Composite))
kable(mc_tab)
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r models_cap`

## Dispersion Across Speakers {#sec-speakers}

A corpus average conceals whoever it averages over, and for a workflow
offered to researchers who record people the question is how much the
error rate varies between the people speaking, not between
utterances. LibriSpeech identifies the reader of every
utterance, so the test-clean split can be repartitioned by speaker at no
cost. Pooling errors and reference words within each reader gives a
word error rate per speaker that is not distorted by utterance length,
which [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer) showed to drive the per-utterance spread together with
the scorer's charge for quotation marks.

```{r speaker-dispersion, include=FALSE}
# Per-speaker pooled WER on the headline corpus, read from the condition
# sweep's raw Large v3 report (wer_report is post_raw, as the setup chunk
# checks).  The utterance id is `<speaker>-<chapter>-<index>`, so the
# reader is recoverable without re-reading the audio.  Pooling within
# speaker weights every reference word equally and removes the
# short-utterance artefact. It keeps the scorer's charge for the
# quotation marks Whisper writes around dialogue, which the paragraphs
# below say in words and without a number, because no committed artefact
# holds the hypotheses. Re-scored from the sweep's own test-clean
# hypotheses (ARC job 8917985, task 0, not committed) with leading and
# trailing apostrophes set aside on both sides, 842 of the 2,030 errors
# go: 836 quotation marks, the apostrophes of two possessive plurals
# (hours', Anders') and the leading apostrophes of four elided forms
# ('Tis three times and 'Twasn't once) that the references write as TIS
# and TWASN'T. The readers' range falls from 12.4 to 8.7 to one, and the
# errors that go are 63% to 80% of the error of each of the four readers
# scored worst. Whether the scorer should keep those apostrophes is the
# maintainer's decision; if it changes, re-derive these paragraphs, the abstract's
# last sentence (and its claims-check entry), the Methods' sentence on
# the apostrophe, the per-utterance paragraph of [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer), the
# whisper_norm, cross-corpus and normaliser-gain paragraphs (with the
# suite-order check and the order of @fig-suites and @tbl-models), the
# caption of @tbl-models, Appendix C and the Discussion's paragraph on
# the readers from the re-scored reports.
spk <- wer_report |>
  mutate(speaker = sub("-.*$", "", name)) |>
  group_by(speaker) |>
  summarise(errors = sum(substitutions + deletions + insertions),
            words  = sum(reference_words),
            n_utt  = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(words > 0) |>
  mutate(wer = errors / words) |>
  arrange(wer)
stopifnot(nrow(spk) > 1, min(spk$wer) > 0,
          nrow(spk) == sc_level$n_readers,
          sum(spk$n_utt) == sc_level$n_utterances)
spk_ratio <- max(spk$wer) / min(spk$wer)
spk_cap <- paste0(
  "Pooled word error rate for each of the ", num_word(nrow(spk)),
  " readers in LibriSpeech test-clean (Whisper Large v3, raw output), ",
  "ordered from the lowest rate to the highest. Each point is one ",
  "reader, and the horizontal line marks the corpus micro-averaged rate.")
```

Across the `r num_word(nrow(spk))` readers of test-clean the
pooled rate runs from `r pct(min(spk$wer))`
to `r pct(max(spk$wer))`, a spread of
about `r big(round(spk_ratio))`
to 1 around a median of
`r pct(median(spk$wer))` (@fig-speakers).
The best-served reader is scored an order of magnitude better than the
worst, on clean read speech in a single language, from a corpus chosen
for being easy. Part of that spread is the scorer's and not the
recogniser's. Pooling removes the weight of short utterances but not
the charge for quotation marks described in [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer), which falls on
each reader according to how much of their reading is dialogue and how
often the recogniser marks it, and those marks make up much of the
error of the readers scored worst.
Nothing in a corpus mean carries information of this kind, and it is
what a researcher planning a study most needs, since it shows how far
a headline rate can fail to transfer to one particular participant,
even among readers of prepared text.

This spread describes volunteers reading prepared English text under
the present scorer. It does not bound the disparity in conversational,
second-language or atypical speech, where the speakers and the
recogniser's errors can differ. Fine-tuning studies document substantial
recognition difficulties on dysarthric speech
[@chungDiagnosisawareMultitaskFinetuning2026], and published contrasts
between speaker groups can be far larger, in percentage points, than
the spread observed here between readers.
@zhaoQuantificationAutomaticSpeech2025 measured a mean word error rate
of 52.6% for d/Deaf and hard-of-hearing speakers against 5.0% for
speakers with normal hearing, over 850 recordings and four commercial
systems, with the largest errors falling on speakers rated low and
medium in speech intelligibility, on those whose hearing loss began
before they acquired speech, and on those whose main mode of
communication was sign language. Their contrast is between groups
where the figure reported here is between individuals, and it pools
