four systems rather than attributing the rate to Whisper alone, so it
documents inequality in the systems and groups tested without
estimating this workflow's error rates or its disparity between
speakers. The present evaluation
cannot estimate disparities between these populations, because its
corpora do not carry the
speaker attributes that would allow the comparison to be made
systematically. That limitation lies in the evaluation and leaves the
workflow untouched, and a subsequent study should measure it first.

\needspace{0.75\textheight}

```{r fig-speakers, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Word Error Rate Across LibriSpeech test-clean Readers"}
spk_plot <- spk |> mutate(rank = dplyr::row_number())
ggplot(spk_plot, aes(x = rank, y = wer)) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(mean = wsum$micro_wer),
             aes(yintercept = mean, linetype = "Corpus mean"),
             colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = NULL, values = c("Corpus mean" = "dashed")) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = rank, y = 0, yend = wer),
               colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, colour = "#1F4E79") +
  # No fixed accuracy: the labels take as many decimals as the spacing
  # of the breaks needs, so ticks at 2.5% and 7.5% do not print as 2% and
  # 8% beside an exact 5%.
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(),
                     limits = c(0, NA),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Reader, ordered by word error rate",
       y = "Pooled word error rate") +
  theme_paper()
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r spk_cap`

## Filler Preservation on Conversational Speech {#sec-disfluency}

The defensive layer is offered on the grounds that it keeps the
hesitations conversation-analytic and clinical designs are built on.
Word error rate cannot test that. It counts how many words differ, not
which, so a condition that deleted every filler and one that kept every
filler can post a similar figure. Scoring it directly requires the
verbatim hypotheses, which the benchmark retains, and a corpus
transcribed verbatim, which among those used here is AMI.

The measurement needs two rates, because two different things can go
wrong. Retention asks how many of the fillers the model emitted survive a
condition's transform. Measured between the untransformed and the
transformed hypothesis, it isolates the post-processing from
recognition error. Reference recall asks how many of the fillers the
human transcriber recorded reach the output, and is bounded by what
the model heard in the first place. Each rate is counted over the
utterances a condition scores, and recall always against the
reference as the transcriber wrote it, never against a version of it
that a condition has normalised. A filler here is any token the
detector counts, which takes in hesitations such as *um*, *uh* and
*hmm* and also the backchannels *mm-hmm* and *uh-huh* with which a
listener signals attention. The model writes most of the transcriber's
backchannels and few of the hesitations, so the pooled recall below is
higher than the recall of the hesitations alone.

```{r disfluency-figures, include=FALSE}
# Fillers the composite keeps but does not bracket: spellings outside
# the bracketing stage's lists, such as a drawn-out "mmm". The paragraph
# below says the composite keeps exactly the fillers the model emitted
# and names how many of them go unmarked, so a run that loses any of the
# model's fillers, adds fillers of its own or marks every one must have
# its wording changed. `retained` is the multiset intersection of the
# model's fillers with the output's, so the first equality fails on a
# loss and the second on an addition.
# The split between backchannels and hesitations is said in words,
# because disfluency.py writes no per-kind counts. Applying its detector
# to the pipeline_full rows of the sweep's AMI dump (ARC job 8917985,
# task 1, not committed) reproduces 4,072 reference fillers and 802
# recovered, and gives 402 of 474 backchannels (mm-hmm, uh-huh) recovered
# against 400 of the other 3,598 (uh 133 of 1,778, um 204 of 1,291).
disfl_unmarked <-dcond("pipeline_full", "output_fillers") -
  dcond("pipeline_full", "output_marked")
stopifnot(dcond("pipeline_full", "retained") ==
            dcond("pipeline_full", "raw_fillers"),
          dcond("pipeline_full", "output_fillers") ==
            dcond("pipeline_full", "retained"),
          disfl_unmarked > 0,
          # "roughly four fifths" of the transcriber's fillers never reach
          # the transcript: the share lost lies within five points of 80%
          abs(1 - dcond("pipeline_full", "reference_recall") - 0.8) < 0.05)
```

On the `r big(dcond("raw", "n_utterances"))`
AMI test utterances, the production composite retained
`r pct(dcond("pipeline_full", "retention"))`
of the fillers the model produced,
`r big(dcond("pipeline_full", "retained"))`
of
`r big(dcond("pipeline_full", "raw_fillers"))`.
The claim about the post-processing therefore holds exactly. The
bracketing stage marks all but `r num_word(disfl_unmarked)` of these
tokens instead of removing them, so they remain both machine-findable
and readable. Those `r num_word(disfl_unmarked)` are spellings that its
list of fillers does not cover, such as a drawn-out *mmm*, and they
stay in the transcript unmarked. @tbl-disfluency gives the three
conditions side by side.

The end-to-end picture is less comfortable. The references record
`r big(dcond("pipeline_full", "reference_fillers"))`
fillers, of which the model emitted only
`r pct(dcond("pipeline_full", "reference_recall"))`.
Whisper is trained on text that has largely been tidied, and it tidies
in turn, so roughly four fifths of the fillers a human transcriber
recorded never reach the transcript at all. No post-processing can
restore them, because they were never emitted. A design that depends on
disfluencies should treat an automatic transcript as a starting point
for correction, since it is no record of them, and the workflow's
contribution here is that it does not compound the loss.

The loss is not peculiar to fillers in meeting speech.
@mcgonigleBenchmarkingAutomaticSpeech2024 found that Whisper missed
almost half the developmentally informative non-speech vocalisations
in natural language samples from toddlers with Down syndrome, and
captured 14% of the words those children produced against 50% for
typically developing children, proportions of words recovered rather
than error rates. Nor is the loss evenly borne.
@liOurCollectiveVoices2025 scored Whisper against verbatim Mandarin
references from 72 speakers who stutter and found that deletions
increased with stuttering severity, which they attribute to the model
smoothing repeated words out of its output. They make the same
methodological point as this section, that removing disfluencies from
reference and hypothesis alike is the conventional practice because it
makes the two easier to align, and that it hides the fluency bias under
study.

How much the loss costs depends on what the transcript is for.
@naffahSpokenLanguageAnalysis2025 compared automatic transcripts of two
speech tasks completed by 238 older adults, produced by Whisper and by
a commercial service, against human-corrected transcripts, and found
the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count features computed from each
converging at an average *r* of .98, with manual tagging of filler words
altering the validity of no category except filler words and netspeak.
That figure pools the two systems, and it is convergence of aggregate
lexical measures rather than transcription accuracy, so it bounds the
damage for designs resting on such measures while leaving untouched the
designs built on the hesitations themselves.

The canonical Whisper normaliser, used for scoring throughout this
literature, is not neutral with respect to any of this. Of the fillers
the model emitted in the utterances it scores, it retains only
`r pct(dcond("whisper_norm", "retention"))`.
It is also inconsistent about which it removes. Applied to each token
in a carrier sentence, it deletes *um*, *uh*, *hmm*, *mm* and *mhm* but
keeps *er* and *ah*. It deletes the backchannel *mm-hmm* and cuts
*uh-huh* to *huh* when they are hyphenated, as AMI and Whisper write
them, but keeps both when they are written as one word. No version
number announces such a pattern. Its more consequential effect falls
on the corpus itself. Because it strips fillers from the reference as
well, an utterance whose reference holds nothing but such fillers
normalises to empty and is discarded. That removed
`r big(dcond("raw", "n_utterances") - dcond("whisper_norm", "n_utterances"))`
of the AMI utterances,
`r pct(1 - dcond("whisper_norm", "n_utterances") / dcond("raw", "n_utterances"))`
of the corpus, and every one of them carried a filler. Those utterances
held
`r pct(1 - dcond("whisper_norm", "raw_fillers") / dcond("raw", "raw_fillers"))`
of all the fillers the model produced, and in them the model
emitted `r pct(disfl_recall_dropped)` of the fillers the transcriber
recorded, against `r pct(disfl_recall_kept)` in the utterances the
normaliser keeps. Scoring a filler-bearing analysis under this
normaliser therefore excludes precisely the material the analysis is
about.

Which normaliser to score under is an audit decision, then, and not a
neutral preliminary. @sloaneCaseStakeholderdrivenAI2026 argue that an
audit of automatic speech recognition cannot presume a single correct
transcript, because a verbatim rendering that preserves hesitations
and a tidied one can each be the right answer, depending on the
research design being served. The normaliser used here retains fillers
by default for that reason, and the figures above record what the
canonical alternative would have removed.

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-disfluency
#| tbl-cap: "Filler Preservation on the AMI Test Split"
# Every row reads the summary's `conditions` block, each condition over
# its own utterances, with recall against the transcriber's reference.
drow <- function(label, key) tibble::tibble(
  Condition = label,
  Utterances = big(dcond(key, "n_utterances")),
  `Reference fillers` = big(dcond(key, "reference_fillers")),
  `Model fillers` = big(dcond(key, "raw_fillers")),
  Retention = pct(dcond(key, "retention")),
  `Reference recall` = pct(dcond(key, "reference_recall"))
)
dplyr::bind_rows(
  drow("Raw model output", "raw"),
  drow("Production composite", "pipeline_full"),
  drow("Whisper normaliser", "whisper_norm")
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", rep("r", 5)))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* Filler preservation on the AMI test split. Retention is the share of the fillers the model emitted that survive the condition. Reference recall is the share of the fillers the human transcriber recorded that reach the output, counted against the reference as the transcriber wrote it, and is bounded by what the model emitted. Each row is scored over the utterances its condition keeps, so the normaliser row covers fewer: it discards those whose reference holds nothing but the fillers it strips.

## Post-Processing Beyond English {#sec-multilingual}

```{r load-multilingual, include=FALSE}
# fleurs_multilingual_summary.json is loaded in setup. Its four arms are
# four states of the code, each recorded in the file with its commit,
# jobs and the GPU of every language: the original composite
# (1_before_fix), the diacritic repair (2_after_fix), the language gate
# (3_after_gate), and the repaired composite run again at the code of
# the condition sweep, on other GPUs (4_after_audit, ARC job 8917984,
# whose settings hpc/runs/fleurs_ml.env records).
ml_langs <- ml$languages
ml_arms  <- ml$benchmark$arms
ml_field <- function(field)
  vapply(names(ml_langs), \(k) one(ml_langs[[k]][[field]],
                                   paste(k, field)), numeric(1))
# The unrounded rates, ratios and shares the summary keeps beside the
# rounded ones, so that no comparison below rests on rounding.
ml_exact <- function(field)
  vapply(names(ml_langs), \(k) one(ml_langs[[k]]$exact[[field]],
                                   paste(k, "exact", field)), numeric(1))
# Order by the severity of the original inflation, worst first.
ml_keys  <- names(ml_langs)[order(-ml_field("ratio_before_fix"))]
r1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", one(x))
ml_worst <- r1(max(ml_field("ratio_before_fix")))
ml_best  <- r1(min(ml_field("ratio_before_fix")))
ml_n     <- length(ml_keys)
ml_de    <- r1(ml_langs[["de_de"]]$ratio_after_fix)
ml_pl_fix <- r1(ml_langs[["pl_pl"]]$ratio_after_fix)
ml_fr_fix <- r1(ml_langs[["fr_fr"]]$ratio_after_fix)
ml_rawlo <- f3(min(ml_field("raw_before_fix")))
ml_rawhi <- f3(max(ml_field("raw_before_fix")))
# How far the raw rate moved across the four arms, the control the text
# leans on: the largest spread of any language, taken on the unrounded
# rates. The text quotes it rounded up to the fourth decimal, so that the
# bound it states holds of the exact rates; rounded to the nearest, a
# spread just above a step would print as that step.
ml_raw_exact  <- vapply(c("raw_before_fix", "raw_after_fix",
                          "raw_after_gate", "raw_after_audit"), ml_exact,
                        numeric(length(ml_langs)))
ml_raw_spread <- max(apply(ml_raw_exact, 1, \(r) diff(range(r))))
ml_raw_bound  <- ceiling(ml_raw_spread * 1e4) / 1e4
# The fourth arm against the third, which the text bounds in the same
# way and says is no larger than the spread of the first three arms (on
# the committed summary, 0.000213 against 0.000216; the four-arm spread,
# 0.000308, comes from the fourth arm, so the four-arm bound alone would
# say nothing about it).
ml_arm4_dev   <- max(abs(ml_raw_exact[, "raw_after_audit"] -
                           ml_raw_exact[, "raw_after_gate"]))
ml_arm4_bound <- ceiling(ml_arm4_dev * 1e4) / 1e4
stopifnot(ml_arm4_dev <=
            max(apply(ml_raw_exact[, c("raw_before_fix", "raw_after_fix",
                                       "raw_after_gate")], 1,
                      \(r) diff(range(r)))))
# Rank correlation between diacritic density and the original
# inflation, quoted in the text as the discriminating evidence for the
# unicode_strip diagnosis. It is taken on the unrounded share and ratio,
# so that rounding cannot create ties (audit finding OUTPUTS-11), and
# gives the same coefficient as the rounded columns of the table. Only
# the coefficient is quoted; it is printed through r_apa(), which, like
# f2(), refuses an NA.
ml_share <- ml_exact("share_words_with_diacritic")
ml_orig  <- ml_exact("ratio_before_fix")
ml_rho <- cor(ml_share, ml_orig, method = "spearman")
ml_after_gate <- ml_field("ratio_after_gate")
ml_after_fix  <- ml_field("ratio_after_fix")

# What the section says in words, checked against the summary.
ml_gpus <- function(arm) unlist(ml_arms[[arm]]$gpus)
stopifnot(
  # Polish writes a diacritic in the most words and was the worst
  # affected, Dutch in the fewest and the only language not doubled
  names(which.max(ml_share)) == "pl_pl", names(which.max(ml_orig)) == "pl_pl",
  names(which.min(ml_share)) == "nl_nl", names(which.min(ml_orig)) == "nl_nl",
  sum(ml_orig < 2) == 1,
  # French writes a diacritic in more words than Spanish, yet was the
  # less inflated of the two
  ml_share[["fr_fr"]] > ml_share[["es_419"]],
  ml_orig[["fr_fr"]] < ml_orig[["es_419"]],
  # once diacritics were kept, German, Polish and French alone stayed
  # above 1.00, German the most
  setequal(names(which(ml_after_fix > 1)), c("de_de", "pl_pl", "fr_fr")),
  names(which.max(ml_after_fix)) == "de_de",
  # with the gate as well the composite prints at 1.00 in every language,
  # and in the fourth arm its rate equals the raw rate exactly
  all(sprintf("%.2f", ml_after_gate) == "1.00"),
  all(abs(ml_exact("ratio_after_audit") - 1) < 1e-12),
  # the wave ran under the English sweep's seed, and the fourth arm ran
  # the condition sweep's code, on GPUs none of the first three arms used
  one(ml$benchmark$seed) == one(wer_summary$benchmark$seed,
                                "the headline summary's seed"),
  one(ml_arms[["4_after_audit"]]$code) == sweep_version,
  length(intersect(ml_gpus("4_after_audit"),
                   c(ml_gpus("1_before_fix"), ml_gpus("2_after_fix"),
                     ml_gpus("3_after_gate")))) == 0)
# Any two arms that decoded a language on the same card scored its raw
# hypothesis alike, to the last binary digit, and at least one such pair
# exists. Only the first three arms form such pairs, since the fourth ran
# on GPUs none of them used (checked above), so the text claims the
# equality of those three and says that nothing isolates the fourth's
# GPUs. The summary's own account of the arm (finding$control) names the
# GPU as the only known difference; the text adds the nodes that hold
# the GPUs, since each node holds one model of card (ARC_NODE_GPU in
# evaluation/footprint.py) and the host processor computes the log-mel
# features before the card sees them, as determinism_cross_accelerator
# records among its differences.
ml_card_pairs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ml_langs), \(k) {
  card <- vapply(names(ml_arms), \(a) one(ml_arms[[a]]$gpus[[k]],
                                          paste(a, k, "GPU")), character(1))
  rate <- vapply(names(ml_arms), \(a) one(
    ml_langs[[k]]$exact[[sub("^[0-9]+_", "raw_", a)]], paste(a, k, "raw")),
    numeric(1))
  ij <- utils::combn(length(card), 2)
  data.frame(same_card = card[ij[1, ]] == card[ij[2, ]],
             same_rate = abs(rate[ij[1, ]] - rate[ij[2, ]]) < 1e-12)
}))
stopifnot(any(ml_card_pairs$same_card),
          all(ml_card_pairs$same_rate[ml_card_pairs$same_card]))

ml_table_cap <- paste0(
  "WER = word error rate. ",
  "Macro-averaged word error rate of the production composite on ",
  num_word(ml_n), " non-English FLEURS test splits (Whisper Large v3), ",
  "expressed as a ratio to the raw hypothesis measured in the same pass, ",
  "before and after each of two repairs, and in a re-run of the repaired ",
  "composite at the code of the English condition sweep, on GPUs the ",
  "earlier passes did not use. A ratio of 1.00 denotes a composite that ",
  "neither helps nor harms. The raw rate shown is the first pass's. ",
  "Languages are ordered by the severity of the original inflation. The ",
  "final column gives the proportion of words ",
  "carrying a diacritic, counted over every reference word of each test ",
  "split as the words holding a letter outside ASCII, the quantity the ",
  "initial damage tracks.")
```

The workflow is offered for multilingual use, since the model is
multilingual and the masking database covers nine languages. The
evidence presented so
far is not. Every corpus in @tbl-models is English, so the composite had
been shown to be near-neutral for a model that does not fail this way, on
English, and nothing more. Post-processing rules written against one language need not
transfer, and the question is empirical, so the composite was scored on
`r num_word(ml_n)` non-English FLEURS test splits
[@conneauFleursFewshotLearning2023] under the same protocol as the
English sweep: Whisper Large v3, the raw hypothesis against the
production composite, seed `r one(ml$benchmark$seed)`, with the
transcription language stated explicitly.

The composite did not merely fail to transfer. It inflated word error
rate on every language tested, by a factor of `r ml_best` at best and
`r ml_worst` at worst, while the raw model output was uniformly strong
across the same splits (macro WER `r ml_rawlo` to `r ml_rawhi`). The
damage was therefore contributed entirely by the post-processing and
not by the recogniser. In practical terms, a researcher transcribing
Polish would have received a transcript with roughly
`r num_word(round(ml_langs[["pl_pl"]]$ratio_before_fix))` times the
error rate of the one the model had produced.

Two independent defects account for it, and the first three arms of
@tbl-multilingual separate their contributions. The first is the
Unicode strip, which removed every codepoint outside the American
Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) and so
deleted diacritics instead of transliterating them, turning `n'était`
into `n'tait` and `Gerät` into `Gert`. Every accented word became a
wrong word. The table supplies the discriminating evidence. If this
stage were responsible, inflation should scale with how often a
language writes a diacritic, and across the `r num_word(ml_n)` splits
it does (Spearman $\rho$ = `r r_apa(ml_rho)`).
Polish, at
`r one(ml_langs[["pl_pl"]]$pct_words_with_diacritic)`%
of words, is the worst affected by a wide margin, and Dutch, at
`r one(ml_langs[["nl_nl"]]$pct_words_with_diacritic)`%,
is the only language the composite left nearly intact. The
correspondence is close without being exact. French writes a diacritic
in more of its words than Spanish
(`r one(ml_langs[["fr_fr"]]$pct_words_with_diacritic)`% against
`r one(ml_langs[["es_419"]]$pct_words_with_diacritic)`%) but was the
less inflated of the two (`r r1(ml_langs[["fr_fr"]]$ratio_before_fix)`
against `r r1(ml_langs[["es_419"]]$ratio_before_fix)`), so density
predicts the ordering without fully determining it.
The prediction that Polish would prove worst was registered before its
split had finished scoring, and it held. The first repair kept
accented letters but still deleted other characters outside ASCII,
numbers among them, and so took the vulgar fractions out of Whisper's
transcripts of one FLEURS sentence. The stage now keeps the letters,
combining marks, punctuation and numbers of every script, fractions
included, with currency and mathematical signs and the degree sign. It
removes emoji and the other symbols, together with control and
formatting codes, the artefacts it was written for, and keeps a joiner
only between two letters, where Persian and the Indic scripts use one.

The second defect is visible only against the repaired baseline, mainly
as a residual inflation of `r ml_de` in German, with smaller ones in
Polish (`r ml_pl_fix`) and French (`r ml_fr_fix`). The clean-text
stages assume an English vocabulary, and one of them rewrites a bare
`im` to the contraction `I'm`, a reasonable repair of a Whisper
artefact in English and a corruption in German, where *im* is a common
preposition. The remedy is a narrower rule, not a better one.
Stages encoding English lexical knowledge run only on transcripts
identified as English, while those encoding orthographic conventions
these languages share, such as sentence capitalisation and punctuation
spacing, run for all of them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-multilingual
#| tbl-cap: "Post-Processing Costs Across Non-English FLEURS Test Splits"
#| tbl-colwidths: [12, 15, 8, 12, 15, 12, 11, 15]
# The table is wider than Pandoc's 72 columns, so it sets each column's
# width; left to the header lengths, the PDF hyphenated "Language",
# "Utterances" and "Original" inside their narrow columns.
ml_get <- function(field) unname(sapply(ml_keys, \(k) ml_langs[[k]][[field]]))
ml_cap <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substring(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))
mltab <- tibble::tibble(
  Language = ml_cap(ml_get("language")),
  Utterances = ml_get("utterances"),
  `Raw WER` = sprintf("%.3f", ml_get("raw_before_fix")),
  `Original` = sprintf("%.2f", ml_get("ratio_before_fix")),
  `Diacritics kept` = sprintf("%.2f", ml_get("ratio_after_fix")),
  `Stages gated` = sprintf("%.2f", ml_get("ratio_after_gate")),
  `Run again` = sprintf("%.2f", ml_get("ratio_after_audit")),
  `Diacritic words` = sprintf("%d%%", ml_get("pct_words_with_diacritic"))
)
kable(mltab)
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r ml_table_cap`

With both repairs in place the composite is neutral, at a ratio of 1.00,
on all `r num_word(ml_n)` languages. The fourth arm, run at the code of
the English condition sweep (`r sweep_version`) on GPUs none of the
first three used, reproduces this exactly, since there the composite
scores every utterance as the raw hypothesis does. The raw hypothesis
supplies the control. Its rate stays within
`r sprintf("%.4f", ml_raw_bound)` across the four arms for every
language. Neither repair touches the recogniser, and any two of the
first three arms that decoded a language on the same model of GPU
scored its raw hypothesis alike. The fourth arm, at the audited code
and on other GPUs, departs from the third by at most
`r sprintf("%.4f", ml_arm4_bound)` in any language, no more than the
first three depart from one another, and the only known differences
from the third that reach the recogniser are its GPUs and the nodes
that hold them, which no pair of arms on one model of GPU isolates. The gate
skips the English-specific stages instead of
supplying equivalents for other languages. A non-English transcript
therefore receives less post-processing than an English one, and not
post-processing tailored to it, so the honest claim is that the
composite is harmless outside English without being helpful there.

The wider point is methodological. Both defects had been present since
the pipeline was written, both survived a test suite that exercised the
stages individually, and neither was visible in any English result,
because the English fixtures contained no diacritics and no word whose
English repair is another language's ordinary vocabulary. What exposed
them was scoring the composite on languages it had never been measured
against. A local workflow that offers multilingual transcription should
be evaluated multilingually, and the post-processing layer is where the
assumption of a single language is most likely to hide.

## Speaker Diarisation and Timestamp Alignment {#sec-benchmark-der}

```{r load-der-ts, include=FALSE}
# Every diarisation and timestamp artefact is loaded, and its fields
# checked, in setup. The default (untuned) configuration on the held-out
# AMI test split (der_summary, der_report) is the headline result;
# der_tuned, der_oracle and der_concat are the comparisons it is read
# against. der_sweep is a wide scan of the clustering threshold on the
# development split, and der_sweep2 a finer grid crossing it with the
# minimum-pause parameter.
# The DER artefacts are the October re-runs, at 9cb43e3 on L40S cards
# (hpc/runs/der_*.env): ARC jobs 8976354 to 8976357 scored the test split
# (defaults, oracle, tuned, concatenation) and 8976358 and 8976362 the
# two development sweeps. Against the August runs they replace, only the
# two meetings in which two speakers share a turn moved (EDER-02), and no
# rate in any summary by more than 5e-5. Every figure in this section is
# computed, and the checks here and in the chunks below stop the render
# where a sentence they cover says in words what the files no longer
# bear out. What they do not cover was re-read against these files by
# hand, and must be again after any re-run: the concatenation as the
# prose describes it (its first twenty-five utterances, which
# hpc/runs/der_concat.env sets, and its half-second gap,
# evaluation/ami_meetings.CONCAT_GAP_S), the statement that in both
# reconstructions the microphone
# channel changes "wherever the speaker does" (each turn is written from
# its own headset clip, in evaluation/ami_meetings.mix_meeting and
# concat_meeting alike, and the unannotated frames are digital silence,
# so the cue is common to both figures), the accounts of why the
# pipeline behaves as it does (the powerset's two-speaker limit,
# clustering forced to merge, and the pause trade being flattered by
# digital silence), and the expectation that a two-person recording,
# which no meeting here is, would sit nearer the favourable end. The
# crosstalk sentences themselves and "within a tenth of a point of the
# optimum", here and in the Discussion, are checked in der-derived.
#
# "Missed speech and confusion account for roughly half and two fifths
# of the total respectively, and false alarm for the small remainder":
# the shares round to those fractions, and false alarm is the smallest.
der_share <- c(missed = der_summary$macro_missed,
               conf   = der_summary$macro_confusion,
               fa     = der_summary$macro_fa) / der_summary$macro_der
stopifnot(round(der_share[["missed"]], 1) == 0.5,
          round(der_share[["conf"]], 1) == 0.4,
          der_share[["fa"]] < min(der_share[["missed"]], der_share[["conf"]]),
          # "confirmed that no meeting was displaced relative to its
          # reference"
          recon_test$summary$n_best_shift_zero == recon_test$summary$n_meetings,
          recon_val$summary$n_best_shift_zero == recon_val$summary$n_meetings)
#
# Per-utterance timestamp records give the coverage of the worst
# truncation and the distribution plotted below.
ts_cov <- (ts_report$pred_end_s - ts_report$pred_start_s) /
  ts_report$ref_duration_s
# Whisper writes its timestamps on a 20 ms step, and every predicted
# boundary lies on it. No hypothesis ends far past its reference: the
# largest overrun is about half a step, where a reference ends between
# two steps and the prediction takes the next one.
ts_step    <- 0.02
on_ts_step <- function(x) all(abs(x / ts_step - round(x / ts_step)) < 1e-6)
ts_overrun <- -min(ts_report$end_error_s)
stopifnot(on_ts_step(ts_report$pred_start_s), on_ts_step(ts_report$pred_end_s),
          ts_overrun > 0, abs(ts_overrun - ts_step / 2) < ts_step / 10)
# The paragraphs below also say in words that the mean end error is more
# than ten times the median, that the errors over half a second make up
# the large majority (here, over three quarters) of their total, and
# that the model starts the large majority of clips at exactly zero.
ts_gross <- abs(ts_report$end_error_s) > 0.5
stopifnot(ts_summary$mae_end > 10 * ts_summary$median_abs_end_error,
          sum(abs(ts_report$end_error_s[ts_gross])) /
            sum(abs(ts_report$end_error_s)) > 3 / 4,
          mean(ts_report$pred_start_s == 0) > 3 / 4)
# The one utterance the benchmark could not score, as
# timestamp_skipped.csv records it: the final chunk carried no end
# timestamp, and the hypothesis is the word "ha" and nothing else. The
# clip's length comes from its id, whose last two fields are its begin
# and end on the meeting timeline in hundredths of a second.
ts_skip_id  <- strsplit(ts_skipped$audio_id, "_", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
ts_skip_s   <- (as.numeric(ts_skip_id[[6]]) - as.numeric(ts_skip_id[[5]])) / 100
ts_skip_tok <- tolower(regmatches(ts_skipped$hypothesis,
                                  gregexpr("[[:alpha:]']+",
                                           ts_skipped$hypothesis))[[1]])
stopifnot(nrow(ts_skipped) == 1, ts_skipped$reason == "untimed_tail",
          length(ts_skip_id) == 6, ts_skip_s > 0,
          length(ts_skip_tok) > 0, all(ts_skip_tok == "ha"))
der_cap <- paste0(
  "DER = diarisation error rate; IHM = individual headset microphone. ",
  "Speaker diarisation on the held-out AMI IHM test split, reconstructed ",
  "on the original meeting timeline. Components are macro averages. The ",
  "oracle row is given the true number of speakers in each meeting and is ",
  "an upper bound on what a known participant count can buy. Collar: ",
  der_collar, " s in total, ", der_collar / 2, " s either side of each ",
  "reference boundary.")
der_meetings_cap <- paste0(
  "DER = diarisation error rate; IHM = individual headset microphone. ",
  "Per-meeting DER decomposition for the ", nrow(der_report), " AMI IHM ",
  "test meetings, ordered by the proportion of reference speech that is ",
  "overlapped (given beneath each label). Bars show missed speech (dark), ",
  "false alarm (mid) and speaker confusion (light). Error rises with ",
  "overlap, and it does so mainly through missed speech.")
stopifnot(nrow(der_report) == der_summary$n_meetings)
```

Speaker diarisation and timestamp alignment are evaluated in two
supplementary benchmarks, both against the AMI
Meeting Corpus [@carlettaAMIMeeting2005], which provides manual speaker
labels and time-aligned reference transcripts across a corpus of
recorded meetings. The individual headset microphone (IHM) release
was used throughout, as it isolates diarisation and alignment
errors from acoustic confounds introduced by distant microphone
capture.

That release distributes AMI one row per speaker turn, never as
whole recordings, with each row carrying that
speaker's headset audio together with the turn's position in the
original meeting timeline. A diarisation benchmark needs a
meeting, so the rows have to be reassembled first, and how they
are reassembled determines what is being measured. Each utterance
was therefore written at its true onset on a shared timeline and
the headset channels summed, so that turns which overlapped in the
original meeting overlap in the reconstruction. Since AMI's own
headset mix is likewise a sum of the individual channels, the
result approximates the signal under which diarisation systems are
conventionally reported on this corpus, and it preserves the
property that makes meeting diarisation difficult. An independent
audit re-derived speech activity from each reconstructed waveform
by short-term energy and confirmed that no meeting was displaced
relative to its reference, the best alignment falling at zero
across a range of candidate shifts down to 10 ms.

The reconstructed test split comprises
`r der_summary$n_meetings` meetings totalling
`r round(der_summary$corpus$audio_hours, 1)` h
of audio and
`r round(der_summary$corpus$speech_hours, 1)` h
of annotated speech, of which
`r pct(der_summary$corpus$overlap_fraction)`
carries two or more simultaneous speakers. Diarisation used the
`pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1` pipeline of `pyannote.audio`
[@bredinPyannoteAudio2025], whose segmentation model is trained under
the powerset formulation described below
[@plaquetPowersetMulticlassCross2023], and accuracy
was measured as the diarisation error rate (DER), the proportion of
reference speech time that is either missed, invented or attributed
to the wrong speaker. Errors were counted outside a collar, a tolerance
around each reference speaker boundary within which small timing
disagreements are forgiven. The scorer, `pyannote.metrics`, takes the
collar as its total width and centres it on the boundary, so the
collar of `r der_collar` s used here forgives `r der_collar / 2` s
either side. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
Rich Transcription scoring tools read the same
figure as the width on each side, so the rates below are scored more
strictly than a NIST collar of `r der_collar` s and correspond to one
of `r der_collar / 2` s there.
Hyperparameters were chosen on the AMI development split and the
resulting configuration scored once on the held-out test split, so
that the reported figure is not the best of several draws on the
data it is reported against.

At the pipeline's shipped settings the macro DER, averaging
per-meeting rates, was
`r pct(der_summary$macro_der)`, and the
micro DER over the pooled reference was
`r pct(der_summary$micro_der)`. The
decomposition attributed
`r pct(der_summary$macro_missed)` to missed
speech, meaning speech the system did not detect at all,
`r pct(der_summary$macro_fa)` to false
alarm, meaning silence it labelled as speech, and
`r pct(der_summary$macro_confusion)` to
speaker confusion, meaning speech it detected but attributed to the
wrong participant. Missed speech and confusion account for roughly
half and two fifths of the total respectively, and false alarm for
the small remainder.

```{r der-correlations, include=FALSE}
# Pearson correlations between overlap and each error component, with
# intervals.  Also computed within meeting series, because the sixteen
# test meetings are four series of four sessions sharing participants,
# room and microphones, and are therefore not sixteen independent
# observations. The chunk sits between paragraphs: placed inside one,
# as it once was, it split a sentence across two paragraphs.
dcor <- local({
  r_ci <- function(x, y) {
    ct <- cor.test(x, y)
    list(r = unname(ct$estimate), lo = ct$conf.int[[1]],
         hi = ct$conf.int[[2]], df = unname(ct$parameter))
  }
  d <- der_report |>
    mutate(series = substr(meeting_id, 1, nchar(meeting_id) - 1))
  within <- d |>
    group_by(series) |>
    summarise(r = if (dplyr::n() > 2) cor(overlap_fraction, der) else NA_real_,
              .groups = "drop")
  list(der    = r_ci(d$overlap_fraction, d$der),
       missed = r_ci(d$overlap_fraction, d$missed_speech),
       fa     = r_ci(d$overlap_fraction, d$false_alarm),
       conf   = r_ci(d$overlap_fraction, d$speaker_confusion),
       n_series      = dplyr::n_distinct(d$series),
       within_median = median(within$r, na.rm = TRUE))
})
# A correlation with its interval, each bound printed as r_apa() prints
# the coefficient (no leading zero, a true minus sign).
rfmt <- function(z)
  sprintf("%s, 95%%&nbsp;CI [%s, %s]", r_apa(z$r), r_apa(z$lo), r_apa(z$hi))
# The paragraph after next describes the design in words ("sixteen test
# meetings are four series of four sessions").
stopifnot(nrow(der_report) == 16, dcor$n_series == 4,
          all(table(substr(der_report$meeting_id, 1,
                           nchar(der_report$meeting_id) - 1)) == 4))
# And the two paragraphs describe the correlations in words: overlap and
# DER covary strongly (r above 0.5), which the closing paragraph of
# qualifications also relies on when it says the error tracks overlap
# closely; missed speech carries the association more than confusion
# does, and false alarm runs the other way; and within series the
# association persists.
stopifnot(dcor$der$r > 0.5,
          dcor$missed$r > dcor$conf$r, dcor$conf$r > 0, dcor$fa$r < 0,
          dcor$within_median > 0)
# "Overlap is substantially confounded with series": series accounts for
# most of the variance in overlap between meetings. "The EN2002 sessions
# being both the most overlapped and among the most error-prone": the
# series' four sessions are the four most overlapped meetings, the
# series has the highest mean DER of the four, and each of its sessions
# lies in the more error-prone half of the meetings.
der_series <- substr(der_report$meeting_id, 1, nchar(der_report$meeting_id) - 1)
der_en2002 <- der_series == "EN2002"
der_series_der <- tapply(der_report$der, der_series, mean)
stopifnot(
  summary(lm(der_report$overlap_fraction ~ der_series))$r.squared > 0.5,
  sum(der_en2002) == 4,
  all(rank(-der_report$overlap_fraction)[der_en2002] <= sum(der_en2002)),
  names(which.max(der_series_der)) == "EN2002",
  all(rank(-der_report$der)[der_en2002] <= nrow(der_report) / 2))
# "Meetings with more overlap also have more and shorter turns", strongly
# enough that the two cannot be separated (|r| above 0.5): turns are the
# report's annotated utterances, counted per second of meeting and
# measured by the speech each carries. speech_s is the union of the
# turns, which counts overlapped time once, so overlap would shorten the
# turns by construction; the overlapped time is therefore added back
# (overlap_fraction is a share of speech_s), counting it twice.
stopifnot(all(c("n_utterances", "duration_s", "speech_s") %in%
                names(der_report)))
der_turns <- with(der_report, c(
  more    = cor(overlap_fraction, n_utterances / duration_s),
  shorter = cor(overlap_fraction,
                speech_s * (1 + overlap_fraction) / n_utterances)))
stopifnot(der_turns[["more"]] > 0.5, der_turns[["shorter"]] < -0.5)
```

Per-meeting rates ranged from
`r pct(min(der_report$der))` to
`r pct(max(der_report$der))`, and
much of that variation goes with how much of a meeting is spoken over
(@fig-der-permeeting). Across the
`r num_word(nrow(der_report))` meetings, overlapped speech and
diarisation error rate covary
strongly, at *r*(`r dcor$der$df`) =
`r rfmt(dcor$der)`. The association is
carried by missed speech
(*r* = `r rfmt(dcor$missed)`) and to a
lesser degree by speaker confusion
(*r* = `r rfmt(dcor$conf)`), while the
association with false alarm is negative
(*r* = `r rfmt(dcor$fa)`).

Those intervals are wide, and they are also optimistic. The 16
test meetings are four series of
four sessions each, recorded with the same participants in the same
room on the same headsets, so they are not 16 independent
observations. The effective sample is closer to four. Overlap is
substantially confounded with series, the EN2002 sessions being both
the most overlapped and among the most error-prone. Within series the
association persists, at a median correlation of
`r r_apa(dcor$within_median)`
across the four, which is reassuring but rests on four observations
apiece. A related predictor cannot be separated from overlap here
either, since meetings with more overlap also have more and shorter
turns, which is independently hard for embedding-based clustering. The
relationship should therefore be read as a robust association in this
corpus, and not as an estimate of an effect size, still less as
evidence that overlap alone causes the error.

The direction of the pattern is nonetheless what the architecture
predicts. Instead of scoring each speaker separately, the
segmentation model of pyannote 3.1 assigns each frame of a 10-s
window to one of an enumerated set of speaker combinations, a powerset
formulation [@plaquetPowersetMulticlassCross2023], and that set admits
at most two speakers at once. Speech from a third concurrent voice
therefore has no category it can be assigned to, and is lost rather
than misattributed, which is why the association is carried by missed
speech. The negative association with false alarm follows
mechanically, since a meeting dense with overlap leaves less silence
in which a false alarm can occur. This relationship could not have
been observed under the utterance-concatenation arrangement described
below, whose reconstructions contain no overlapping speech at all.

```{r der-derived, include=FALSE}
# Every figure quoted in the three paragraphs below, read from the same
# artefacts the tables use.  Quoting them by hand is how the sweep
# values and the prose drift apart between runs.
sw <- function(df, thr, pause = NULL, col = "macro_der") {
  # The defaults row of each sweep carries NA for every hyperparameter,
  # so the matches below must tolerate NA rather than propagate them into
  # the subset.
  near <- function(x, target) !is.na(x) & abs(x - target) < 1e-9
  keep <- near(df$clustering_threshold, thr)
  if (!is.null(pause)) keep <- keep & near(df$min_duration_off, pause)
  one(df[[col]][keep], paste(col, "at threshold", thr, "pause", pause))
}
oracle_worse <- local({
  m <- dplyr::inner_join(der_report[, c("meeting_id", "der")],
                         der_oracle_report[, c("meeting_id", "der")],
                         by = "meeting_id", suffix = c("_base", "_oracle"))
  stopifnot(nrow(m) == nrow(der_report), nrow(m) == nrow(der_oracle_report))
  list(n_worse = sum(m$der_oracle > m$der_base),
       n_total = nrow(m),
       best_base = min(m$der_base),
       best_oracle = m$der_oracle[which.min(m$der_base)])
})
# Defaults row in the second sweep carries no threshold value.
sweep2_default <- one(der_sweep2$macro_der[is.na(der_sweep2$clustering_threshold)],
                      "defaults row of the second DER sweep")
pct2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * one(x))
pct1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * one(x))
# The design of the two development sweeps, described in words below.
# The scan's setting rows, without its defaults row.
der_scan        <- der_sweep[!is.na(der_sweep$clustering_threshold), ]
der_grid1_thr   <- sort(unique(der_scan$clustering_threshold))
der_grid2_thr   <- sort(unique(na.omit(der_sweep2$clustering_threshold)))
der_grid2_pause <- sort(unique(na.omit(der_sweep2$min_duration_off)))
der_n_configs   <- der_sel$n_configurations + der_sel2$n_configurations
stopifnot(der_sel$n_configurations == nrow(der_sweep),
          der_sel2$n_configurations == nrow(der_sweep2),
          # the second grid is its thresholds crossed with its pauses,
          # plus the defaults row
          nrow(der_sweep2) ==
            length(der_grid2_thr) * length(der_grid2_pause) + 1)
# What tuning bought against what the reconstruction moved (MS-08): the
# development-selected configuration against the shipped defaults on
# the held-out split, and on the development split itself.
der_tune_gain_test <- der_tuned$macro_der - der_summary$macro_der
der_tune_gain_dev  <- sweep2_default - sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0)
der_recon_effect   <- der_concat$macro_der - der_summary$macro_der
# Claims the next paragraphs make in words, kept true of the artefacts:
# every meeting's speaker count was overestimated; the oracle left
# missed speech and false alarm unchanged to five decimals and more
# than doubled confusion; tuning lost on the held-out split, by under a
# tenth of a point (in the Discussion, "indistinguishable from them and
# fractionally worse"), and gained under a tenth of a point on the
# development split.
stopifnot(
  all(der_report$hyp_n_speakers > der_report$n_speakers),
  round(der_oracle$macro_missed, 5) == round(der_summary$macro_missed, 5),
  round(der_oracle$macro_fa, 5) == round(der_summary$macro_fa, 5),
  der_oracle$macro_confusion > 2 * der_summary$macro_confusion,
  der_tune_gain_test > 0, der_tune_gain_test < 0.001,
  der_tune_gain_dev >= 0, der_tune_gain_dev < 0.001)
# And of the development sweeps: the scan is lowest at a threshold of
# 0.7, and 0.8 finds fewer speakers but more error; the finer grid's best
# cell is 0.70 with no minimum pause, which is the configuration scored
# as tuned on the test split; at 0.70 a half-second pause recovers missed
# speech but adds more false alarm, so the total rises; and the
# reconstruction moves macro DER by far more (over tenfold) than tuning
# gained. Where a file lacks a setting, one() stops instead of letting
# an empty comparison pass.
der_best2 <- c(thr   = one(der_sel2$best$clustering_threshold),
               pause = one(der_sel2$best$min_duration_off))
der_tuned_set <- c(
  thr   = one(der_tuned$hyperparameters$clustering$threshold),
  pause = one(der_tuned$hyperparameters$segmentation$min_duration_off))
stopifnot(
  abs(der_scan$clustering_threshold[which.min(der_scan$macro_der)] - 0.7) < 1e-9,
  sw(der_sweep, 0.8, col = "mean_hyp_speakers") <
    sw(der_sweep, 0.7, col = "mean_hyp_speakers"),
  sw(der_sweep, 0.8) > sw(der_sweep, 0.7),
  abs(der_best2[["thr"]] - 0.7) < 1e-9, der_best2[["pause"]] == 0,
  abs(der_tuned_set - der_best2) < 1e-9,
  sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0.5, "macro_missed") < sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0, "macro_missed"),
  sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0.5, "macro_fa") - sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0, "macro_fa") >
    sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0, "macro_missed") - sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0.5, "macro_missed"),
  sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0.5) > sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0),
  der_recon_effect > 10 * der_tune_gain_dev)
# The response to the threshold, "falling gradually to its minimum and
# climbing steeply beyond it": on the scan, and on the finer grid at
# each pause, DER falls at every step up to its lowest point and rises
# at every step after it, and every step down is shallower than every
# step up.
der_asymmetric <- function(thr, der) {
  o <- order(thr)
  slope <- diff(der[o]) / diff(thr[o])
  k <- which.min(der[o])
  down <- slope[seq_len(k - 1)]
  up <- slope[seq_along(slope) >= k]
  length(down) > 0 && length(up) > 0 && all(down < 0) && all(up > 0) &&
    max(-down) < min(up)
}
der_grid2_cells <- der_sweep2[!is.na(der_sweep2$clustering_threshold), ]
stopifnot(
  der_asymmetric(der_scan$clustering_threshold, der_scan$macro_der),
  all(vapply(der_grid2_pause, \(p) {
    cell <- der_grid2_cells[abs(der_grid2_cells$min_duration_off - p) < 1e-9, ]
    der_asymmetric(cell$clustering_threshold, cell$macro_der)
  }, logical(1))))
# "The released defaults already sit within a tenth of a point of the
# optimum of this grid", and in the Discussion "within a tenth of a point
# of the optimum of the grid": the defaults row is within 0.001 of the
# lowest macro DER the second sweep records, the defaults row included,
# so the wording also holds if a re-run makes the defaults the best.
# They are not at it on the committed files, which put the defaults
# 0.065 points above the best cell, as the August files did.
stopifnot(sweep2_default - min(der_sweep2$macro_der) < 0.001)
# "Fourteen distinct configurations": the scan and the grid share the
# threshold of 0.70 with no pause, which both scored, and the pipeline's
# own settings, as the headline run records them, are none of the grid's
# cells, so the defaults row adds one, counted once even when both sweeps
# carry it, as a re-run of the scan does. The text prints the defaults'
# threshold and says they set no minimum pause. The settings are compared
# rounded to six decimals, so that a value written with more digits or
# carried through floating point still matches.
der_default_set <- c(
  thr   = one(der_summary$hyperparameters$clustering$threshold),
  pause = one(der_summary$hyperparameters$segmentation$min_duration_off),
  size  = one(der_summary$hyperparameters$clustering$min_cluster_size))
der_cell_keys <- function(df) {
  df <- df[!is.na(df$clustering_threshold), ]
  paste(round(df$clustering_threshold, 6), round(df$min_duration_off, 6),
        df$min_cluster_size)
}
der_keys_scan <- der_cell_keys(der_sweep)
der_keys_grid <- der_cell_keys(der_sweep2)
der_keys_both <- intersect(der_keys_scan, der_keys_grid)
der_default_key <- paste(round(der_default_set[["thr"]], 6),
                         round(der_default_set[["pause"]], 6),
                         der_default_set[["size"]])
der_n_distinct <- length(unique(c(der_keys_scan, der_keys_grid))) + 1
der_n_shared <- length(der_keys_both) + der_defaults_both
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(der_keys_scan), !anyDuplicated(der_keys_grid),
          length(der_keys_both) == 1,
          der_keys_both == paste(0.7, 0, one(der_sel2$best$min_cluster_size)),
          !der_default_key %in% c(der_keys_scan, der_keys_grid),
          der_default_set[["pause"]] == 0,
          der_n_distinct == nrow(der_sweep) + nrow(der_sweep2) - der_n_shared,
          der_n_configs == nrow(der_sweep) + nrow(der_sweep2))
# The finer grid meeting by meeting (der_sweep2.csv) must be the file its
# summary was written from: each cell holds every development meeting
# once, and their mean is the cell's macro DER to the six decimals both
# files keep. From it come the spread the tuning difference is set
# against, which is the same number of whole points under the best cell
# and under the defaults ("under either setting"), and the number of
# speakers each development meeting holds, which the scan's 0.8 comes
# within a speaker of on average, and closer than 0.7 does ("close to
# the truth").
stopifnot("config_id" %in% names(der_sweep2))
der_pm <- split(der_sweep2_meetings, der_sweep2_meetings$config_id)
stopifnot(
  setequal(names(der_pm), der_sweep2$config_id),
  all(vapply(der_pm, \(x) nrow(x) == der_dev_meetings &&
               !anyDuplicated(x$meeting_id), logical(1))),
  all(abs(vapply(der_pm[der_sweep2$config_id], \(x) mean(x$der), numeric(1)) -
            der_sweep2$macro_der) < 2e-6))
der_dev_span <- vapply(
  c(best     = sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0, "config_id"),
    defaults = one(der_sweep2$config_id[is.na(der_sweep2$clustering_threshold)])),
  \(id) round(100 * diff(range(der_pm[[id]]$der))), numeric(1))
stopifnot(der_dev_span[["best"]] == der_dev_span[["defaults"]])
der_dev_span_pp <- der_dev_span[["best"]]
der_dev_spk <- unique(der_sweep2_meetings[, c("meeting_id", "n_speakers")])
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(der_dev_spk$meeting_id),
          nrow(der_dev_spk) == der_dev_meetings)
der_dev_true_spk <- mean(der_dev_spk$n_speakers)
der_spk_off <- abs(c(t07 = sw(der_sweep, 0.7, col = "mean_hyp_speakers"),
                     t08 = sw(der_sweep, 0.8, col = "mean_hyp_speakers")) -
                     der_dev_true_spk)
stopifnot(der_spk_off[["t08"]] < 1, der_spk_off[["t08"]] < der_spk_off[["t07"]])
# "Roughly a minute of audio per meeting" in the concatenation.
stopifnot(round(one(der_concat$corpus$audio_hours) * 60 /
                  one(der_concat$n_meetings)) == 1)
# "A recording with little crosstalk tends towards the favourable end of
# the range observed here and a busy group discussion towards the other,
# though not every quiet meeting here scored well", and the Discussion's
# "tends to sit below the corpus average and a busy discussion above it":
# the least overlapped quarter of the meetings averages below the macro
# DER and the most overlapped quarter above it, while at least one of the
# least overlapped scores above the macro DER. "A two-person interview,
# which no meeting here resembles": every meeting has three speakers or
# more.
local({
  q    <- nrow(der_report) %/% 4
  o    <- order(der_report$overlap_fraction)
  low  <- der_report$der[head(o, q)]
  high <- der_report$der[tail(o, q)]
  stopifnot(q >= 2, mean(low) < der_summary$macro_der,
            mean(high) > der_summary$macro_der,
            any(low > der_summary$macro_der),
            all(der_report$n_speakers >= 3))
})
```

A common intuition holds that diarisation would improve if the system
were simply told how many people are present, and two results bear on
it. The pipeline overestimated the speaker count in every one of the
`r num_word(nrow(der_report))` meetings, finding
`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(der_report$hyp_n_speakers))`
speakers on average where
`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(der_report$n_speakers))`
were present, which makes the intuition an attractive one. It does not
survive measurement. Constraining the pipeline to the true count
raised macro DER to
`r pct(der_oracle$macro_der)`,
worsening `r oracle_worse$n_worse` of the
`r oracle_worse$n_total` meetings and taking the
best of them from
`r pct1(oracle_worse$best_base)` to
`r pct1(oracle_worse$best_oracle)`. Missed speech and false alarm were unchanged to five
decimal places, as they must be when segmentation is untouched, so the
entire increase fell on speaker confusion, which more than doubled to
`r pct(der_oracle$macro_confusion)`.
The development sweep points the same way from the other direction.
Raising the clustering threshold to 0.8 brought the mean number of
hypothesised speakers down to
`r sprintf("%.1f", sw(der_sweep, 0.8, col = "mean_hyp_speakers"))`,
close to the truth, yet DER rose from
`r pct1(sw(der_sweep, 0.7))` to
`r pct1(sw(der_sweep, 0.8))`. Agglomerative clustering forced towards a
smaller number of clusters must merge until it reaches one, and
merging two distinct speakers is far more costly under DER
than leaving several spurious small clusters, which the optimal
speaker mapping largely discounts. Getting the speaker count right is
not the same thing as getting the diarisation right, and a workflow
that offers a speaker-count option, as this one does, should not
present it as a free improvement.

Tuning was attempted and did not repay the effort.
`r Num_word(der_n_distinct)` distinct configurations were scored on the
`r num_word(der_dev_meetings)` development meetings: the pipeline's
own defaults, which set the threshold at
`r sprintf("%.3f", der_default_set[["thr"]])` with no minimum pause, a
scan of the clustering threshold from `r min(der_grid1_thr)` to
`r max(der_grid1_thr)`, and a grid crossing thresholds of
`r and_list(sprintf("%.2f", der_grid2_thr))` with a minimum
pause of `r and_list(as.character(der_grid2_pause))` s. The scan and
the grid share one cell, a threshold of 0.70 with no pause`r if (der_defaults_both) ", and both scored the defaults beside their own cells" else ""`. The response
to the threshold is
asymmetric, falling gradually to its minimum and climbing steeply
beyond it, with macro DER of `r pct1(sw(der_sweep, 0.5))`
at 0.5, `r pct1(sw(der_sweep, 0.7))`
at 0.7 and `r pct1(sw(der_sweep, 0.9))`
at 0.9. The best cell, a threshold of 0.70 with no minimum pause,
reached `r pct2(sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0))`
against `r pct2(sweep2_default)` for
the shipped defaults, a difference of under a tenth of a percentage
point, where the development meetings themselves differ by as much as
`r num_word(der_dev_span_pp)` points under either setting. Raising the
minimum pause behaved exactly as
its definition implies, recovering missed speech by merging short
gaps into turns, from
`r pct2(sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0, "macro_missed"))`
to `r pct2(sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0.5, "macro_missed"))`
at a threshold of 0.70, while adding more false alarm than it
recovered, from
`r pct2(sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0, "macro_fa"))`
to `r pct2(sw(der_sweep2, 0.7, 0.5, "macro_fa"))`,
so that the total rose. That trade is if anything flattered here,
because the silence between annotated turns in the reconstruction is
digital, with no room tone in it. Scoring the development-selected
configuration once on the held-out test split gave a macro DER of
`r pct2(der_tuned$macro_der)`,
against
`r pct2(der_summary$macro_der)`
for the untuned pipeline, a difference of
`r sprintf("%.4f", 100 * der_tune_gain_test)` percentage points and in
the unfavourable direction. All four
configurations are set out together in @tbl-der-summary. The released
defaults already sit within a tenth of a point of the optimum of this
grid, so a workflow that adopts them has little to gain from tuning
them, and the effort is better spent on the reconstruction of the
evaluation corpus, which moves the figure far more, as the next
paragraph shows.

How the corpus is reconstructed matters more than any tuning of these
settings. Running the same pipeline over the same
`r num_word(nrow(der_report))` meetings
rebuilt instead by concatenating the first 25 utterances of
each with a half-second silent gap, the arrangement this benchmark
used initially, gives a macro DER of
`r pct(der_concat$macro_der)`
and a micro DER of
`r pct(der_concat$micro_der)`,
with every component higher. Concatenation removes all overlapping
speech and leaves roughly a minute of audio per meeting from which to
estimate speaker embeddings, and the penalty for those departures from
the real task, `r ppt(der_recon_effect)` percentage points of macro
DER, exceeds by far the `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * der_tune_gain_dev)`
points that tuning gained on the development split. Both
reconstructions also change the microphone channel wherever the speaker
changes, as the next paragraph explains, so that cue is present in both
figures. It may still help more in the concatenation, where a
half-second silent gap separates every change of channel and no speech
overlaps. The figure concatenation produces should not be read as a diarisation
result, and it is reported here only to quantify the distance between
the two protocols.

Several things qualify the headline figure. Because the release
distributes only annotated spans, the gaps between turns in the
reconstruction are digital silence and not room tone. An audit of the
reconstructed audio against its annotation confirmed it: in every one
of the `r recon_test$summary$n_meetings` test and
`r recon_val$summary$n_meetings` development meetings, the share of
unannotated frames whose samples are all exactly zero is
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(recon_test$summary$min_silence_exact_zero, recon_val$summary$min_silence_exact_zero))`,
and the alignment of audio with annotation is best at no shift in
`r recon_test$summary$n_best_shift_zero + recon_val$summary$n_best_shift_zero`
of the `r recon_test$summary$n_meetings + recon_val$summary$n_meetings`
meetings. Voice activity detection therefore faces an easier problem
in those gaps than it would on a continuous recording, and the false
alarm component should be read as a lower bound. Each turn is also
written from its speaker's own headset, so the channel changes wherever
the speaker does, a cue the speaker-embedding model can use and that a
single shared microphone would not provide. The collar, at
`r der_collar / 2` s either side of each boundary, is narrower than
the NIST collar of the same nominal size and wider than the
collar-free convention used in some diarisation reporting, so these
values are directly comparable with published figures computed under
neither. Finally,
overlapped regions are scored throughout, which is the
stricter of the two conventions and the reason the error tracks
overlap so closely.

In practice the implication is that a single headline rate is a poor
guide. Error rises with simultaneous speech, so a recording with little
crosstalk tends towards the favourable end of the range observed here
and a busy group discussion towards the other, though not every quiet
meeting here scored well. A two-person interview, which no meeting here
resembles, would be expected to sit nearer the favourable end, an
expectation this corpus cannot test.
Researchers relying on speaker labels should verify DER on a
representative subsample of their own recordings instead of assuming
the corpus average, and should treat the labels as an aid to
navigation, never as evidence in their own right.

Repairing the attribution after the fact is no substitute for that
check. @efstathiadisLLMbasedSpeakerDiarization2025 fine-tuned a
language model to correct speaker attribution in already-transcribed
conversations and cut word-level attribution error substantially on
transcripts from the recognisers the correction had been trained on,
while an ensemble of those models reduced the same error by only about
6% on a recogniser it had not seen. A correction layer of that kind
therefore inherits the recogniser it was fitted to, much as the
lexical post-processing of [the Post-Processing Beyond English section](#sec-multilingual) inherits its language.

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-der-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Speaker Diarisation on the AMI IHM Test Split"
der_row <- function(label, s) {
  tibble::tibble(
    Configuration = label,
    `Macro DER`   = pct(s$macro_der),
    `Micro DER`   = pct(s$micro_der),
    Missed        = pct(s$macro_missed),
    `False alarm` = pct(s$macro_fa),
    Confusion     = pct(s$macro_confusion)
  )
}
dplyr::bind_rows(
  der_row("Pipeline defaults", der_summary),
  der_row("Tuned on development split", der_tuned),
  der_row("Known speaker count (oracle)", der_oracle),
  der_row("Utterance concatenation, defaults", der_concat)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", rep("r", 5)))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r der_cap`

\needspace{0.75\textheight}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3.4}
#| label: fig-der-permeeting
#| fig-cap: "Diarisation Error Components Across AMI Test Meetings"
component_cols <- c(
  "Missed"      = "#2c3e50",
  "False alarm" = "#7f8c8d",
  "Confusion"   = "#bdc3c7"
)
der_report |>
  arrange(overlap_fraction) |>
  mutate(meeting = factor(
    sprintf("%s\n%s", meeting_id,
            scales::percent(overlap_fraction, accuracy = 1)),
    levels = sprintf("%s\n%s", meeting_id,
                     scales::percent(overlap_fraction, accuracy = 1))
  )) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(missed_speech, false_alarm, speaker_confusion),
    names_to  = "component",
    values_to = "rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(component = dplyr::recode(component,
    missed_speech     = "Missed",
    false_alarm       = "False alarm",

  ) |> factor(levels = names(component_cols))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = meeting, y = rate, fill = component)) +
    geom_col() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = component_cols, name = NULL) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "DER component") +
    theme_paper() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r der_meetings_cap`

The timestamp benchmark evaluated segment-boundary accuracy for
Whisper Large v3 on
`r ts_summary$n` utterances of the same AMI IHM test split, all from
its first meeting, `r ts_ami$meetings`, so the figures below describe
one meeting and its `r num_word(length(ts_ami$speakers))` speakers.
Start boundaries came in at a mean absolute error
of
`r round(ts_summary$mae_start * 1000, 1)` ms. At the
end boundary the mean absolute error was
`r round(ts_summary$mae_end * 1000, 0)` ms, but
that figure describes neither the typical utterance nor the failure,
and the distribution behind it matters more than its average. Median
absolute end error is
`r round(ts_summary$median_abs_end_error * 1000, 0)`
ms, so half the utterances land within a hundredth of a second of the
reference boundary. The mean is more than 10 times larger because
`r round(ts_summary$gross_end_error_rate * 100, 1)`%
of utterances are out by more than half a second, and those few
contribute the large majority of it. What the end boundary shows is
therefore a small number of gross failures, with no systematic offset
behind it, which also means that no constant correction could remove it.
Subtracting the mean would move the many accurate boundaries away
from the truth in order to flatter the few inaccurate ones.

Those failures all run in one direction. The
error is measured as the reference duration minus the hypothesised
end, so a positive value means the model stopped before the speech did,
and on this corpus every gross end error was of that sign. The
truncation rate,
`r round(ts_summary$truncation_rate * 100, 1)`%,
equals the gross error rate exactly. In the worst cases the
hypothesis covered
`r pct(min(ts_cov))`
of the reference segment. The
failure is thus early truncation, the model ceasing to transcribe
part-way through an utterance. That it is never instead a run-on past
the true boundary is a property of the benchmark and not a finding
about the model. Each utterance is scored as an isolated clip whose
reference end coincides with the end of the audio, so there is no
material beyond the boundary for the model to continue into, and the
largest negative end error over the whole set is
`r round(1000 * ts_overrun)` ms, about half of the
`r round(1000 * ts_step)` ms step on which Whisper places its
timestamps. The one utterance left unscored shows the failure the
design cannot score: on a `r sprintf("%.1f", ts_skip_s)` s clip whose
reference is the single word *yeah*, Whisper wrote *ha*
`r length(ts_skip_tok)` times and never closed the segment with an end
timestamp. Whether Whisper over-runs a boundary inside continuous audio
is a question this design cannot ask, and it shares that limitation
with the start boundary discussed below. The root-mean-square error at
the end boundary, which squares each error before averaging and so
weights the tail heavily, is correspondingly large at
`r round(ts_summary$rmse_end * 1000, 0)` ms and
reflects the same few utterances. @fig-timestamps shows the
distribution directly, as a near-vertical rise at the origin holding
most of the corpus, then a long right tail and nothing to the left of
it.

```{r timestamp-captions, include=FALSE}
# Captions for the figure and table below, built from the artefacts:
# how many utterances were scored, and which meeting and speakers they
# come from, read from the utterance ids of the per-utterance report.
stopifnot(nrow(ts_report) == ts_summary$n, length(ts_ami$meetings) == 1,
          # the text says every gross end error was a truncation
          ts_summary$truncation_rate == ts_summary$gross_end_error_rate)
ts_fig_cap <- paste0(
  "IHM = individual headset microphone. ",
  "Empirical cumulative distribution of signed segment-end error over the ",
  big(ts_summary$n), " AMI IHM test utterances (Whisper Large v3), all of ",
  "which come from the single meeting ", ts_ami$meetings, ". Positive ",
  "values mean the hypothesis ended before the reference did. The dashed ",
  "line marks the half-second threshold above which an error is counted as ",
  "gross. The horizontal axis is clipped at one second, beyond which a ",
  "small number of utterances continue out to the maximum error.")
ts_tbl_cap <- paste0(
  "IHM = individual headset microphone. ",
  "Timestamp alignment benchmark summary for Whisper Large v3 on ",
  big(ts_summary$n), " AMI IHM test utterances. The benchmark reads the ",
  "test split in order and stops at ", big(ts_first), " utterances, of ",
  "which ", big(ts_summary$n), " are scored, so every utterance comes from ",
  "the first meeting, ", ts_ami$meetings, ", and from its ",
  num_word(length(ts_ami$speakers)), " speakers, so the figures describe ",
  "one meeting rather than the split. Errors are in milliseconds. The ",
  "median and the tail rates are reported beside the means because the ",
  "end-boundary distribution is dominated by a small number of gross ",
  "failures.")
```

\needspace{0.75\textheight}

```{r fig-timestamps, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.0, fig.cap="Distribution of Segment-End Error on the AMI IHM Test Sample"}
ts_ecdf <- tibble::tibble(err = ts_report$end_error_s) |>
  arrange(err) |>
  mutate(cdf = (dplyr::row_number() - 0.5) / dplyr::n())

end_lines <- tibble(
  boundary = c(0, 0.5),
  meaning = c("Reference end", "Gross-error threshold"))

ggplot(ts_ecdf, aes(x = err, y = cdf)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.6, colour = "#1F4E79") +
  geom_vline(data = end_lines, aes(xintercept = boundary, linetype = meaning),
             colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = NULL,
    breaks = end_lines$meaning,
    values = c("Reference end" = "solid", "Gross-error threshold" = "dashed")) +
  # Labels as precise as the breaks need (a quarter-second step prints
  # as 0.25, not 0.2), with a true minus for any negative tick.
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.1, 1.0), oob = scales::oob_keep,
                     labels = label_number(style_negative = "minus")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(x = "Segment-end error (s), positive = stopped early",
       y = "Cumulative share of utterances") +
  theme_paper()
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r ts_fig_cap`

@tbl-ts-summary collects these quantities. Early truncation bears on
what a workflow can do about it. The repetition-detection
stage of the post-processing pipeline suppresses run-on
continuations, which is the opposite failure and therefore no remedy
here. Truncation leaves the transcript short, and
post-processing cannot restore words the model never emitted. What
the workflow can do is notice. The review pass compares the end of the
final segment against the duration of the recording, and a transcript
that stops well short of it is flagged for the analyst before it is
passed on as complete.

The start-boundary figure deserves a caveat, not a boast.
Each utterance is scored as an isolated clip whose reference starts
at zero, and the model returns a start of exactly zero for the large
majority of them, so the start error is zero by construction in
those cases and the millisecond-scale mean says little about how
well the model would locate a boundary inside continuous audio. The
end boundary, which the model has to locate for itself, is where the
informative signal lies.

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-ts-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Timestamp Alignment on the AMI IHM Test Sample"
# Every field is checked in setup, so none can fall back to a
# placeholder here.
ts_val <- function(key, digits = 1, scale = 1000)
  as.character(round(one(ts_summary[[key]], key) * scale, digits))
tibble::tribble(
  ~Metric,                              ~Value,
  "Utterances evaluated",               as.character(ts_summary$n),
  "Mean absolute error, start (ms)",    ts_val("mae_start"),
  "Mean absolute error, end (ms)",      ts_val("mae_end"),
  "Median absolute end (ms)",           ts_val("median_abs_end_error"),
  "90th percentile end (ms)",           ts_val("p90_abs_end_error"),
  "Gross end errors > 0.5 s (%)",       ts_val("gross_end_error_rate", 1, 100),
  "Early truncations (%)",              ts_val("truncation_rate", 1, 100),
  "Root-mean-square error, start (ms)", ts_val("rmse_start"),
  "Root-mean-square error, end (ms)",   ts_val("rmse_end"),
  "ASR model",                          ts_summary$model
) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Metric", "Value"), align = c("l", "r"))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r ts_tbl_cap`

The modular structure of the evaluation pipeline means that these
metrics can be updated independently of the WER evaluation as
model versions change. Each timestamped JSON the workflow writes
carries a provenance block naming the model, the Hub snapshot it was
loaded from and, when speakers are attributed, the source and
snapshots of the diarisation pipeline, so that a change of model or
snapshot is reflected in the artefacts.

## Evaluating the Masking Layer {#sec-masking}

```{r load-masking, include=FALSE}
# The three masking summaries (dictionary only, case-insensitive, and
# with the zero-shot NER stage) are loaded and checked in setup. They
# are the benchmark as regenerated after the audit (a08265c): names are
# also placed after an opening quotation mark or parenthesis, the
# dictionary pool holds the curated names under three characters, and
# held-out names carry a label of their own (audit findings EPRIV-10,
# T1-07, EPRIV-19). The seed-42 sample drew none of those short names,
# though (the shortest name in masking_report.csv has three letters), so
# the benchmark does not probe them, and nothing here says it does.
# A whole-number percentage without its sign, for the masking prose. It
# is named apart from the setup chunk's pct(), which it once shadowed
# for the rest of the document (audit finding MS-18).
pct0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * one(x))
stopifnot(ms$seed == 42L)   # "the same seed" as the sweep's --seed 42
m_recall  <- pct0(ms$overall$recall)
m_leak    <- pct0(ms$overall$leakage)
m_title   <- pct0(ms$by_casing$title$recall)
ci_recall <- pct0(msci$overall$recall)
ci_lower  <- pct0(msci$by_casing$lower$recall)

# What the section says in words, kept true of the summaries. The
# masker redacts an injected name if and only if it is title-cased and
# in the dictionary: no held-out or lower-case name is redacted, and
# every in-dictionary title-case one is (half the in-dictionary
# injections, since every name is injected in both casings). Every
# subset that cuts across both conditions, the bare and possessive
# forms and each carrier position, the quoted and bracketed ones among
# them, reproduces the pooled rate, compared as counts so that no
# rounding enters. Relaxing the capitalisation costs no precision on
# these carriers, and the gated NER stage redacts no lower-case name.
# Each test is wrapped in isTRUE() because these fields are not among
# those setup requires, and a comparison with a missing one is empty,
# which stopifnot() would let pass.
m_positions <- names(ms$by_position)
m_pooled <- function(cell)
  isTRUE(cell$hits * ms$overall$n == ms$overall$hits * cell$n)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(ms$by_in_db$out_of_db$hits == 0),
  isTRUE(ms$by_casing$lower$hits == 0),
  isTRUE(ms$by_casing$title$n == ms$by_casing$lower$n),
  isTRUE(ms$overall$hits == ms$by_in_db$in_db$n / 2),
  all(c("bare", "possessive") %in% names(ms$by_morphology)),
  all(c("quoted", "bracketed") %in% m_positions),
  all(vapply(c(ms$by_morphology[c("bare", "possessive")], ms$by_position),
             m_pooled, logical(1))),
  isTRUE(msci$overall$false_positives == 0),
  isTRUE(msner$by_casing$lower$hits == 0))

# The masking arms whose summaries record a working tree with uncommitted
# changes, which the Data and code availability section names; the
# sentence there needs at least one, and is to be dropped if a clean
# re-run leaves none.
ms_dirty <- c(default            = ms$run_metadata$git_dirty,
              `case-insensitive` = msci$run_metadata$git_dirty,
              `named-entity`     = msner$run_metadata$git_dirty)
stopifnot(is.logical(ms_dirty), length(ms_dirty) == 3, !anyNA(ms_dirty))
if (!any(ms_dirty))
  stop("No masking arm now records a dirty tree; drop the sentence on ",
       "uncommitted changes in Data and code availability", call. = FALSE)
# The sentence explains the flag: the record counts any changed tracked
# file (provenance.git_commit, git status --untracked-files=no), and an
# arm records it after an earlier arm of the same run has rewritten the
# committed results in output/evaluation. At 2e5e852 the default arm
# recorded a clean tree and the case-insensitive arm, at the same commit,
# a dirty one; the named-entity arms ran at 41cb9ae and eaef44a, which
# touch only tests/, and a08265c then committed the eight result files.
# That explanation holds only while the default arm, which runs first,
# records a clean tree. The verb and pronouns follow the number of arms.
stopifnot(!ms_dirty[["default"]])
ms_dirty_one <- sum(ms_dirty) == 1
ms_dirty_txt <- paste0(
  "The ", and_list(names(ms_dirty)[ms_dirty]),
  if (ms_dirty_one)
    " arm of the masking benchmark also records that its working tree held uncommitted changes when it ran"
  else
    " arms of the masking benchmark also record that their working tree held uncommitted changes when they ran")

# The optional zero-shot NER stage, which addresses the closed-dictionary
# blind spot.
ner_recall  <- pct0(msner$overall$recall)
ner_out     <- pct0(msner$by_in_db$out_of_db$recall)
ner_prec    <- pct0(msner$overall$precision)
ner_leak    <- pct0(msner$overall$leakage)
ner_title   <- pct0(msner$by_casing$title$recall)

# The NER stage's false positives on the transcript of a podcast episode
# whose two voices are synthetic (see Ethics), read from the
# measurement's own record (output/case_study/ner_false_positive_test.md):
# the redactions and genuine names of the dictionary alone and of the
# NER stage without and with the capitalisation gate, from its
# three-column results table. Only that table is read: the recalls the
# note quotes further down predate the regenerated benchmark (a08265c).
# The note calls the transcript "natural speech"; the text does not.
# The measurement ran over output/case_study/ep05_raw_text.txt, the text
# of the August run of the case study (ARC job 8441879), which stays
# committed beside the note for that reason, as the Availability section
# says. The case study's other files are those of the re-run of
# 18 October 2026 (9124852), whose text differs from it in places, and
# the note says the measurement was not repeated on that text. Should it be, update the
# note's table and re-check the two paragraphs on the NER stage's false
# positives below and that Availability sentence.
md_table_row <- function(lines, label) {
  rows <- strsplit(trimws(lines[startsWith(trimws(lines), "|")]), "|",
                   fixed = TRUE)
  rows <- lapply(rows, \(x) trimws(x[nzchar(trimws(x))]))
  hit <- Filter(\(x) length(x) == 3 && x[[1]] == label, rows)
  if (length(hit) != 1)
    stop("ner_false_positive_test.md has no single row '", label, "'",
         call. = FALSE)
  as.integer(hit[[1]][2:3])
}
ner_dict    <- md_table_row(ner_fp_note, "Dictionary only")
ner_ungated <- md_table_row(ner_fp_note, "\\+ NER, no capitalisation gate")
ner_gated   <- md_table_row(ner_fp_note,
                            "\\+ NER, capitalisation gate (shipped default)")
ner_fp_extra   <- ner_ungated[[1]] - ner_dict[[1]]
ner_fp_genuine <- ner_dict[[2]]
ner_dict_fp    <- ner_dict[[1]] - ner_dict[[2]]
# "every one of the further redactions was a false positive": the
# ungated stage found no genuine name the dictionary had not. "Under
# that gate the stage adds no redaction to this transcript at all": the
# gated stage redacts exactly what the dictionary does. "one was not:
# *Jordan*" and "The one false redaction left": exactly one of the
# dictionary's redactions names no one, and the note names that word as
# the third. The Availability section says the count was not repeated
# on the later run's text, as the note does.
stopifnot(ner_ungated[[2]] == ner_dict[[2]], ner_dict_fp == 1,
          identical(ner_gated, ner_dict),
```
