```{r load-masking, include=FALSE}
          any(grepl("The third is \"Jordan\"", ner_fp_note, fixed = TRUE)),
          any(grepl("the measurement was not repeated on it", ner_fp_note,
                    fixed = TRUE)))
masking_cap <- paste0(
  "Name-masking layer scored as a personally-identifying-information ",
  "detection task by reproducible name injection (seed ", ms$seed, "). ",
  "Recall is the proportion of injected names redacted, leakage its ",
  "complement, and *n* the number of injections in the subset. Precision is ",
  "undefined, and its cell left blank, wherever the masker proposed no ",
  "redaction at all in the subset; where it is defined it is an upper ",
  "bound, because the carrier sentences contain no confusable content ",
  "tokens.")
```

The personal-name masking described in the Methods is the workflow's
privacy contribution, and it is evaluated here as a detection task,
not asserted. Because a hand-annotated gold standard would be
small and subjective, the masker is probed by injection. Personal
names, some drawn from the curated dictionary and some from a held-out
list of names absent from it, are inserted into carrier sentences at
`r num_word(length(m_positions))` positions and in both title-case and
lower-case. Two of the positions put the name directly after an
opening quotation mark or parenthesis, as in reported speech or an
aside, where an earlier version of the masker looked for the capital
on the mark, not on the name, and so let such names through. The
masker is then run, and a redaction of the injected token is scored
as a hit. The
realised design holds
`r big(ms$by_in_db$in_db$n)`
in-dictionary against
`r big(ms$by_in_db$out_of_db$n)`
out-of-dictionary injections, divided evenly between title-case and
lower-case. Recall
is the proportion of injected names redacted, precision the proportion
of redactions that fell on an injected name, and leakage the
complementary false-negative rate that a confidentiality-bound
researcher cares about most.

The result is given in @tbl-masking, and it is governed entirely by the
two design choices the masker makes explicit. The dictionary is closed,
so a name it has never seen is never redacted, and recall on the
held-out names is zero. The detector also requires an initial capital,
so a name the recogniser happens to emit in lower case is never
redacted, and recall on lower-cased names is zero against
`r m_title`% on title-cased names. On these carriers the two
conditions are together necessary and sufficient, so the masker
redacts an injected name if and only if it is title-cased and in the
dictionary. The rule is exact for a name that stands as a word of its
own, judged once any surrounding punctuation and a possessive ending
are set aside. A name joined to a neighbouring word by a hyphen or a
slash, with no space between them, is looked up together with that
word as a single token the dictionary does not hold, and so escapes
even when it is capitalised and listed. The injected carriers contain
no such case. Every subset of
@tbl-masking follows from that rule. Any subset violating either
condition scores zero. The in-dictionary and title-case subsets score
`r pct0(ms$by_in_db$in_db$recall)`% and
`r m_title`% because each still contains names that fail the other
condition. The bare and possessive subsets cut across both conditions
and reproduce the pooled figure exactly, and so does each of the
`r num_word(length(m_positions))` carrier positions, the quoted and
bracketed ones included.

That determinism is what makes the pooled figure across the whole
injected set, `r m_recall`% redacted against `r m_leak`% leaked, a
poor summary. It is an arithmetic consequence of how many injections
fell in each cell, and not an estimate of a rate in the world, and it
would move with any change to the mix of title-case and lower-case or
of in-dictionary and held-out names. The quantities that describe the
masker are the conditional ones, and they are stark, with complete
recall where both conditions hold and none at all where either fails.
What a researcher should take from this is the shape of the failure,
which no percentage conveys, since natural transcripts differ from
these carriers in exactly the respects that decide the outcome.

The injection uses clean, well-punctuated carriers with no confusable
content tokens, so the precision reported here is an upper bound and
not a false-positive rate on natural speech. The experiment is
designed to expose the recall floor, not to estimate the precision
ceiling.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-masking
#| tbl-cap: "Personal-Name Masking by Injection Subset"
# Precision is 0/0 wherever the masker proposed no redaction in a
# subset; printing it as 0.00 would read as a false-positive problem
# where in fact nothing was proposed at all. The cell is left blank, as
# APA 7 asks of a value that does not apply, and the caption says why;
# the "---" it once held printed as an em dash.
cells <- list(ms$overall, ms$by_in_db$in_db, ms$by_in_db$out_of_db,
              ms$by_casing$title, ms$by_casing$lower,
              ms$by_morphology$bare, ms$by_morphology$possessive)
grab <- function(field) vapply(cells, \(x) x[[field]], numeric(1))
prec <- ifelse(grab("replaced_total") > 0,
               sprintf("%.2f", grab("precision")), "")
mtab <- tibble::tibble(
  Subset = c("All injected names", "In dictionary", "Out of dictionary",
             "Title-case", "Lower-case", "Bare", "Possessive"),
  n         = format(grab("n"), big.mark = ","),
  Recall    = sprintf("%.2f", grab("recall")),
  Precision = prec,
  Leakage   = sprintf("%.2f", grab("leakage"))
)
kable(mtab, col.names = c("Subset", "*n*", "Recall", "Precision", "Leakage"),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r masking_cap`

Two of these failure modes are addressable and one is not. An audit of
the files the pipeline emits (`evaluation.audit_artefacts`) recovered,
from the masking logs, the names the pipeline had masked and searched
the de-identified transcripts for them. It found a possessive form
surviving in a transcript whose bare form had been redacted, because
the trailing clitic defeated the dictionary lookup. Stripping the
clitic before the lookup closes that gap, and the benchmark confirms
it, with possessive recall equal to bare-name recall. The
capitalisation requirement can likewise be relaxed. Doing so lifts
overall recall from `r m_recall`% to `r ci_recall`% and lower-case
recall from zero to `r ci_lower`%, at no measurable precision cost on
these carriers, although on natural transcripts a case-insensitive
match would redact more common nouns and the trade-off would be real.
The closed-dictionary blind spot is the hard one, because
redacting names the dictionary has never seen cannot be done by a
larger list. It requires recognising a person from context. The
workflow therefore offers an optional second stage that does so, using
a zero-shot named-entity model small enough to run on a processor
[@zaratianaGLiNERGeneralistModel2024]. It is additive by construction, proposing
further words to redact and never withdrawing one the dictionary
caught, so it can raise recall and can cost precision but cannot
silently reduce what was already removed. Each row of the masking log
records which of the two stages was responsible.

```{r ner-result, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf(
"Scored on the same injected names, the second stage lifts overall
recall from %s%% to %s%% and, more to the point, recall on the held-out
names from zero to %s%%: the blind spot that no larger list could have
addressed is partly closed. Recall on title-cased names rises from %s%%
to %s%%.\n",
m_recall, ner_recall, ner_out, m_title, ner_title))
```

Deciding how far to trust that stage required a second measurement, and
it changed the design. A model asked for people returns person
*references*, not personal *names*, and the difference is invisible on
injected carriers because they contain nothing that could be mistaken
for a name. Run instead over the transcript of a conversational
podcast episode about transcription research, whose two voices are
synthetic (see Ethics), an ungated version of the
stage proposed `r num_word(ner_fp_extra)` further redactions beyond the
dictionary's `r num_word(ner_dict[[1]])`, and every one of the
`r num_word(ner_fp_extra)` was a false positive: *speaker one*, *the
researcher*, *the user*, even *we*. Those are all references to people,
and none is a name. Of the dictionary's own `r num_word(ner_dict[[1]])`,
`r num_word(ner_fp_genuine)` were genuine names and
`r num_word(ner_dict_fp)` was not: *Jordan*, which a speaker gave as an
example of a word a masker might take for a person when the talk is of
the country. These counts come from the measurement's written record,
`output/case_study/ner_false_positive_test.md`, and not from a file an
evaluation module produces.

Every such reference was lower-case and every genuine name was
capitalised, so the stage is held to the same capitalisation gate the
dictionary already applies, and the same option relaxes both together.
Under that gate the stage adds no redaction to this transcript at all,
which is what makes it safe to offer. The one false redaction left,
*Jordan*, is the dictionary's own, and no capitalisation gate could
remove it, because the word is capitalised. The cost is that lower-case
names stay outside the stage's reach, exactly as they are outside the
dictionary's. Relaxing the gate brings them back within reach, at a
false-positive cost at least as high as the ungated stage's just
described, since the relaxed configuration masks every word that stage
masked, and the choice is left to the reader instead of made silently
on their behalf.

The masking layer therefore remains an aid to the analyst's review,
short of a guarantee. It removes the names it recognises, by
whichever route, and this evaluation states both how far that reaches
and what the reaching costs.

The same audit makes a second point about the artefacts themselves.
The masked transcript and its Word rendering are de-identified, but the
timestamped JSON and the WebVTT captions are written from the raw model
output before masking is applied, so they retain whatever names the
recording contained. This is deliberate, because those machine-readable
artefacts exist to support evaluation against a faithful record of what
the model produced, but it means that a researcher who exports the
output tree wholesale exports unredacted material alongside the masked
transcript. Each such JSON declares itself unredacted, and the
workflow also writes a redacted parallel set,
carrying the same timings and speaker labels with the names masked, so
that there is a de-identified artefact to share as well as a
faithful one to evaluate against. A flag suppresses the unredacted set
altogether for deployments that must not retain it. The two are
distinguished inside the file as well as by name, through a top-level
`redacted` field, so a consumer need not infer the status from the
path it was read from.

## Anonymising the Voice {#sec-anonymisation}

```{r load-anon, include=FALSE}
# anonymisation_summary.json and anonymisation_report.csv are loaded and
# checked in setup, where the summary is tied to its report meeting by
# meeting. They come from the benchmark's multi-meeting configuration
# (hpc/runs/anonymisation.env), which takes the first usable utterances
# of every AMI test meeting up to a cap per meeting (audit finding
# EPRIV-03), so that a probe can be searched against recordings from
# other meetings as well as its own (EPRIV-15).
anon_alphas <- names(anon$by_alpha)
anon_get <- function(field)
  vapply(anon_alphas, \(a) one(anon$by_alpha[[a]][[field]],
                               paste("alpha", a, field)), numeric(1),
         USE.NAMES = FALSE)
anon_at <- function(a, field) one(anon$by_alpha[[a]][[field]],
                                  paste("alpha", a, field))
# Lower alpha warps the voice further. anon_contrast is the strongest
# warp short of the strongest, where the text sets self-similarity
# against linkage. anon_up orders the alphas from the strongest warp to
# the mildest, anon_by_strength from the mildest to the strongest.
anon_strong   <- anon_alphas[[which.min(as.numeric(anon_alphas))]]
anon_mild     <- anon_alphas[[which.max(as.numeric(anon_alphas))]]
anon_milder   <- anon_alphas != anon_strong
anon_contrast <- anon_alphas[anon_milder][[
  which.min(as.numeric(anon_alphas[anon_milder]))]]
anon_up          <- order(as.numeric(anon_alphas))
anon_by_strength <- order(as.numeric(anon_alphas), decreasing = TRUE)
stopifnot(all(anon_report$uid %in% anon_report$uid[anon_report$alpha ==
                                                   min(anon_report$alpha)]),
          length(unique(anon_report$uid)) == anon$n_utterances,
          !anyNA(anon_report$level_ratio))
# One row per utterance, for what does not depend on alpha: the
# baseline, the speaker and the meeting. A series is a meeting without
# its session letter (EN2002 for EN2002a to EN2002d).
anon_base <- anon_report[anon_report$alpha == min(anon_report$alpha), ]
anon_series_of <- function(meeting) sub("[a-z]$", "", meeting)

# The sample as the caption and the limitations describe it. AMI ids end
# in the utterance's begin and end times in hundredths of a second, so
# anon_minutes is how far into its meeting the sample reaches. Taking
# each meeting's opening utterances leaves a few speakers dominant.
anon_ends <- vapply(strsplit(anon_base$uid, "_", fixed = TRUE),
                    \(p) if (length(p) == 6) as.numeric(p[[6]]) else NA_real_,
                    numeric(1))
stopifnot(!anyNA(anon_ends))
anon_minutes <- ceiling(max(anon_ends) / 100 / 60)
anon_top3 <- sum(head(sort(table(anon_base$speaker), decreasing = TRUE), 3))
anon_solo_meetings <- sum(tapply(anon_base$speaker, anon_base$meeting,
                                 \(s) length(unique(s))) == 1)

# Linkage and its chance level for each set of candidates a probe is
# searched against: "all" is every other original recording,
# "cross_meeting" only those from other meetings, and
# "cross_meeting_cross_channel" those from other meetings on another
# headset channel (EPRIV-15). Chance is the rate at which a candidate
# drawn at random from those searched shares the probe's speaker,
# averaged over the probes, and a probe whose speaker has no other
# recording among them is left out (EPRIV-04). Both depend on the labels
# alone, so each set has one chance level and one count of probes, the
# same at every alpha and for the untransformed ceiling, and the table
# prints chance once.
anon_link <- function(set, field = "linkage_rate")
  vapply(anon_alphas, \(a) one(
    anon$by_alpha[[a]][["linkage_by_candidates"]][[set]][[field]],
    paste("alpha", a, set, field)), numeric(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
anon_ceiling <- function(set, field = "linkage_rate")
  one(anon$linkage_ceiling[[set]][[field]], paste("ceiling", set, field))
anon_label <- function(set, field) {
  v <- unique(c(anon_link(set, field), anon_ceiling(set, field)))
  if (length(v) != 1)
    stop("anonymisation_summary.json: the ", field, " of the '", set,
         "' candidates differs between alphas or from the ceiling",
         call. = FALSE)
  v
}
anon_chance <- function(set) anon_label(set, "chance")
anon_ratio  <- function(set) anon_link(set) / anon_chance(set)
# The share of the untransformed ceiling's lead over chance that a warp
# leaves standing, near zero where linkage is near chance.
anon_kept_lead <- function(set)
  (anon_link(set) - anon_chance(set)) /
    (anon_ceiling(set) - anon_chance(set))
anon_cross_drop <- max(anon_link("all") - anon_link("cross_meeting"))
# The bound the text gives that fall, in hundredths. It is rounded up,
# not to the nearest, so that "at most" holds of the exact rates, which
# rounding to the nearest hundredth can understate, and of the table's
# rounded cells alike. Rounding to six places first absorbs binary noise.
anon_cross_bound <- ceiling(round(100 * anon_cross_drop, 6)) / 100
# The speakers recorded on a different headset channel in different
# meetings, whose utterances are the probes of the cross-channel set.
anon_switchers <- anon[["speaker_channels"]][["change_channel"]]
anon_switch_series <- unique(anon_series_of(
  anon_base$meeting[anon_base$speaker %in% anon_switchers]))
stopifnot(length(anon_switch_series) == 1,
          anon_label("cross_meeting_cross_channel", "trials") ==
            sum(anon_base$speaker %in% anon_switchers))

# The loop screen (EPRIV-16). Pooling errors over reference words caps
# what substitutions and deletions can add, but not insertions, so a
# recogniser that loops on a short reference can set the corpus rate on
# its own. The benchmark marks a baseline transcript as looped when it
# runs to at least `length_floor` words and more than `length_factor`
# times its reference, writes the mark into the report
# (degenerate_baseline), and computes the guarded figures of the summary
# over the utterances it did not mark, in every arm. Only the baseline
# is screened: a warp that provokes a loop has damaged the transcript,
# and dropping those would hide the cost being measured. The three
# marked here have references of two and three words and hypotheses of
# 148 to 247 (word error rates of 74.0 to 82.3), against 4.0 for the
# worst of the rest, so any length factor from 2 to 73, or any floor up
# to 148 words, marks the same three.
anon_crit <- anon$degenerate_baseline_criterion
anon_loops <- function(hyp, ref)
  hyp >= one(anon_crit[["length_floor"]]) &
    hyp > one(anon_crit[["length_factor"]]) * pmax(ref, 1)
anon_marked <- anon_base[anon_base$degenerate_baseline == 1, ]
anon_kept   <- anon_report[anon_report$degenerate_baseline == 0, ]
anon_n_looped <- nrow(anon_marked)
anon_looped_share <- sum(anon_marked$errors_control) /
  sum(anon_base$errors_control)
stopifnot(
  # the prose speaks of them in the plural
  anon_n_looped >= 2,
  # the mark belongs to an utterance, whatever the alpha
  all(tapply(anon_report$degenerate_baseline, anon_report$uid,
             \(x) length(unique(x))) == 1),
  # the screened arm, the resynthesis control, transcribes exactly as the
  # unmodified audio does, so the text can speak of the latter
  all(anon_report$errors_original == anon_report$errors_control),
  all(anon_report$hypothesis_words_original ==
        anon_report$hypothesis_words_control),
  # the mark is the summary's criterion applied to that arm, and the
  # summary counts what the report marks
  identical(anon_base$degenerate_baseline == 1,
            anon_loops(anon_base$hypothesis_words_control,
                       anon_base$reference_words)),
  all(anon_get("n_degenerate_baselines") == anon_n_looped),
  all(abs(anon_get("degenerate_baseline_error_share") -
            anon_looped_share) < 1e-4))
# "two or three", for the reference lengths of the marked utterances.
anon_word_range <- function(x) {
  r <- range(x)
  if (r[[1]] == r[[2]]) return(num_word(r[[1]]))
  paste(num_word(r[[1]]), if (r[[2]] - r[[1]] == 1) "or" else "to",
        num_word(r[[2]]))
}

# The guarded figures are read from the summary. Re-pooled here from the
# report's errors they agree to the four decimals the summary keeps; its
# cost is the difference of two rounded rates, so it may differ in the
# last of them.
anon_repool <- anon_kept |>
  dplyr::group_by(alpha) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    base   = sum(.data$errors_control) / sum(.data$reference_words),
    warped = sum(.data$errors_anonymised) / sum(.data$reference_words),
    .groups = "drop")
anon_repool <- anon_repool[match(anon_alphas,
                                 as.character(anon_repool$alpha)), ]
anon_guarded_base <- unique(anon_get("wer_baseline_guarded"))
stopifnot(!anyNA(anon_repool$base), length(anon_guarded_base) == 1,
          all(abs(anon_repool$base - anon_guarded_base) < 1e-4),
          all(abs(anon_repool$warped -
                    anon_get("wer_anonymised_guarded")) < 1e-4),
          all(abs(anon_repool$warped - anon_repool$base -
                    anon_get("wer_cost_guarded")) < 2e-4))
# The guarded cost from the mildest warp to the strongest, for the
# sentence that walks through it.
anon_cost_seq <- anon_get("wer_cost_guarded")[anon_by_strength]

# Loops the warp provokes: utterances the baseline did not loop on whose
# warped transcript meets the same criterion. They stay in the guarded
# cost, and anon_wloops gives, for each alpha, how many there are and the
# share of the guarded cost, the warped arm's errors beyond the
# baseline's, that they carry.
anon_wloops <- anon_kept |>
  dplyr::mutate(loop  = anon_loops(.data$hypothesis_words_anonymised,
                                   .data$reference_words),
                extra = .data$errors_anonymised - .data$errors_control) |>
  dplyr::group_by(alpha) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = sum(.data$loop),
                   share = sum(.data$extra[.data$loop]) / sum(.data$extra),
                   .groups = "drop")
anon_wloops <- anon_wloops[match(anon_alphas,
                                 as.character(anon_wloops$alpha)), ]
stopifnot(!anyNA(anon_wloops$n))

# The level the transform returns against its input's, as RMS ratios:
# the summary's mean over the utterances for each alpha, and each
# utterance's in the report. The limiter that keeps the output within
# full scale compresses the samples above its knee, which lowers the
# level of a loud recording. anon_low_series is the meeting series of
# the quietest utterance, and anon_knee_share the part of each alpha's
# compressed samples that lie in it.
anon_lvl_txt <- unique(sprintf("%.2f", anon_get("level_ratio")))
anon_lvl <- anon_report
anon_lvl$series <- anon_series_of(anon_lvl$meeting)
anon_lvl_low <- anon_lvl[which.min(anon_lvl$level_ratio), ]
anon_low_series <- anon_lvl_low$series
anon_lvl_rest <- min(anon_lvl$level_ratio[anon_lvl$series != anon_low_series])
anon_knee_share <- vapply(split(anon_lvl, anon_lvl$alpha), \(d)
  sum(d$knee_samples[d$series == anon_low_series]) / sum(d$knee_samples),
  numeric(1))
stopifnot(length(anon_lvl_txt) == 1)
# A bound in whole percentages that a value cannot exceed, for "no more
# than". Rounding to six places first absorbs binary noise, such as
# 1 - 0.99 coming out a hair above 0.01.
anon_pct_bound <- function(x) paste0(ceiling(round(100 * one(x), 6)), "%")

# Claims the section makes in words, kept true of the artefacts.
anon_claims <- c(
  # the caption: the first per_meeting_cap usable utterances of every
  # test meeting
  cap_met = isTRUE(anon_cap_met),
  # the linkage rate "sits above chance" at every alpha, in both sets the
  # table shows, "by little at the strongest", where "its point estimate
  # stays above chance". The probes cluster on a few speakers and the
  # report keeps no probe's match, so no interval clustered by speaker
  # can be drawn from the artefacts, which the limitations paragraph
  # says; the strongest setting's lead is therefore claimed only as a
  # point estimate.
  above_chance = all(anon_ratio("all") > 1) &&
    all(anon_ratio("cross_meeting") > 1),
  # the limitations paragraph: the probes are "drawn mostly from a few
  # speakers", the three commonest supplying more than half of the probes
  # (a speaker with a single recording, left out of the probes, cannot be
  # among the three), and "the report keeps no probe's match", so no
  # column of the per-utterance report names a probe's nearest candidate
  probes_clustered = anon_top3 > anon_label("all", "trials") / 2,
  no_match_kept = !any(grepl("match|nearest|neighbo", names(anon_report),
                             ignore.case = TRUE)),
  # "far above" chance at the milder settings and "near chance" only at
  # the strongest: more than three times chance there against less than
  # twice, with under a tenth of the ceiling's lead over chance standing
  near_only_strongest = all(anon_ratio("all")[anon_milder] > 3) &&
    all(anon_ratio("cross_meeting")[anon_milder] > 3) &&
    all(anon_ratio("all")[!anon_milder] < 2) &&
    all(anon_ratio("cross_meeting")[!anon_milder] < 2) &&
    all(anon_kept_lead("all")[!anon_milder] < 0.1),
  # at alpha = anon_contrast self-similarity "suggests that little of the
  # voice survives", so the method "would have looked successful" there:
  # under a third of the 1 a recording scores against itself
  contrast_flatters = anon_at(anon_contrast, "mean_self_similarity") < 1 / 3,
  # the mildest setting "hides almost nothing"
  mild_hides_little = anon_kept_lead("all")[anon_alphas == anon_mild] > 0.9,
  # "the cost rises with the strength of the warping"
  cost_rises = all(diff(anon_cost_seq) > 0),
  # the strongest warp "destroys the transcript"
  strongest_destroys = anon_at(anon_strong, "wer_anonymised_guarded") > 0.5,
  # "Warping those ... happens to interrupt the loop", at every alpha
  marked_unlooped = !any(anon_loops(
    anon_report$hypothesis_words_anonymised[anon_report$degenerate_baseline == 1],
    anon_report$reference_words[anon_report$degenerate_baseline == 1])),
  # the warp's own loops carry "most of the cost" at every alpha
  wloops_most = all(anon_wloops$share > 0.5),
  # the low series holds "nearly all of the samples" the limiter
  # compressed, at every alpha
  knee_in_series = isTRUE(all(anon_knee_share > 0.95)),
  # restricted to other meetings, linkage "falls" at every alpha
  cross_lower = all(anon_link("cross_meeting") < anon_link("all")),
  # it "falls by at most" the printed bound, and no difference between
  # the table's rounded cells, which a reader can take, exceeds it either
  cross_bound = anon_cross_drop <= anon_cross_bound &&
    max(as.numeric(sprintf("%.2f", anon_link("all"))) -
          as.numeric(sprintf("%.2f", anon_link("cross_meeting")))) <=
      anon_cross_bound + 1e-9,
  # across meetings and channels "identity survives" at the milder ones
  channel_survives =
    all(anon_ratio("cross_meeting_cross_channel")[anon_milder] > 3),
  # and at the strongest it is "a larger multiple" of chance "than either
  # search of the table shows", on probes "too few to tell whether it
  # lies near chance or far above it": an exact binomial 95% interval for
  # it, which ignores the clustering of the probes by speaker and so is
  # if anything too narrow, runs from under twice chance to over three
  # times it, the two yardsticks of near_only_strongest
  channel_strongest_open = local({
    cc <- "cross_meeting_cross_channel"
    n  <- anon_label(cc, "trials")
    ci <- binom.test(round(anon_link(cc)[!anon_milder] * n), n)$conf.int /
      anon_chance(cc)
    anon_ratio(cc)[!anon_milder] >
      max(anon_ratio("all")[!anon_milder],
          anon_ratio("cross_meeting")[!anon_milder]) &&
      ci[[1]] < 2 && ci[[2]] > 3
  }),
  # "Every speaker's recordings come from one series of meetings"
  one_series = all(tapply(anon_series_of(anon_base$meeting),
                          anon_base$speaker,
                          \(s) length(unique(s))) == 1),
  # the model the text names is the one the run used
  embedding = identical(anon$embedding_model,
                        "pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM"))
if (!all(anon_claims))
  stop("Anonymisation section: no longer true of the artefacts: ",
       paste(names(anon_claims)[!anon_claims], collapse = ", "),
       call. = FALSE)

anon_cap <- paste0(
  "McAdams voice transformation on ", big(anon$n_utterances), " AMI ",
  "test utterances, the first ", num_word(anon$per_meeting_cap),
  " usable ones of each of the ", num_word(anon$n_meetings),
  " test meetings, spoken by ", num_word(anon$n_speakers), " people. ",
  "Self-similarity is the mean cosine similarity between a transformed ",
  "recording and its own untransformed source. Linkage is the proportion ",
  "of transformed utterances, the probes, whose nearest untransformed ",
  "recording of another utterance is the same speaker's, searched among ",
  "all the others or only among those from other meetings, and chance ",
  "is the rate at which a candidate drawn at random from the recordings ",
  "searched shares the probe's speaker. A probe whose speaker has no ",
  "other recording among the candidates is left out. The untransformed ",
  "row matches the original recordings against each other, the ceiling ",
  "the transformation starts from. Lower $\\alpha$ warps the voice ",
  "further. In both searches, only $\\alpha$ = ", anon_strong,
  " brings linkage near chance.")
```

Masking removes a name from a transcript, and leaves the recording
untouched. Where the audio itself is shared or archived, the voice
remains an identifier in its own right, so the workflow also offers an
optional transformation of the waveform. The method is the McAdams
coefficient transformation used as a baseline in the VoicePrivacy
Challenge [@patinoSpeakerAnonymisationUsing2021]. The speech is
modelled as a linear-predictive filter, the angles of that filter's
complex poles are raised to a power $\alpha$, and the signal is
resynthesised. Values of $\alpha$ below one shift the formants and
alter the perceived voice while leaving the words in place. It runs on
a processor in real time, downloads nothing and is deterministic,
which makes it attractive for a workflow of this kind.

Whether it anonymises is a separate question, and it has to be asked
of the right quantity. The obvious measurement, how similar a
transformed recording is to itself before transformation, flatters the
method badly. At $\alpha$ = `r anon_contrast` that similarity falls to
`r f2(anon_at(anon_contrast, "mean_self_similarity"))`,
which suggests that little of the voice survives. The question an
adversary actually asks is different, being whether the original
speaker can be picked out of a set of candidates given a transformed
recording. That is the linkage rate, and it is the quantity reported in
@tbl-anonymisation. Each transformed utterance is embedded with the
diarisation pipeline's own speaker model,
`pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM`, and matched against the
nearest untransformed recording of a different utterance. The search
runs once among all of them and once only among those from other
meetings, so that a match cannot rest on the session alone. A third
search, confined to recordings from other meetings on another headset
channel, is possible only for the speakers whose channel changed
between meetings, and is taken up with the limitations below. The run
reported here loaded the speaker model directly, because a damaged
copy of the pipeline's configuration in the cluster's model cache kept
the pipeline itself from loading. Once the cache was restored, the two
routes gave bit-identical embeddings of the same test signals
(`hpc/runs/anonymisation.env`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-anonymisation
#| tbl-cap: "Speaker Linkage After McAdams Voice Transformation"
# alpha is written as math, as in the prose: the PDF's text font has no
# Greek, so a literal alpha would print as a blank there.
anon_f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
tibble::tibble(
  `Setting` = c(paste0("$\\alpha$ = ", anon_alphas[anon_up]),
                "Untransformed", "Chance"),
  `Self-similarity` = c(anon_f2(anon_get("mean_self_similarity")[anon_up]),
                        "", ""),
  `Linkage, all recordings` = anon_f2(c(anon_link("all")[anon_up],
                                        anon_ceiling("all"),
                                        anon_chance("all"))),
  `Linkage, other meetings` = anon_f2(c(anon_link("cross_meeting")[anon_up],
                                        anon_ceiling("cross_meeting"),
                                        anon_chance("cross_meeting")))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r anon_cap`

At every coefficient tested the measured linkage rate sits above
chance, by little at the strongest, and at the `r num_word(sum(anon_milder))`
milder settings far above it,
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(anon_ratio("all")[anon_milder]))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(anon_ratio("all")[anon_milder]))` times chance,
reaching `r f2(anon_link("all")[anon_alphas == anon_mild])` at
$\alpha$ = `r anon_mild` against a chance level of
`r f2(anon_chance("all"))` and an untransformed ceiling of
`r f2(anon_ceiling("all"))`. At $\alpha$ = `r anon_contrast`, where
self-similarity suggested otherwise, linkage is still
`r f2(anon_link("all")[anon_alphas == anon_contrast])`,
`r num_word(round(anon_ratio("all")[anon_alphas == anon_contrast]))`
times chance. Only the most aggressive setting brings linkage near
chance, to `r f2(anon_link("all")[anon_alphas == anon_strong])`, and
that setting also does the transcript the most harm, as the cost
reported below shows. Short of it, the transformation changes how a
voice sounds but leaves enough of what identifies it for linkage far
above chance, and had self-similarity been reported alone, the method
would have looked successful at $\alpha$ = `r anon_contrast`, where it
fails.

The other side of the trade is what the transformation costs the
transcript, and there is reason not to assume it is small. Common
signal perturbations, pitch shift and time stretching among them, have
been found to raise the rate at which a recogniser fabricates content
[@atwanyLostTranscriptionFound2025], so a warp of the waveform is a
change a transcript can be expected to register. Measuring the cost
turned out to be harder than measuring the
privacy. Two defects had to be removed first, and both are worth
reporting, because each produced a result that looked like warped audio
transcribing *better* than the audio it came from, a gain in
intelligibility that degrading the audio should not bring. The first
was in the transformation itself, which scaled its output by that
output's own peak. Because the synthesis filter rings at
frame boundaries, a single sample could set the gain for a whole file.
At a realistic input level the anonymised audio came back around 20
times quieter, and a recogniser hallucinates less into near-silence, so
the loudness change was doing the work the warping was being credited
with. It reached the shipped feature and not only the benchmark. The
intended control, resynthesis without warping, could not have caught it,
because passing a signal through an unchanged filter and back is
algebraically the identity. The transformation matches the level of
its input, and the benchmark measures the ratio it achieves instead of
assuming it. Averaged over the utterances, that ratio is
`r anon_lvl_txt` at every setting reported here, and outside the
`r anon_low_series` meetings no utterance comes back more than
`r anon_pct_bound(1 - anon_lvl_rest)` quieter than it went in. Those
meetings hold nearly all of the samples that the limiter keeping the
output within full scale had to compress, and there single utterances
come back up to `r pc0(1 - anon_lvl_low$level_ratio)` quieter at
$\alpha$ = `r as.character(anon_lvl_low$alpha)`.

The second defect was in the estimator. Pooling errors over reference
words, as [the Dispersion Across Speakers section](#sec-speakers) also does, stops one short utterance
setting the corpus rate through substitutions and deletions, since the
reference length caps both. It does not cap insertions. Of the
`r big(anon$n_utterances)` utterances,
`r num_word(anon_n_looped)` have references of
`r anon_word_range(anon_marked$reference_words)` words and drew
hypotheses of `r big(min(anon_marked$hypothesis_words_original))` to
`r big(max(anon_marked$hypothesis_words_original))` words from the
recogniser on unmodified audio, and between them they supply
`r pc0(anon_looped_share)`
of all the error in the baseline condition. Warping those
`r num_word(anon_n_looped)` happens to
interrupt the loop, which is not a fact about intelligibility. The
benchmark therefore marks a baseline transcript as a loop when it runs
to at least `r num_word(anon_crit[["length_floor"]])` words and more
than `r num_word(anon_crit[["length_factor"]])` times its reference,
and the cost is reported over the utterances it did not mark. Only the
baseline is screened, since a warp that provokes a loop has genuinely
damaged the transcript and excluding those would hide the very cost at
issue. On that basis the transformation costs
`r f2(anon_cost_seq[[1]])`
in word error rate at $\alpha$ = `r anon_mild`, rising through
`r and_list(vapply(anon_cost_seq[-c(1, length(anon_cost_seq))], f2, ""))`
to
`r f2(anon_cost_seq[[length(anon_cost_seq)]])`
at $\alpha$ = `r anon_strong`, against a screened baseline of
`r f2(anon_guarded_base)`.
The cost rises with the strength of the warping, and the setting that
comes nearest to chance linkage is the one that destroys the
transcript, with a screened word error rate of
`r f2(anon_at(anon_strong, "wer_anonymised_guarded"))` against the
baseline's `r f2(anon_guarded_base)`. The warp also sends utterances
into loops of its own, ones the baseline transcribed without looping.
They are few,
`r num_word(anon_wloops$n[anon_alphas == anon_strong])` at
$\alpha$ = `r anon_strong` and
`r num_word(anon_wloops$n[anon_alphas == anon_mild])` at
$\alpha$ = `r anon_mild`, but they carry between
`r pc0(min(anon_wloops$share))` and `r pc0(max(anon_wloops$share))` of
the cost at each setting.

Read together, the two sides settle the question. The mildest setting
tested hides almost nothing, leaving linkage at
`r f2(anon_link("all")[anon_alphas == anon_mild])` against
`r f2(anon_ceiling("all"))` for untransformed recordings, and still
costs `r f2(anon_cost_seq[[1]])` in word error rate. The most
aggressive brings linkage near chance only at a cost that destroys the
transcript, and even there its point estimate stays above chance. For
this AMI sample and fixed speaker model, no tested setting combined
linkage near chance with transcription accuracy close to the unmodified
baseline.

Some limits apply to both sides of the comparison. Each meeting gives
its first `r num_word(anon$per_meeting_cap)` usable utterances, all
from its first `r num_word(anon_minutes)` minutes, so the sample is
unbalanced: three speakers supply `r big(anon_top3)` of the
`r big(anon$n_utterances)` utterances,
`r num_word(anon_solo_meetings)` meetings yield a single speaker, and
within a meeting a candidate drawn at random shares the probe's
speaker `r pc0(anon_chance("within_meeting"))` of the time. The
linkage rates are therefore weighted towards a few voices, and a
comparison confined to one meeting would be a weak test. The same
clustering leaves open whether, at the most aggressive setting,
linkage lies above chance at all, since it leads chance by little
there, probes drawn mostly from a few speakers are not independent,
and the report keeps no probe's match from which an interval clustered
by speaker could be drawn. A speaker
model can also key on the recording conditions as much as on the
voice, and two restrictions of the candidates test how far the linkage
rests on them. Searched only among recordings from other meetings,
linkage falls by at most `r f2(anon_cross_bound)` at any setting
(@tbl-anonymisation). The
`r num_word(length(anon_switchers))` `r anon_switch_series` speakers,
the only ones whose headset channel changed between meetings, are
still linked across meetings and channels at
`r and_list(vapply(anon_link("cross_meeting_cross_channel")[anon_up], f2, ""))`
from the strongest setting to the mildest, against a chance of
`r f2(anon_chance("cross_meeting_cross_channel"))` over the
`r big(anon_label("cross_meeting_cross_channel", "trials"))`
utterances they supply. At the milder settings, then, identity
survives without the session or the headset to carry it. At the
strongest, `r f2(anon_link("cross_meeting_cross_channel")[!anon_milder])`
is
`r num_word(round(anon_ratio("cross_meeting_cross_channel")[!anon_milder]))`
times that chance, a larger multiple than either search of the table
shows, but `r big(anon_label("cross_meeting_cross_channel", "trials"))`
utterances from `r num_word(length(anon_switchers))` speakers are too
few to tell whether it lies near chance or far above it. Every
speaker's recordings come from one series of meetings, held in one
room [@carlettaAMIMeeting2005], so linkage across rooms is not
measured here. Finally, the intelligibility figures turn on a few
utterances. The
`r num_word(anon_n_looped)` looped baselines would dominate an
unscreened rate, which is why the screen is declared here and applied
in the open, and after it a handful of loops that the warp provokes
still carry most of the cost. The figures give the direction of the
trade, not a precise cost.

These rates measure linkage with a fixed speaker model. The VoicePrivacy
2026 protocol tests an attacker fine-tuned on anonymised speech and
measures speaker verification by equal error rate, alongside separate
measures of linguistic and emotional utility
[@miaoVoicePrivacyChallengeEvaluation2026]. A low linkage rate here
therefore does not establish protection against an attacker adapted to
the transformation.

The wider implication is for how such features should be offered. The
transformation is retained in the workflow because it has legitimate
uses, in masking a voice for presentation or for participant comfort,
but it is documented as a perceptual disguise and not as a
de-identification measure, and it should not be relied on where
re-identification is the risk being managed.

## Computational Footprint {#sec-footprint}

```{r load-footprint, include=FALSE}
# footprint_summary.json, the ledger it was estimated from and the
# per-job report are loaded and checked in setup, where fp_jobs joins the
# ledger to the report and fp_gpu_jobs keeps the jobs that held a GPU.
# The ledger was captured on 4 October 2026, after every job of the
# main evaluation had finished, and prices each GPU at the board of its
# node. The three jobs of the follow-up of 17 and 18 October 2026 (ARC
# 9124828 and 9124851, test-suite runs on processor cores, and 9124852,
# the case study's re-run on one L40S for 17 min 51 s) came later and
# are not in it, as the scope paragraph says.
# It replaced a capture of June 2026 that held 38 jobs, among them none
# of the re-runs behind the results now reported, and labelled every GPU
# a100 (MS-11, OUTPUTS-05, ESTATS-06, REGEN-07).
fp_f0 <- function(x) format(round(one(x)), big.mark = ",")
fp_f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", one(x))
fp_gpuh   <- fp_f0(fp$overall$gpu_hours)
fp_kwh    <- fp_f0(fp$overall$energy_kwh)
fp_kg     <- fp_f1(fp$overall$carbon_kg)
fp_km     <- fp_f0(fp$equivalence$car_km_average_passenger)
fp_prod   <- fp_f0(fp$productive$gpu_hours)
fp_njobs  <- one(fp$overall$n_jobs)
fp_nfail  <- one(fp$overhead$n_jobs)
fp_ohpct  <- sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fp$overhead$gpu_hours / fp$overall$gpu_hours)
fp_pue    <- sprintf("%.2f", one(fp$parameters$pue))
fp_ci     <- sprintf("%.0f", one(fp$parameters$carbon_intensity_g_per_kwh))
fp_days   <- sprintf("%.1f", one(fp$overall$gpu_hours) / 24)
# The ledger's window opens on the day of the evaluation's first job, a
# run of the test suite (evaluation/footprint.py), and the jobs it leaves
# out were cancelled while still queued, so held no allocation and drew
# no power, as the scope paragraph says.
fp_window <- sub(".*--starttime ([0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}).*", "\\1",
                 one(fp$provenance$sacct_query, "the ledger's sacct query"))
fp_first_job <- fp_jobs[order(as.integer(sub("_.*$", "", fp_jobs$job_id)),
                              fp_jobs$job_id), ][1, ]
fp_n_queued  <- length(fp$provenance$left_out_never_allocated)
stopifnot(grepl("^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$", fp_window),
          fp_first_job$category == "Test suite and smoke tests",
          isTRUE(fp$provenance$workdir_checked),
          length(fp$provenance$left_out_outside_project_dirs) == 0,
          fp_n_queued > 0)
# "the jobs behind every other result reported above": the ledger holds
# every job the multilingual summary and the determinism comparison name
# (an array job by its tasks), and a category with jobs for each other
# experiment the Results report.
fp_has_job <- function(id)
  any(fp_jobs$job_id == id | startsWith(fp_jobs$job_id, paste0(id, "_")))
fp_named_jobs <- c(unlist(lapply(ml$benchmark$arms, \(a) a[["arc_jobs"]])),
                   sub("^([0-9]+).*$", "\\1",
                       vapply(det_rn, det_meta, character(1), key = "job")))
fp_cat_n <- vapply(fp$by_category, \(k) one(k$n_jobs, "a category's jobs"),
                   numeric(1))
fp_cat_h <- vapply(fp$by_category, \(k) one(k$gpu_hours, "a category's GPU-hours"),
                   numeric(1))
stopifnot(length(fp_named_jobs) > 0,
          all(vapply(fp_named_jobs, fp_has_job, logical(1))),
          all(fp_cat_n[c("Diarisation (DER)", "Diarisation sweep (DER)",
                         "Timestamp accuracy", "Voice anonymisation",
                         "Case study", "Determinism check")] > 0),
          sum(fp_cat_n) == fp_njobs,
          abs(sum(fp_cat_h) - fp$overall$gpu_hours) < 1e-6)
# The table's disfluency row, which the scope paragraph sets apart: its
# jobs decoded AMI for an earlier version of the filler-preservation
# scoring (hpc/submit_disfluency.sh), and the committed scoring reads the
# condition sweep's own transcripts instead (its summary's source).
fp_disfl_jobs <- fp_jobs[fp_jobs$category == "Disfluency evaluation", ]
stopifnot(nrow(fp_disfl_jobs) > 0,
          all(fp_disfl_jobs$job_name == "disfluency"),
          grepl("wer_hypotheses_ami_whisper-large-v3",
                one(disfl$source, "the filler scoring's source")))
# The condition sweep's passes, and the word error rate work as a whole:
# the sweep, its pilot and the multilingual wave, as the paragraph names
# them. The first pass's category also holds an earlier run of one
# model's part of it, which the first aggregate does not draw on
# (output/evaluation/README.md: sweep_aggregate_prefix was fed by three
# array jobs, one a model): that category holds one array job more than
# the models, and each later pass one a model.
fp_sweep_cats <- names(fp_cat_h)[startsWith(names(fp_cat_h),
                                            "WER condition sweep")]
fp_wer_cats   <- names(fp_cat_h)[startsWith(names(fp_cat_h), "WER")]
fp_sweep_share <- sum(fp_cat_h[fp_sweep_cats]) / fp$overall$gpu_hours
fp_wer_share   <- sum(fp_cat_h[fp_wer_cats]) / fp$overall$gpu_hours
fp_sweep_arrays <- vapply(fp_sweep_cats, \(k)
  length(unique(sub("_.*$", "", fp_jobs$job_id[fp_jobs$category == k]))),
  numeric(1))
stopifnot(setequal(setdiff(fp_wer_cats, fp_sweep_cats),
                   c("WER (pilot)", "WER multilingual (FLEURS)")),
          fp_sweep_share > 1 / 2,
          fp_sweep_arrays[["WER condition sweep"]] == n_sweep_models + 1,
          all(fp_sweep_arrays[setdiff(fp_sweep_cats, "WER condition sweep")]
              == n_sweep_models))
# The cards the GPU jobs ran on, by board: how many jobs each ran and how
# many GPU-hours, and the board that ran the most jobs and the one that
# ran the most GPU time, named as the prose names them (each must be
# unique). Board powers are data-sheet maxima (evaluation/footprint.py).
fp_board_name <- c(`p100-pcie` = "Tesla P100 PCIe",
                   `v100-pcie` = "Tesla V100 PCIe",
                   `v100-sxm2` = "Tesla V100 SXM2", `a100-pcie` = "A100 PCIe",
                   `a100-sxm4` = "A100 SXM4", rtx8000 = "Quadro RTX 8000",
                   `rtx-titan` = "TITAN RTX", a6000 = "RTX A6000",
                   l40s = "L40S", `h100-pcie` = "H100 PCIe",
                   `h100-nvl` = "H100 NVL", `h100-sxm` = "H100 SXM5")
fp_board_n <- c(table(fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_type))
fp_board_h <- tapply(fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_hours, fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_type, sum)
fp_tdp_range <- range(fp_gpu_jobs$tdp_w)
stopifnot(all(names(fp_board_n) %in% names(fp_board_name)),
          sum(fp_board_n == max(fp_board_n)) == 1,
          sum(fp_board_h == max(fp_board_h)) == 1)
fp_most_jobs <- names(which.max(fp_board_n))
fp_most_time <- names(which.max(fp_board_h))
# "failed, were cancelled or reached their time limit", and full
# utilisation: every device is charged its full power for its whole
# allocation, which is an assumption and not a measured upper bound.
stopifnot(setequal(fp$overhead$states, c("FAILED", "CANCELLED", "TIMEOUT")),
          one(fp$parameters$gpu_util) == 1,
          isTRUE(fp$parameters$cpu_util == 1))
fp_cap <- paste0(
  "GPU = graphics processing unit; CPU = central processing unit; ",
  "CO2e = carbon dioxide equivalent. ",
  "Estimated computational footprint by experiment category, from the ",
  "committed scheduler ledger under the Green Algorithms model: each GPU ",
  "job is charged the maximum board power of the card in its node (",
  fp_tdp_range[[1]], " to ", fp_tdp_range[[2]], " W), at utilisation ",
  sprintf("%.1f", one(fp$parameters$gpu_util)),
  ", a power-usage effectiveness of ", fp_pue, " and the UK 2023 ",
  "generation intensity of ", fp_ci, " gCO2e/kWh. Pre-flights, probes and ",
  "test-suite runs are categories of their own. GPU-hours weight ",
  "wall-clock by allocated GPUs. Every device is charged its full power ",
  "for its whole allocation, which assumes full utilisation and is not a ",
  "measured upper bound.")
# The scope paragraph places the masking benchmark and the
# filler-preservation scoring on a desktop machine, outside the cluster.
# Their summaries record the platform they ran on, which on the cluster
# is Linux.
fp_off_cluster <- vapply(list(ms, msci, msner, disfl), \(s)
  startsWith(one(s$run_metadata$platform, "a summary's run platform"),
             "Windows"), logical(1))
if (!all(fp_off_cluster))
  stop("Footprint section: a masking or filler-preservation summary no ",
       "longer records a desktop platform, so the sentence placing them ",
       "off the cluster is no longer true", call. = FALSE)
```

The case for a local workflow rests in part on its being
inexpensive to run, and that cost is quantified here instead of left
implicit. Every cluster job of the evaluation ran under one scheduler,
whose accounting database records each job's wall-clock runtime, its
allocated GPU, central processing unit (CPU) and memory and the node it ran on. The site does not
meter energy. The estimates below use those allocations and the model of
@lannelongueGreenAlgorithmsQuantifying2021 to combine GPU, CPU and
memory power over each job's runtime. Both utilisation factors are held
at one, and every GPU job is charged the rated board power of the card
in its node, which runs from `r fp_tdp_range[[1]]` W to
`r fp_tdp_range[[2]]` W. These assumptions specify full utilisation
without establishing an upper bound on energy consumption. Every physical
constant is a documented parameter a reader can substitute and re-run.

The committed ledger holds every cluster job of the evaluation that
held an allocation before its capture, `r fp_njobs` in all. Its window
opens on `r long_date(fp_window)`, with the evaluation's first job, a
run of the test suite, and it was captured on
`r long_date(fp$provenance$captured)`, after the last job of the main
evaluation had finished. Three jobs of a follow-up on 17 and 18 October
2026 came later and are not in it: two runs of the test suite, on
processor cores alone, and the re-run of the case study, which held one
L40S card for 18 minutes.
The `r num_word(fp_n_queued)` jobs it leaves out were cancelled while
still queued and drew no power. Besides the
`r num_word(length(fp_sweep_cats))` passes of the condition sweep and
an earlier run of part of the first, which that pass's aggregate does
not draw on, it holds the pilot runs of the word error rate benchmark
and the jobs
behind every other result reported above, and the pre-flights, probes
and test-suite runs are categories of their own (@tbl-footprint). Its
`r big(nrow(fp_gpu_jobs))` GPU jobs ran on `r num_word(fp_n_boards)`
models of card, the `r fp_board_name[[fp_most_jobs]]` running the most
of them, `r big(fp_board_n[[fp_most_jobs]])`, and the
`r fp_board_name[[fp_most_time]]` the most GPU time,
`r fp_f0(fp_board_h[[fp_most_time]])` GPU-hours. All the jobs together
are estimated at `r fp_gpuh` GPU-hours, `r fp_kwh` kWh and `r fp_kg`
kgCO~2~e, assuming a power-usage effectiveness of `r fp_pue` and a grid
intensity of `r fp_ci` gCO~2~e/kWh. That is comparable to driving
roughly `r fp_km` km in an average car. The condition sweep's
`r num_word(length(fp_sweep_cats))` passes, with that earlier run,
account for `r pc0(fp_sweep_share)` of the GPU time, and the word error rate work
as a whole, with its pilot and the multilingual wave, for
`r pc0(fp_wer_share)`, because the sweep re-transcribes
`r num_word(n_sweep_suites)` corpora under
`r num_word(n_sweep_models)` models while the diarisation and timestamp
benchmarks reuse a single pass. Of the `r fp_njobs` jobs,
`r fp_nfail` failed, were cancelled or reached their time limit, so
`r fp_ohpct`% of the GPU time went to runs that did not complete, and
the completed jobs used `r fp_prod` GPU-hours. What matters here is the
scale. These runs amount to about `r fp_days` days of continuous
single-GPU time, and the marginal cost of transcribing one further
recording with the deployed workflow is a small fraction of that, which
is the property that makes the approach practical to run inside an
institution. The ledger records the cost of these benchmark runs and
not the cost the workload requires. The benchmark transcribes one
utterance at a time, and an optimised serving stack for Whisper has
been reported to reach more than 50% higher throughput than existing
implementations [@zhangEfficientDeploymentLarge2025], so a deployment
that cared about the figure could lower it without changing the model.
The masking benchmark and the filler-preservation scoring ran on a
desktop machine and used no cluster time of their own, so the total is
the cost of the evaluation's cluster jobs and not of every computation
behind the paper. The table's
`r num_word(nrow(fp_disfl_jobs))` disfluency jobs decoded AMI for an
earlier version of that scoring, which now reads the condition sweep's
own transcripts. Their GPU time is in the total, but none of the
reported results comes from them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-footprint
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated Computational Footprint by Experiment"
fp_cats <- fp$by_category
catnames <- names(fp_cats)
ftab <- tibble::tibble(
  Category = catnames,
  Jobs = sapply(catnames, \(k) fp_cats[[k]]$n_jobs),
  `GPU-hours` = sapply(catnames, \(k) fp_cats[[k]]$gpu_hours),
  `Energy (kWh)` = sapply(catnames, \(k) fp_cats[[k]]$energy_kwh),
  `kgCO2e` = sapply(catnames, \(k) fp_cats[[k]]$carbon_g / 1000)
) |>
  mutate(across(c(`GPU-hours`, `Energy (kWh)`, `kgCO2e`),
                \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)))
kable(ftab)
```

`\noindent`{=latex} *Note.* `r fp_cap`

# Discussion

```{r discussion-derived, include=FALSE}
# Figures the Discussion quotes that no Results chunk computes, read from
# the artefacts loaded in setup, so that the summary cannot drift from
# them, and the counts its determinism sentences put into words.
#
# The interval on the corpus rate, beside which the contraction stage's
# cost before its repair passed for noise.
disc_ci_width <- one(wer_ci$ci_hi - wer_ci$ci_lo,
                     "width of the corpus interval")
# The multilingual re-run at the sweep's code (the summary's fourth arm):
# the composite scores exactly as the raw hypothesis does in every
# language, which the exact block of each language shows unrounded. The
# text ties the claim to that code and not to the two repairs, because
# with both in their first form (the third arm) Spanish was not exact:
# the Unicode strip still deleted the vulgar fractions of one sentence.
disc_ml_n <- length(ml$languages)
disc_ml_code <- one(ml$benchmark$arms[["4_after_audit"]][["code"]],
                    "code of the multilingual re-run")
if (!identical(disc_ml_code, sweep_version))
  stop("The multilingual re-run (", disc_ml_code, ") and the English ",
       "sweep (", sweep_version, ") ran different code", call. = FALSE)
disc_ml_neutral <- all(vapply(names(ml$languages), \(k) {
  e <- ml$languages[[k]][["exact"]]
  one(e[["pipeline_full_after_audit"]],
      paste(k, "composite after the audit")) ==
    one(e[["raw_after_audit"]], paste(k, "raw after the audit"))
}, logical(1)))
# The voice transformation as linkage over chance at each coefficient.
# The most aggressive setting is the lowest alpha: the text gives the
# range over the other settings and that one's own figures, with the
# word error rate over the utterances whose baseline did not loop.
disc_anon <- local({
  a   <- names(anon$by_alpha)
  get <- function(f) vapply(a, \(k) one(anon$by_alpha[[k]][[f]],
                                         paste("alpha", k, f)), numeric(1))
  ratio  <- get("linkage_rate") / get("chance")
  strong <- a[[which.min(as.numeric(a))]]
  list(ratio  = ratio,
       strong = strong,
       lo     = min(ratio[a != strong]),
       hi     = max(ratio[a != strong]),
       link   = get("linkage_rate")[[strong]],
       chance = one(unique(get("chance")),
                    "one chance level across the coefficients"),
       base   = get("wer_baseline_guarded")[[strong]],
       wer    = get("wer_anonymised_guarded")[[strong]])
})
# The determinism paragraphs. The seed of the check's V100 run, whose
# first decode the comparison reads, against that of the sweep's decode
# it reproduced.
det_seed_check <- one(det_cross$meta$runs$v100_seed0$seeds[[1]],
                      "the first seed of the check's V100 run")
det_seed_sweep <- one(det_cross$meta$runs$v100$seeds, "the sweep's seed")
stopifnot(startsWith(det_cross$runs$v100_seed0$inputs$dump$file,
                     paste0("seed", det_seed_check, "_")),
          det_seed_check != det_seed_sweep)
# Each run's error rate on one utterance, read from every comparison that
# finds two runs differing on it, to the three decimals of the H100's
# log; a run that agrees with every other on the utterance has none.
det_rates_on <- function(uid) {
  rates <- list()
  for (pair in c(det_cross$text, det_cross$wer_level)) {
    d <- pair$differing_utterances
    if (!is.data.frame(d) || !uid %in% d$uid) next
    w <- d$wer[d$uid == uid, , drop = FALSE]
    for (run in names(w))
      rates[[run]] <- unique(c(rates[[run]], round(w[[run]], 3)))
  }
  if (length(rates) == 0 || any(lengths(rates) != 1))
    stop("determinism_cross_accelerator.json gives no single error rate ",
         "for each run on ", uid, call. = FALSE)
  unlist(rates)
}
# The utterances on which the H100's logged rates differ from the L40S's
# and from the sweep's decode, and on the second of them the two groups
# the runs fall into: those that score it as the H100 does (early) and
# the rest (late), with the commits each group ran at.
det_h_uids <- function(pair)
  sort(det_cross$wer_level[[pair]]$differing_utterances$uid)
det_uid_h_l <- det_h_uids("h100_vs_l40s")
det_uid_h_v <- det_h_uids("h100_vs_v100")
det_split <- local({
  r <- det_rates_on(det_uid_h_v)
  grp <- split(names(r), r)
  early <- grp[[which(vapply(grp, \(g) "h100" %in% g, logical(1)))]]
  late  <- setdiff(names(r), early)
  list(rates = r, n_groups = length(grp), early = early, late = late,
       n_early_commits = length(unique(det_commit[early])),
       n_late_commits  = length(unique(det_commit[late])))
})
# What the paragraphs say of these: the L40S differs from the sweep's
# decode, the check's V100 run and the processor run on the same
# utterances, by the same number of word edits each; the H100's rates
# differ from the L40S's on one of them and from each of the other three
# runs' on the other; on that other every run has a rate and the runs
# fall into two groups, the H100 and L40S runs, made at the earliest
# commits, against the rest, made at later ones and at none of the same.
det_l40s_uids <- sort(det_x$differing_utterances$uid)
stopifnot(
  all(vapply(c("l40s_vs_v100_seed0", "cpu_vs_l40s"), \(p) {
    d <- det_cross$text[[p]]$differing_utterances
    identical(sort(d$uid), det_l40s_uids) &&
      all(as.integer(d$word_edits) == det_x_edits[[1]])
  }, logical(1))),
  all(det_x_edits == det_x_edits[[1]]),
  length(det_uid_h_l) == 1, length(det_uid_h_v) == 1,
  det_uid_h_l != det_uid_h_v,
  setequal(c(det_uid_h_l, det_uid_h_v), det_l40s_uids),
  all(vapply(c("h100_vs_v100_seed0", "cpu_vs_h100"),
             \(p) identical(det_h_uids(p), det_uid_h_v), logical(1))),
  setequal(names(det_split$rates), det_rn), det_split$n_groups == 2,
  setequal(det_split$early, c("h100", "l40s")),
  !any(det_commit[det_split$early] %in% det_commit[det_split$late]),
  max(det_date[det_split$early]) < min(det_date[det_split$late]))
```

A low corpus WER and a high one each invite over-confident
readings. The model has not solved transcription in the first
case, and it has not become unfit for purpose in the second. A
probabilistic model trained on a heterogeneous web corpus assigns
most of its probability mass to the most frequent configurations
of its training distribution. When the audio at hand resembles that
distribution, errors will be few and concentrated in predictable
places, namely proper nouns, specialist terminology, code-switching
and overlap. When the audio departs from it, errors will be more
frequent and more varied, but they will still be concentrated in
places that an experienced analyst can anticipate. What a defensive
layer can do is act on that anticipation, and whether it does so is a
question for measurement and not for design. The question
worth asking is therefore what an auditable record built around such a
model actually buys.
The answer here is uneven, and the most instructive parts of it are
the failures.

The clearest result in this paper is a defect in the workflow's own
post-processing, and the way it came to light generalises beyond this
workflow. The contraction repair reads from its specification like a
safe orthographic tidy, and in aggregate it cost
`r ppt(pf_lsc)` percentage points on test-clean before its repair,
small enough to pass for noise beside an interval about
`r ppt(disc_ci_width)` points wide on the corpus rate. A reader given
that figure alone would have had no reason to look any further at it.
What settled the matter was the per-utterance signature reported in [the Word Error Rate section](#sec-wer), since a
stage that never once improves an utterance and only ever adds
substitutions is not disagreeing with the reference orthography at
all. Seven of its keys were ordinary English words, and the stage had
run over every English transcript the tool produced.

The existing tests checked the repair table against its intended
substitutions and passed because the code followed that table. A test
requiring correct English words to survive unchanged could have detected
the faulty specification, and that invariant now guards the repair.
Scoring each stage against reference speech supplied independent
evidence of its effects and exposed the source of the excess error.
That decomposition is useful when the measure can detect the property
under test. A stage that adds errors without improving any utterance
warrants inspection, while an unchanged word error rate requires a
separate test of any benefits or harms the scorer cannot see.

Accuracy is in any case the wrong instrument for the property this
layer is recommended on, and the claim that it protects disfluency was
never in contact with the evidence offered for it. Scored on that
property directly the layer does hold up, preserving every filler
the recogniser emits. The figure a researcher needs is the end-to-end
one, and it is far lower, because the recogniser supplies only
`r pct(dcond("pipeline_full", "reference_recall"))`
of the fillers a human transcriber recorded, and a smaller share still
of the hesitations among them. The loss happens before any
post-processing runs. The general lesson is that a layer
offered on a property has to be scored on that property, which here
meant keeping the verbatim hypotheses a conventional benchmark throws
away and declining to score them under a normaliser that removes the
phenomenon under study from the reference as well as the hypothesis.
Fabrication is the other property an error rate fails to track. Across
more than 20 recognisers @atwanyLostTranscriptionFound2025 found
that a high error rate can accompany few hallucinations and a low one
can conceal them, which is why they propose reporting a hallucination
rate alongside the error rate in high-stakes settings.

A layer of lexical rules carries the language it was written in,
whether or not that language is ever declared. The inflation reported
in [the Post-Processing Beyond English section](#sec-multilingual), reaching a factor of `r ml_worst` at its worst,
was contributed by the workflow and not by the model it wraps, and it
had been present for as long as the workflow had. What generalises is
where an assumption of that kind hides. A recogniser declares the
languages it covers and is tested against them, while a text-processing
layer inherits its author's language in silence, so a tool whose model
is multilingual should not be released on the strength of an English
benchmark however thorough that benchmark is. Scored again at the code
behind the English sweep, the layer leaves the error rate in all
`r num_word(disc_ml_n)` languages exactly where the raw output puts
it, but gating the English-specific stages supplies none of the
processing another language would need in their place, which is the
limit of what the repairs can be said to have achieved.

What a headline rate cannot carry is the variation between the
individual people recorded.
Across the `r num_word(nrow(spk))` readers of LibriSpeech test-clean,
every one of them reading prepared text, the pooled error rate as
scored ran about `r big(round(spk_ratio))`
to 1 from the best-served to the worst. Quotation marks contribute
to that spread and also to the normaliser's apparent gains. The exploratory
rescoring reduced Whisper Large v3's gains sharply on both LibriSpeech
splits and little on AMI,
showing that an accuracy claim needs its scoring convention alongside it.
The remaining variation describes these readers
and their material without predicting its size in conversational,
second-language or atypical speech. Speaker attribution also varies widely
across recordings, for the separate reason set out below.
A researcher should therefore read a published rate as
a property of a corpus and estimate the rate that matters by
hand-correcting a subsample of their own recordings. Where an analysis
compares groups of speakers the dispersion threatens the comparison
itself, because transcription quality that differs widely between
speakers can manufacture a difference that will be read as
substantive, and the subsample should then cover every group
and not the recordings as a whole. The threat is not confined to
accuracy. @koeneckeCarelessWhisperSpeechtoText2024 found fabricated
phrases in 1.7% of transcriptions from speakers with aphasia against
1.2% from controls, and in 1.8% against 1.1% once the two groups were
matched on demographic characteristics, so a recogniser's failure rate
need not be distributed evenly across the clinical groups a study sets
out to compare.

For the speaker-attribution component the decisive choice turned out
to be the evaluation protocol and not the parameters.
A sweep of `r num_word(der_n_distinct)` configurations on the
development meetings left the shipped defaults within a tenth of a
point of the optimum of the grid, and the
configuration selected there proved, on the held-out split,
indistinguishable from them and fractionally worse. Rebuilding the same
`r num_word(nrow(der_report))` test meetings by concatenating short
excerpts instead of restoring the original timeline moved macro
diarisation error by `r ppt(der_recon_effect)` percentage points, where
choosing the best configuration of the grid over the shipped defaults
gained `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * der_tune_gain_dev)` of a point on the
development meetings and nothing on the held-out ones. A
diarisation figure is thus a statement about how the evaluation audio
was assembled quite as much as about the system that processed it, and
a report giving its hyperparameters but not its reconstruction has
described the less important half. The timestamp benchmark carries the
same warning in a milder form, because how its evaluation clips were
cut decides which boundary errors it is in any position to see.

Local execution sits awkwardly with reproducibility unless the
sources of variation are pinned. The precise version of the model,
the hardware, the audio decoder and even the floating-point
precision can all influence the transcript that comes out. The
workflow records the model identifier and version in the
transcript header, writes the raw timestamped output before any
post-processing, and integrates the evaluation pipeline with a
Quarto manuscript whose tables and figures are regenerated from the
committed evaluation outputs on every render. A reader who wishes to
recompute the WER may do so from the published JSON output without
re-accessing the audio. That the same audio yields the same words was
checked and never assumed. `r Num_word(det_n)` AMI utterances were
transcribed twice under a fixed seed and again under a second seed, in
separate runs on an `r det_gpu_name`, an `r det_card_names[["l40s"]]`,
a `r det_card_names[["v100_seed0"]]` and an `r det_cpu_name` processor,
and within each of those `r num_word(length(det_own))` runs the decodes
agreed on every utterance, character for character. The agreement
across seeds should be read for what it is. Decoding here is greedy,
with no temperature fallback configured, so the seed sets only the
libraries' random state and decides no sampling step, and a decoder
allowed to fall back to sampling would test it where this check could
not.

The words did change from one hardware configuration to another, though
not between every pair. The check's run on the V100 reproduced, on all
`r num_word(det_n)` utterances, the words of the condition sweep's
decode on the same node, although it ran under seed
`r det_seed_check` where the sweep ran under seed `r det_seed_sweep`,
at a later commit, and in a job of its own where the sweep decoded the
whole split in one process. On that node, then, the seed, the code and
the process changed nothing. The processor run, in
`r det_cpu_precision`, gave the same words on all `r num_word(det_n)`
as well. The L40S run differs from those three on
`r num_word(det_x$differing)` utterances, each by
`r num_word(det_x_edits[[1]])` edits to the words as written,
punctuation included. The error rates logged by the H100 run, whose
transcripts were lost, can show a difference but never agreement, and
they differ from the L40S run's on one of those utterances and from
those of the other three runs on the other. On that other utterance the
runs part by code version as well as by hardware. The H100 and L40S
runs, made at the `r num_word(det_split$n_early_commits)` earliest of
the `r num_word(length(unique(det_commit)))` commits, score it alike,
and the `r num_word(length(det_split$late))` runs made at the later
`r num_word(det_split$n_late_commits)` score it alike but differently.
The check's V100 run shares the L40S run's seed and kind
of job, so the difference between those two lies in the hardware or in
the code between their commits, and no pair of runs separates a card
from the node that holds it. Over the `r num_word(det_n)` utterances,
the pooled WER of the `r num_word(det_n_runs)` runs ranged from
`r f3(min(det_pooled))` to `r f3(max(det_pooled))`, a spread of
`r ppt(max(det_pooled) - min(det_pooled))` percentage points, so
reproducibility held within each configuration in which it was
measured and should not be assumed across them.

What the workflow offers on privacy needs stating with the same care,
because two quite different claims are easily run together. The first
is about custody, and it holds. Audio never leaves the institution
under which the recording was made, and downloading model weights is
an outbound-only operation carrying no user data. That is the property
which bears on the obligations the General Data Protection Regulation
and its counterparts place on an
institutional data controller, and it is a claim about where the data
goes, not about what the transcript reveals. Where speaker
diarisation depends on the gated `pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1`
model [@bredinPyannoteAudio2025], a HuggingFace access token is read
from a local file and not embedded in any artefact the workflow emits.

The second claim is about de-identification, and it does not hold.
[The Evaluating the Masking Layer section](#sec-masking) shows a name masker that, on injected names, redacts one
if and only if it is title-cased and already in its dictionary, and
that, because it looks each word up whole, can miss even such a name
when it is joined to a neighbouring word. [The Anonymising the Voice section](#sec-anonymisation) shows a voice transformation that
leaves speakers linkable at `r sprintf("%.1f", disc_anon$lo)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", disc_anon$hi)` times the chance level at every
setting but the most aggressive. That setting lowers linkage to
`r f2(disc_anon$link)` against a chance level of
`r f2(disc_anon$chance)`, but only by destroying the transcript, whose
word error rate it raises from `r f2(disc_anon$base)` to
`r f2(disc_anon$wer)`. Keeping custody of a recording is not
the same as de-identifying it, and a workflow that does the first well
can still hand an analyst a transcript and an audio file from which
participants are recoverable. Neither feature should be relied on
where re-identification is the risk being managed, and the paper
reports both as bounded for that reason.

The remaining limitations are practical. On the desktop,
throughput is bounded by the host machine, and a long interview
will take longer than its real-time duration on a CPU-only laptop.
On a high-performance computing cluster, throughput is bounded by queue waiting times, by
the partition's time limits and, since the batch worker decodes on
processor cores alone, by the speed of those cores, and adapting the
submission scripts to a new cluster requires editing the module
load lines and the partition names in the templates under
`hpc/`. The graphical interface assumes a single audio file at a
time, which suits the qualitative researcher working with a small
number of interviews and is inappropriate for the methodologist
seeking to process hundreds of recordings, for whom the Slurm
array submission script remains the right tool. Future work will
explore tighter integration between the two modes so that a user
with intermittent cluster access can dispatch a job from the
graphical interface when convenient and process locally when not.

No headline figure in this paper should be read as a guaranteed
performance bound, and several are bounded in ways worth restating
together. The English word error rates come from a sweep run after the
contraction repair and after both repairs the multilingual work
prompted, at the code its aggregate records as `r sweep_version`, and
what the defects cost is quoted from the earlier runs that exposed
them, as history. The condition comparisons are paired and
therefore precise, but they are precise about one corpus and one
model. The intervals in @tbl-condition-ci describe LibriSpeech
test-clean under Whisper Large&nbsp;v3, and neither the sign nor the
size of a stage's effect need carry to another corpus. The
deduplication window costs a little on test-clean and helps on AMI
([Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a)), and [the Post-Processing Beyond English section](#sec-multilingual) and @tbl-models
show the size of an effect moving a long way between languages and
between models. Injection into clean carriers produced the masking
figures, which describe a deterministic rule, not a rate that would
transfer to natural transcripts. The timestamp benchmark scores isolated clips
whose reference end is the end of the audio, so it cannot observe a
model running past a boundary, and all of them come from one meeting.
The determinism comparison covers
`r num_word(det_n_gpu_configs)` GPU configurations and
`r num_word(length(det_proc_run))` processor, all on the cluster, and
`r num_word(det_n)` utterances of a single meeting, so it shows that a
transcript can change between configurations without estimating how
often it does. Its processor run, in the `r det_cpu_precision` that a
desktop machine without a CUDA device and the cluster's batch worker
both use, gave the V100's words, but it ran on one processor model, an
`r det_cpu_name`, and nothing here shows that another would agree.

Of those bounds, two matter directly to a reader planning work.
Diarisation error varies across meetings with how much of the speech is
spoken over, so a recording with little crosstalk tends to sit below
the corpus average and a busy discussion above it, and the label
stream deserves the same spot check as any other measurement taken on
unfamiliar material. The end-boundary errors in timestamp alignment are
concentrated in a small proportion of utterances where the model stops
transcribing early, and no post-processing can repair that, since the
words were never emitted. The only defence is detection, so the end of
a transcript should be checked against the duration of its recording
before the transcript is treated as complete.

# Ethics {.unnumbered}

This study analysed only publicly available recordings. The speech
corpora are third-party public releases: LibriSpeech
[@panayotovLibrispeechASRCorpus2015], FLEURS
[@conneauFleursFewshotLearning2023], VoxPopuli
[@wangVoxpopuliLargescaleMultilingual2021] and the AMI Meeting Corpus
[@carlettaAMIMeeting2005]. The one other recording, on whose
transcript [the Evaluating the Masking Layer section](#sec-masking) counts false redactions, is an episode of the
author's own published podcast, *Codex Mentis*, whose two voices were
generated with NotebookLM. No participants were recruited and no new
human recordings were collected for this study. Ethical approval was
not sought. The name-masking benchmark injects name strings into
constructed carrier sentences.
